docs.title: ThingStudio
docs.text:
ThingStudio is a visual, low-code way to program microcontrollers. You build a program, called a flow, in a node-based editor in your web browser. Nodes are functional blocks, and wires carry data between them. The design is inspired by Node-RED.

ThingStudio converts the flow to MicroPython, a version of Python for microcontrollers, compiles it, and sends it to your board. The flow is saved on the board. It will then run without the editor connected, and will start again after a reset or power cycle.

The editor: nodes to drag in on the left, your flow in the middle, and on the right the selected node's settings and the board's console. Click to see it full size. Tour the editor labels every part.

In a hurry?

Getting started takes you from a new board to a blinking LED in six steps.

ThingStudio is designed to be private, and as open and hackable as possible:

  • Fully local. Development happens on your computer. There's no cloud service and no account.
  • Works offline. Once installed, it needs no internet connection, docs included.
  • Git friendly. ThingStudio's files, your programs and your board definitions, are plain, indented JSON that you save where you like. They diff cleanly and sit happily in a git repository. Passwords and other credentials are stored separately, so a committed program holds no secrets.
  • Made to be extended. Write your own custom nodes, and add your own boards and processors. You drop their files into a folder. There's nothing to rebuild.
  • Free and open source. ThingStudio is under the Apache 2.0 license. You can use it, change it and build on it, including in commercial products.

Already know the background?

If you know Node-RED, MicroPython or Arduino, read what's different for you, or go straight to Getting started.

  • Node-RED
  • MicroPython
  • Arduino and C

docs.title: Who ThingStudio is for, and who it isn't
docs.text: ThingStudio is designed for developers with a reasonable amount of programming experience, it doesn't aim to teach programming fundamentals. You should also have some level of experience in working with microcontrollers. You don't have to be an EE graduate, but you should be comfortable wiring a breadboard. You should also be able to do basic commands from the terminal or PowerShell.

docs.title: What's different about programming with ThingStudio?
docs.text:
A typical microcontroller program, in Arduino for example, has a setup() section that runs once at boot, then a main loop that runs forever. The loop might:

  • read the sensors
  • check the buttons
  • update the outputs
  • check the network
  • go round again

Each new job makes the loop longer. A slow step, such as a network call, holds up everything else, and the timing gets hard to reason about.

ThingStudio programs respond to events instead. When a button is pressed, turn on a light. Every ten seconds, read the temperature. When a message arrives from the network, update the display. Each response runs only when its event happens, and the board waits for many events at once. This is event-driven programming.

MicroPython supports this style natively with asyncio. An asyncio program no longer reads top to bottom, which makes it harder to see what it does. ThingStudio's graphical editor of events, functions and outputs makes an event-driven program easier to build and follow.

docs.title: Events, nodes and wires
docs.text:
A program is made of nodes joined by wires. There are three types of node:

  • Sources start messages when something happens: a timer fires, a button is pressed, an MQTT message arrives.
  • Transforms take a message in and send a message on: a function, a filter, a delay.
  • Sinks act on a message: switch a pin, update a display, publish to MQTT.

A wire joins one node's output to the next node's input. The nodes and wires together make a flow. A flow can hold any number of chains, each starting at a source.

Nodes pass messages along the wires. A message is a dict, with its main value in payload. Messages are covered in more detail in flows, nodes and messages.

This way of working comes from Node-RED, a popular tool for home automation and IoT. In Node-RED, flows run on a server or a Raspberry Pi. In ThingStudio, they run on the microcontroller.

docs.title: Including your own code
docs.text:
There are a number of ready made functions available built-in nodes . There is also the function node, which will take regular MicroPython and runs your it on each message that arrives:

# payload arrives in degrees C, leaves in degrees F
msg['payload'] = msg['payload'] * 1.8 + 32
return msg

msg is a dict, with the main value in msg['payload']. Return it to pass it on, or return nothing to stop it. A function node can also keep state between messages and have more than one output. The only rule to remember is not to use blocking calls in a function node, that would make the entire flow wait on the operation.

To reuse code across flows, make it a custom node. A custom node has its own place in the palette and its own properties in the property panel. It can access custom hardware, transform messages, act on them, or send them on a schedule.

You can also stop the flow and run the python REPL directly on the board from the editor for debugging. See Commands and the Python prompt.

docs.title: Running on the board
docs.text:
The microcontroller runs a MicroPython image with a ThingStudio runtime on top. You can flash the image from the editor or use one of your own choosing. The runtime sends the flow to the board and manages running it. It also sends back status and debugging information. We also provide custom Micropython images with the runtime included, which are more efficient in memory usage.

When you click Deploy, the editor converts your flow into MicroPython and compiles it. It sends the compiled flow to the board over USB or WiFi, and the board swaps it in, and starts running it. There's no new firmware to flash, so changing a flow and trying it again takes seconds. The board keeps the flow and runs it again after a restart.

docs.title: Built on standard parts
docs.text:
ThingStudio tries not to reinvent the wheel.

  • MicroPython's asyncio provides the event-driven primitives.
  • Tried and tested libraries provide extra functionality and hardware drivers, such as Peter Hinch's mqtt_as and micropython-async, and drivers from micropython-lib.
  • What comes out is plain MicroPython. You can read it in the editor's Compiled source panel.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A board with one of the processors in Supported hardware. Other boards that run MicroPython may work.
  • A USB cable that carries data, not only power.

docs.title: Writing flows with an AI assistant
docs.text: This page is for an AI assistant (or a person) writing a ThingStudio flow file or a custom node in the user's folder, without the editor. It is complete on its own, with two companions: the generated node catalog, and the thingstudio-compile command (Check a flow without the editor). With a board attached, device_cli.py deploys and runs the flow (Command line). The whole docs set is also one file at /llms-full.txt on the docs site, with an index at /llms.txt.

docs.title: Setting up your assistant
docs.text:
Paste this into the assistant's standing instructions (a project's instructions, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, or a custom GPT/Gem), so it reads this page before it writes a flow:

When I ask for a Thingstudio flow or custom node, first read the Thingstudio authoring guide:
https://docs.thingstudio.net/ai-authoring/ (the whole docs set is one file at https://docs.thingstudio.net/llms-full.txt).
Write the flow as a .flow.json file, run the thingstudio-compile check with --board for my board and
--layout, fix every error and layout warning until it prints OK, then tell me: the board id you checked against, which credential
names I must create, what you assumed about wiring, and what you could not check.
Never say a flow works on the board unless you deployed it there and saw its output; otherwise say it
passes the check. No HTTPS in http_request.

Claude users can add the ThingStudio skill instead: thingstudio-flow-author-<version>.zip, from the releases page, carries this guide, the node catalog, the examples and the check command, so the assistant needs nothing else. Upload the zip as a skill in Claude, or unzip it into ~/.claude/skills/ for Claude Code. Use the skill whose version matches your editor. Otherwise the check needs Node and the built thingstudio-compile.mjs.

docs.title: The loop
docs.text:
1. Write the flow as a .flow.json file.
  2. Run node dist-cli/thingstudio-compile.mjs --board board:lolin-s2-mini --layout my.flow.json (the board ids are board:cyd, board:freenove-s3-4in, board:lolin-s2-mini, board:pico, board:pico-2 and board:pico-w, or processor:esp32, esp32-c3, esp32-s2, esp32-s3, rp2040, rp2350 for a bare chip; --list-boards shows the current list). Read every error: it names the node and says what is wrong. Fix them all, and every layout: warning, and run it again until it prints OK.
  3. Tell the user to open the file in the editor (File → Open), choose the board, and deploy. If a board is attached and the user asks you to test it, deploy it with device_cli.py instead, and report what the board printed. That result is for that board only.

The check is the same compile the editor runs, so a flow that passes it opens and compiles in the editor. It loads the user's custom node packages the way the editor does. It can't check credentials, what a custom node's Python does on the board, or the hardware. Don't claim a flow works on a board unless you deployed it there and saw it run; otherwise say it passes the check.

docs.title: The flow file
docs.text:
A JSON object. These keys matter:

Key What formatVersion 1 flowName A name for the flow. nodes [{ "id", "type", "properties" }]. id is any unique string. type is thingstudio/<kind>. edges [[fromId, outputNumber, toId, inputNumber]]. Numbers start at 0, in the order the catalog lists the ports. configs [{ "id", "type", "properties" }]: shared settings (I2C bus, WiFi, MQTT broker, touch panel). screens The pages of any GUI screen, keyed by that node's id. See GUI. panes, paneOf Optional. Tabs in the editor and which tab each node is on; leave them out and everything lands on one tab. When you edit a file that has them, put new nodes in paneOf too (copy the pattern). layout { "<nodeId>": { "pos": [x, y] } }. Optional, but give positions: without them every node lands at 0,0. notes Optional text shown in the editor's Notes panel. Say what the flow is for and how it is wired.

A property you leave out gets the default listed in the catalog. Use the catalog's names and types exactly: intervalMs, not interval. Values and ranges are checked by the compile, which says what is allowed.

Give every node a position, laid out as described in Layout.

A complete flow, a blinking LED on a LOLIN S2 Mini (its LED is pin 15):

{
  "formatVersion": 1,
  "flowName": "blink",
  "nodes": [
    { "id": "tick", "type": "thingstudio/timer", "properties": { "intervalMs": 500 } },
    { "id": "flip", "type": "thingstudio/function",
      "properties": { "code": "msg['payload'] = msg['payload'] % 2\nreturn msg", "outputCount": 1 } },
    { "id": "led", "type": "thingstudio/gpio_out", "properties": { "pin": 15 } }
  ],
  "edges": [["tick", 0, "flip", 0], ["flip", 0, "led", 0]],
  "layout": { "tick": { "pos": [80, 200] }, "flip": { "pos": [300, 200] }, "led": { "pos": [520, 200] } },
  "configs": []
}

docs.title: Layout
docs.text:
The user reads the flow on the editor's canvas, and the editor shows it exactly where the file puts it. It does not rearrange the nodes or zoom to fit. Lay it out the way a careful person would:

  • Left to right. Sources (timers, inputs, subscriptions) on the left, outputs on the right, and every wire running to a node further right. Don't wrap a long chain back to the left edge on a second row.
  • Columns about 220 px apart, left edge to left edge. Nodes are 84-132 px wide, so that leaves about 90 px for the wire. Use the same column positions for the whole flow, so columns line up.
  • Tight rows. Nodes are 34 px tall (a function node with several outputs is taller). Stack branches in one column about 36 px apart (y about 70 apart), and separate chains about 66 px apart (y about 100 apart).
  • One chain per job, stacked top to bottom: inputs and processing first, display or output last. Unwired nodes (GUI buttons that only appear on a screen, for example) go together at the bottom left.
  • Straight wires. A node fed by one node sits at that node's y. When one node feeds several, the first sits level with it and the rest stack below; a node fed by several sits level with the first of them, or between them.
  • Start near (80, 80), so the flow is on screen when it opens.

--layout checks these rules and reports problems as layout: warnings. --relayout rewrites the positions to follow them, which makes a good first pass for a new flow. When you edit the user's own flow, keep their layout: place only the nodes you add, and don't relayout it unless they ask.

docs.title: Which node
docs.text: To... Use send a message every so often, or once at start timer, startup, inject read a BME280 / BMP280 bme280 (payload is a dict with temperature, humidity, pressure; pick one out in a function) read another I2C chip i2c on a shared i2c-bus config react to a switch or button eswitch (a debounced switch: open and close events); ebutton for press, release, long-press and double-click; interrupt for raw edges drive a pin gpio_out (on/off), pwm_out change or route a message function; filter to pass only changes; delay keep a number's history journal, shown by a histogram (gui_trend) show the time ntp (two for time and date: format time and date) talk MQTT / HTTP / UDP mqtt_publish, mqtt_subscribe, http_request, http_in and http_response, udp_send, udp_receive draw on a screen gui_screen with gui_* widgets, wired to display_spi

docs.title: Messages and the function node
docs.text:
Every message is a dict: msg = {'payload': ..., 'topic': ...}. payload is what nodes read; topic is a string, '' when there is nothing to say. Other keys ride along.

A function node's code is the body of a function in MicroPython (a subset of Python with a small standard library). Return msg to pass it on, or None to stop. With outputCount above 1, return a list with one entry per output (None for nothing, a list of messages for several). context keeps state for the node, flow for the whole flow. See function. A syntax error in the code is caught by the check.

A wire is refused if the payload types can't meet (for example a bool into a bytes input). The check reports it. Numbers go into bool inputs (zero is off), and an int into a number; a number into an int is refused.

Addresses are written two ways, because the nodes differ: the bme280 address is a plain number (118 is 0x76); a touch panel config's address is text ("0x38"). The catalog notes which.

A node that uses the network (mqtt_publish, http_request, http_in and so on) uses the flow's WiFi: add a WiFi config to configs and it is picked up; the node has no WiFi property of its own.

Things to know before you pick a node:

  • http_request is plain http:// only (no HTTPS), GET or POST. A reply with any status is passed on with an integer msg['status']; a failed connection or a timeout sends nothing on and logs an error. So test msg['status'] == 200 in a function, and expect no message at all when the server is unreachable.
  • mqtt_subscribe payloads arrive as text when they decode, otherwise bytes. For a number, use float(msg['payload']) in a function.
  • function code can import standard modules (json, framebuf, time) inside the body.
  • http_in gives a payload of None and http_response sets no Content-Type. Use port 80 unless something else on the board already uses it.
  • bme280 has no input: it reads on its own interval. To answer a web request with a current value, keep the latest reading with flow.set('temp', ...) in a function after the sensor, and read it with flow.get('temp') in a function between http_in and http_response (send a 503 before the first reading arrives).
  • To print text on a display_i2c (SSD1306), draw with framebuf in a function and send the buffer: see display i2c. Its address property is addr, a plain number (60 is 0x3C).

docs.title: Pins: take them from the board
docs.text:
Never guess a pin. List the boards with --list-boards, run --board-info board:<id> for what each pin does (the LED, the buttons, the display, the I2C pins) and which to avoid, and check the finished flow with --board board:<id>. If the user's board is not listed, say so, ask for the pins, and point them to the MicroPython documentation for their board (docs.micropython.org). Don't pretend a board is supported.

Things the pin check cannot catch: a pin that exists but is wired to something else on the user's board. When the user has told you the wiring, use it; when they haven't, say what you assumed.

docs.title: Config nodes and credentials
docs.text:
A node that needs shared settings names a config by id: "i2cConfigId": "cfg-i2c", with the config in configs:

{ "id": "cfg-i2c", "type": "thingstudio/config/i2c-bus", "properties": { "bus": 0, "scl": 15, "sda": 16, "freq": 100000 } }

The catalog lists each config type's fields. WiFi and MQTT configs hold a credential name:

{ "id": "cfg-wifi", "type": "thingstudio/config/wifi", "properties": { "credentialName": "home", "security": "password" } }

Never write a password, SSID or broker secret into a flow file. Write a credentialName and tell the user which names to create in the editor's credential store (they are saved there, not in the file). The check uses stand-ins for them and says so.

docs.title: GUI screens
docs.text:
A touch or plain display is two nodes wired together, gui_screen then display_spi, plus widget nodes (gui_label, gui_readout, gui_bar, gui_trend, gui_led, gui_button) that you wire data into. Where each widget sits is in screens:

"screens": { "<screenId>": { "pages": [
  { "name": "main", "elements": [
    { "card": true, "row": 0, "col": 0, "rowSpan": 1, "colSpan": 12 },
    { "kind": "text", "text": "Living room", "row": 0, "col": 0, "colSpan": 8 },
    { "kind": "widget", "node": "<readoutId>", "row": 1, "col": 0, "rowSpan": 4, "colSpan": 12 },
    { "kind": "pagedots", "row": 15, "col": 4, "colSpan": 4 }
  ] }
] } }

Rules that cause most failures:

  • The screen's width and height are the panel's own size (320 × 480 for the Freenove 4") whatever the orientation. Portrait needs nothing more: leave orientation empty and use the board's rotation (1 for the Freenove). To turn the picture, set the orientation property of display_spi to "90", "180" or "270" (clockwise), not the screen's size.
  • A navigate button's target is next, prev, back, home or the name of a page in screens; when you edit an existing flow, read the page names from its screens section.
  • Fonts are chosen to fit an element's cells; nothing in a layout is in pixels. A character no font has is an error.
  • A widget is placed once per page, drawn the same on every page it is on. Its cells decide its size.
  • A page is a cell grid: the gui screen has gridColumns (12 by default) and gridRows (0 = from the display's shape). Every element has row, col (0-based) and spans; an element outside the grid, two on the same cells, or one whose text cannot fit is an error naming it and the page.
  • With an orientation, xstart and ystart must be -1, which means "no offset" (the CYD example flow uses 0, which an orientation refuses; -1 is always allowed). At "90" or "270" the picture is the panel turned, so a 320 x 480 panel gives 480 wide by 320 high to lay out.
  • A modal is laid out in screens.<screenId>.modals, not in pages: see the format below.
  • A histogram (gui_trend) takes a journal's first output, and a journal takes numbers: sensor → journal → histogram.

A modal (gui_modal, with screen set to the gui_screen node's id) is listed next to pages. Its elements are what it shows, and not the modal node itself:

"modals": [ { "node": "<modalNodeId>", "elements": [
  { "kind": "text", "text": "Too hot", "row": 0, "col": 0, "rowSpan": 2, "colSpan": 8 },
  { "kind": "widget", "node": "<labelId>", "row": 2, "col": 0, "rowSpan": 2, "colSpan": 12 }
] } ]

Any message opens it; a message with payload None closes it; timeout (seconds, 0 for never) closes it by itself; a navigate button with target back acknowledges it. Its output sends 'ack', 'timeout' or 'closed'.

Placement keys, in screens (a page is {"name", "elements": [...]}; a modal is {"node", "elements": [...]}):

Element Keys any element row, col (0-based cells), rowSpan, colSpan (default 1), card (draw a panel behind), align widget kind: "widget", node (the widget node's id) text kind: "text", text page dots kind: "pagedots" panel card: true (no node or text)

No element takes a font, height, width, gap or padding: fonts follow the cells and spacing is the screen's gutter. The button's own behaviour (mode, target, onValue, ...) is on the node: see the catalog. For a toggle that follows a real device (a smart plug), gui.md has the wiring.

Read GUI nodes for the details, and copy from test-flows/gui-headliner-sensor-freenove-s3-4in.flow.json (a sensor display with histograms, a clock and MQTT) and test-flows/gui-touch-freenove-s3-4in.flow.json (buttons).

docs.title: Custom nodes
docs.text: If no node does the job and a function node is not enough, write a custom node: <name>.node.json and <name>.node.py. Writing custom nodes is complete on its own. The two files go in ~/.thingstudio/custom-nodes/ on the computer running ThingStudio. The check command loads that folder (or the one given with --custom-nodes <dir>), so check a flow that uses the node: a bad descriptor is reported by file, and the node's wires, properties and compile hook are checked like a built-in's. What the Python does on the board isn't checked: test its body on its own with sample messages.

docs.title: When you hand the flow back
docs.text: Tell the user, briefly: that it passes the check (and with which --board), which credential names to create, which board to choose in the editor, what you assumed about wiring, and what you could not check.

docs.title: Boards and processors
docs.text:
Each board and processor has a definition file that says which pins a flow may use. This page covers picking a board, seeing its pins, what gets checked, and writing your own definition files.

ThingStudio checks every pin in a flow against the board the flow is for. If a pin doesn't exist on that board, or using it would crash the board, the compile stops and says why.

Each board has a definition file, and so does each processor. ThingStudio comes with definitions for the boards and processors below. You can change them or add your own.

docs.title: Picking the board
docs.text:
Pick the board a flow is for from the Board menu in the toolbar. The default, Auto, uses the connected board. Auto recognises a board by the name MicroPython reports for it, and the menu shows what it found, for example Auto: LOLIN S2 Mini.

Some boards report only their processor. The CYD, for example, reports itself as a generic ESP32. Pick those boards from the menu by hand. You can also pick a processor without a board, for example ESP32 (any board).

The board menu picks pins, not memory. A classic ESP32 board with no PSRAM can run a GUI flow by flashing the custom firmware for classic ESP32, which carries the runtime and the flow libraries in the firmware.

A board picked by hand stays picked when you reconnect. If you then connect a board with a different processor, the menu goes back to Auto and the console says so.

If no board is connected and none is picked, pins are only checked against the range 0–48.

docs.title: Seeing a board's pins
docs.text:
Click Pins… next to the Board menu. It opens the pin cheat sheet, in its own tab, for the board or processor picked there. The cheat sheet lists, in order:

  • the pins the board names, such as its LED
  • for boards whose definition has a header, such as the Pico family, the physical pins, laid out like the board, with power and ground marked
  • every pin, with whether it's free, reserved or best avoided, and why
  • which pins each SPI and I2C bus can use

The page is read from the definition files each time you click. After changing a file, click Pins… again.

If ThingStudio knows the board's processor but not the board, the page shows the processor's pins and says the board's own ones, like its LED, are missing. It gives a starter file to add them: see Adding a board. If it doesn't know the processor either, the page says what the board reports: see Adding a processor.

docs.title: What gets checked
docs.text:
These stop the compile:

  • a pin the board or processor doesn't have
  • a reserved pin, such as a pin wired to the flash chip
  • an output on an input-only pin
  • an SPI or I2C bus the processor doesn't have, or a pin that bus can't use
  • an SPI speed the processor can't run on those pins

These give a warning, but the flow still compiles:

  • a pin to avoid, such as a strapping pin that changes how the board starts
  • a pull-up or pull-down on a pin that has no internal pull resistor

A node that needs hardware the board doesn't have, such as an ESP-NOW node on a Pico, is refused the same way. The palette greys out such a node while the board is known.

Warnings appear in the console when you deploy, and at the end of the compiled source.

In the properties panel, a pin field shows the board's name for that pin, such as LED. It also flags reserved pins and pins to avoid. On a board whose pins are named rather than numbered, the field is a dropdown of the board's pins. See Pins that aren't numbers.
