docs.text:
Processor GPIO Reserved ESP32 0–19, 21–23, 25–27, 32–39 (34–39 input only) 1, 3 (USB serial), 6–11 (flash) ESP32-S2 0–21, 26–46 (46 input only) 27–32 (flash) ESP32-S3 0–21, 26–48 27–32 (flash) ESP32-C3 0–21 12–17 (flash) ESP32-C5 0–28 16–22 (flash and PSRAM) RP2040 0–29 none RP2350 0–47 (0–29 on the RP2350A) none STM32F405 X1–X22, Y1–Y12 (named pins, not numbers) none nRF52840 0–47 (P1.x is 32 + x) none

The ESP32 runs SPI at up to 27 MHz on most pins. Faster speeds need the bus's own fast pins (SCK 14 and MOSI 13 on bus 1, SCK 18 and MOSI 23 on bus 2).

On the RP2040 and RP2350, each SPI and I2C bus can only use certain pins. The compile error lists the pins that work.

On the nRF52840, any pin works for SPI and I2C. SPI uses buses 2 and 3, up to 8 MHz; I2C uses buses 0 and 1.

The definition files list every pin to avoid, with the reason.

docs.title: Your definition files
docs.text:
Definition files live in ~/.thingstudio/boards/ and ~/.thingstudio/processors/. When ThingStudio starts, it writes every built-in file there, replacing a file of the same name, so an upgrade's changes arrive on the next start.

To keep your own version of a built-in board, save it under a different name (for example my-cyd.json) and give it its own name in the file. It is then a board of its own in the Board menu, and is never overwritten. Editing a built-in file in place lasts until the next start.

ThingStudio reads these files when the editor starts, when you connect, and when you deploy. If a file has a mistake, it isn't loaded and the built-in is used instead. The console says what's wrong, and the Board menu lists the file under Invalid files.

docs.title: Adding a board
docs.text:
Save a JSON file in ~/.thingstudio/boards/. The file name, without .json, is the board's id. Use lowercase letters, digits, - and _.

A board file can't build on another one. To describe a built-in board with parts you have wired to it, copy the built-in's file, give it a new file name and name, and add a name in pins for each part, such as "POT": 0. Kitchen-sink board is a built-in made this way.

{
  "name": "My weather station",
  "processor": "esp32-c3",
  "match": [],
  "pins": { "LED": 8, "SENSOR_SDA": 4, "SENSOR_SCL": 5 },
  "avoid": { "9": "Wired to the BOOT button." },
  "notes": "Hand-built, rev 2."
}

The fields are:

Field Meaning name Name shown in the Board menu. Required. processor Id of the processor, such as esp32 or rp2040. Required. match Board names MicroPython reports, for Auto. Use [] to pick the board by hand. Required. pins Names for pins, shown in the properties panel. Required, can be {}. capabilities Hardware this board adds to its processor, such as ["wifi"]. A board with no radio usually sets wifi to false instead. gpio The pins this board has, if fewer than its processor. For example ["0-29"]. reserved Pins that must not be used, each with a reason. avoid Pins that give a warning, each with a reason. free Pins the processor reserves or warns about that are fine on this board. For example ["12-13"] on an ESP32-C3 board whose flash doesn't use them. notes Anything else worth knowing. variant The MicroPython build that Tools → Install firmware… picks for this board, such as esp32-c3-generic. Copy it from a built-in board with the same chip, or leave it out. wifi false if the board has no WiFi. Hides connecting over WiFi for it. Leave it out if unsure. headerOrder "down" if the right-hand row is numbered top to bottom, like the left. Leave it out for a header numbered down the left and back up the right, like the Pico's. usb Where the USB connector is, with pin 1 at the top left: "top" or "bottom". Shown on the Pins… page. Needs header. header What each physical pin carries: a pin (a GPIO number, or a named pin), or a label such as "GND" or "3V3". Shown on the Pins… page. For example { "1": 0, "3": "GND", "40": "VBUS" }. A string that's one of the board's pins is that pin; any other string is a label.

Naming a pin in pins turns off the processor's warning for it, on the grounds that the board uses it on purpose. If the warning still matters, such as a strapping pin on a shield header, repeat it in the board's avoid.

Numbers in header are physical pin numbers, as printed on the board or its datasheet. A header numbered 1 to N is drawn in two columns, like the Pico's. For a board with several connectors, name the pins "P3-1" and so on.

Pin lists take numbers and ranges: [0, 2, "4-7"]. In reserved and avoid, the key is a pin or a range: { "6-11": "Wired to the flash chip." }. A processor whose pins are named uses the names in the same places: see Pins that aren't numbers.

To find the name MicroPython reports, connect the board and look for chipType in the console's [HELLO] line. The board name is the part before " with ".

docs.title: Adding a processor
docs.text:
Save a JSON file in ~/.thingstudio/processors/, named the same way as a board file. The built-in files in that folder are good examples.

The fields are:

Field Meaning name Name shown in the Board menu. Required. match Text in the processor name MicroPython reports, such as ESP32S3. Case, spaces and - are ignored. Required. nativeArch The mpy-cross -march value, such as xtensawin. Required. gpio Every pin the processor has. Numbers, or names on a processor whose pins aren't numbered. Required. inputOnly Pins that can't drive an output. noPull Pins without internal pull resistors. capabilities Hardware the chip has, such as ["wifi", "ble", "espnow"] or ["pio"]. A node that needs one the board lacks is refused. adc2 Pins on a second ADC that can't be used while WiFi is up (ESP32 family). reserved, avoid As for boards. spi, i2c Bus numbers, pins each bus can use, and SPI speed limits.

docs.title: Pins that aren't numbers
docs.text:
Some processors, such as the STM32 on a pyboard, name their pins (X1, A13) instead of numbering them. In a definition file, a pin is either a number, a range "4-7", or a name: a string that starts with a letter and contains only letters, digits, _ and -. Names go wherever numbers do — gpio, pins, reserved, avoid, a bus's pins — and a list can mix both. Ranges work for numbers only; list named pins one by one.

{
  "name": "Pyboard",
  "match": ["STM32F405"],
  "nativeArch": "armv7emsp",
  "gpio": ["X1", "X2", "X3", "X4", "Y1", "Y2", "Y3", "Y4"]
}

In the editor, a pin field on a named-pin board is a dropdown of the board's pins rather than a number input.

docs.title: Check a flow without the editor
docs.text: thingstudio-compile compiles and checks a flow file from the command line, with the same errors the editor gives. Use it in a script, in CI, or to let an AI assistant check a flow it has written.

docs.title: Build it
docs.text:
From the editor/ folder:

npm ci --ignore-scripts
npm run build:cli

This writes dist-cli/thingstudio-compile.mjs, one script that needs only Node 22 or later.

docs.title: Use it
docs.text:
node dist-cli/thingstudio-compile.mjs my-flow.flow.json

A good flow prints one line:

OK  my-flow.flow.json: 25 nodes, 21 wires, 4 configs, 38980 bytes of MicroPython, 0 warnings

A bad one lists every problem it found:

FAIL  my-flow.flow.json: 2 errors
  error: wire from node t1 output 4 to node g1 input 1: node t1 has no output 4 (it has 1)
  error: node x1: unknown node type "thingstudio/teleporter"

The exit code is 0 for a valid flow, 1 for a flow with errors, and 2 for a bad command or a file it can't read.

docs.title: Options
docs.text:
• --board board:freenove-s3-4in checks pins against that board. --list-boards shows the choices. Without a board, pins are checked against the widest range and a warning says so.
  • --board-info board:freenove-s3-4in prints that board's labelled pins (the LED, the display, the I2C pins), the GPIOs that exist, and the ones to avoid or that are reserved, as JSON.
  • --out flow.py writes the generated MicroPython.
  • --json prints the result as JSON: ok, errors, warnings, notes, stats and the source.
  • --strict makes warnings fail the check.
  • --layout also checks the layout: wires run left to right, nodes are close but don't overlap, and the flow starts on screen. Problems come back as layout: warnings (so --strict fails on them). The rules are in Layout.
  • --relayout rewrites each file's node positions to follow those rules, then checks it. It changes positions only, and it overwrites the file.
  • --describe timer prints a node's type, ports and properties with their defaults. --describe-all prints every node and config node (add --json for JSON). The same list is on the node catalog page, generated from the code.
  • --custom-nodes ~/my-nodes loads custom node packages from that folder. Without it, the check loads ~/.thingstudio/custom-nodes/ when it exists, as the editor does. --no-custom-nodes loads none.
  • --no-syntax skips the MicroPython syntax check. --arch sets its -march; the default is the --board's processor (rv32imc for an ESP32-C3 or C5), or xtensawin without a board.

docs.title: What it checks
docs.text:
• The file is a flow file, and every node type exists.
  • Every wire joins real ports, and is one the editor would accept. The editor drops a wire it refuses when it opens the file.
  • A property the file leaves out gets the editor's default, as when you open the file in the editor.
  • The flow compiles: pins, properties, GUI layouts, nodes with nothing wired to them.
  • Custom node packages load as they do in the editor. A package that doesn't load is named with its file and the reason, and its nodes' wires and properties are checked like a built-in node's.
  • The generated code is valid MicroPython. This uses the same mpy-cross the editor deploys with, and catches a typo in a function node's code before you deploy.

docs.title: What it doesn't check
docs.text:
• WiFi and MQTT credentials. The secrets are in the backend, so the check uses stand-in values and says so in a note. A missing credential shows up when you open the flow in the editor.
  • What a custom node's Python does. It is checked for syntax, not run. Test its body on its own with sample messages.
  • A real board. It can't tell you the display is wired right, or that the memory is enough. Deploy does that; Command line can deploy and run a flow without the editor.

docs.title: Command line
docs.text: Options for starting ThingStudio, a way to install the runtime and run flows without the editor, and a check for a flow file. To check a flow file from the command line, see Check a flow without the editor.

docs.title: Starting options
docs.text:
Add these after thingstudio (or thingstudio-backend, from source). thingstudio --help lists them all.

Option What it does --no-browser Don't open the editor in a browser. Open http://127.0.0.1:8765/ yourself. --port N Serve the editor on port N instead of 8765. --data-dir DIR Use DIR instead of ~/.thingstudio. See The ThingStudio folder. --log-level LEVEL How much ThingStudio prints in its terminal: DEBUG, INFO (default), WARNING or ERROR.

If you restart ThingStudio with the editor still open, that tab reconnects and no new one opens.

docs.title: Installing the runtime from the command line
docs.text:
Useful for scripting, or setting up several boards at once. It needs a copy of the source repository. Click Disconnect in the editor first, so the port is free.

pip install mpremote
python3 test-flows/deploy_runtime.py --port PORT

PORT is the board's port, as shown in the editor's port list. When it finishes, click Connect in the editor.

device_cli.py runtime install does the same thing and resets the board afterwards; see below.

docs.title: Deploy and run a flow without the editor
docs.text:
device_cli.py is a small command line for a board on USB serial. It does what the editor does, without a browser: find the board, check the runtime, deploy a flow, fire inject nodes, run console commands and watch the output.

python3 test-flows/device_cli.py list          # USB serial ports
python3 test-flows/device_cli.py hello         # runtime version, chip, running flow
python3 test-flows/device_cli.py flow deploy my-flow.flow.json \
    --mpy-cross ~/mpy-src/mpy-cross/build/mpy-cross
python3 test-flows/device_cli.py trigger inject0001
python3 test-flows/device_cli.py exec "settings.namespaces()"
python3 test-flows/device_cli.py watch
  • If there is one USB serial port, --port is not needed. Use --port or THINGSTUDIO_PORT otherwise.
  • flow deploy compiles the .flow.json with the same compiler as the editor, then deploys it. It takes the flow name from the file's own flowName. That name is also the settings namespace, so check it is what you expect.
  • --trigger NODE_ID (repeatable) fires inject or startup nodes after deploy, for testing without clicking.
  • --json prints one JSON object per line, for scripts.
  • Disconnect in the editor first: only one program can hold the serial port.
  • flow deploy needs a native mpy-cross. The build recipe is in device-runtime/test/README.md, or set THINGSTUDIO_MPY_CROSS to one you already have.

python3 test-flows/device_cli.py <command> --help lists every option. test-flows/README.md has ready-made test flows and their expected output.

docs.title: Step 4: Connect your board
docs.text:
Connect the board over USB so the editor can talk to it. Start ThingStudio if it isn't running: see step 1.

To connect:

  1. Plug the board in.
  2. Check the port list in the toolbar. When the editor opens it looks for boards, and selects yours if it's the only USB device plugged in. If you plugged the board in afterwards, click ⟳ next to the port list.
  3. Click Connect. It changes to Connected · Disconnect. Click that to disconnect.

With more than one USB device plugged in, pick your board from the port list. Port names depend on your operating system and the board's USB chip. To tell which port is your board, unplug it, click ⟳, plug it back in and click ⟳ again. The port that appears is your board.

docs.title: What the console says
docs.text:
A board with MicroPython but no ThingStudio runtime gives this message:

No reply from the runtime. MicroPython but no Thingstudio runtime: Tools → Install runtime…

You install the runtime in the next step.

If the console says nothing came back, or the board replied but isn't running MicroPython, go back to step 3: install MicroPython. Other messages are explained in Board won't connect.

Once the runtime is installed, the console shows which flow the board is running, if any.

Once a board with WiFi is set up, you can also connect to it over WiFi. See Connecting over WiFi.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Step 5: install the runtime.

docs.title: Custom firmware
docs.text:
A ThingStudio custom image is MicroPython with ThingStudio's runtime and every flow library built in. Stock MicroPython loads the runtime, the libraries and the flow into RAM. With a custom image, the runtime and libraries run from flash instead, which leaves the RAM for the flow. On a small board, that is the difference between a flow starting and failing with MemoryError.

There is one image per chip:

Chip Image Written at classic ESP32, 4 MB, no PSRAM thingstudio-classic-esp32-…bin 0x0 ESP32-C3, 4 MB thingstudio-esp32-c3-…bin 0x0 ESP32-C5, 4 MB, no PSRAM thingstudio-esp32-c5-…bin 0x2000

On stock MicroPython, flows that fit in memory run as usual. Back to stock MicroPython says how to return to it.

The technique works on any board that runs MicroPython: freeze the runtime and the flow libraries into the firmware. firmware/ in the repository builds these images, and its README says how to add a chip.

docs.title: What it changes
docs.text:
The runtime and the flow libraries are frozen into the firmware, so MicroPython runs them from flash instead of copying them into RAM.

Because the libraries are already there, Deploy does not send them. The console says so after connecting:

[libraries] this flow uses font_body12, … st7796py -- already on the board: font_body12, … st7796py

Two things follow from that:

  • Deploying over a running flow fits where stock MicroPython runs out. On stock MicroPython, the runtime, the libraries and the flow fight over the same memory: an ESP32-C5 redeploying a BLE flow fails with MemoryError. On the custom image, the same board redeploys it with 100 KB to spare.
  • The first deploy after flashing has more memory to work with than any later one. Judge a flow by a deploy over another flow, not by the first one.

The image carries no board-specific settings. Pins and displays come from the board definition, so one image serves any board with that chip.

Each image is rebuilt and tested on a board at every runtime version. The runtime version an image carries is its Version in the Install firmware dialog.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A board with one of the chips in the table above. The S2, S3 and C6 have no custom image, and neither do RP2040 or RP2350 boards.
  • A USB cable that carries data.

docs.title: Install from the editor
docs.text:
Flashing erases the board: its saved flow and all settings are gone afterwards.

  1. Put the board in download mode if it needs it: hold BOOT and tap RESET.
  2. Choose Tools → Install firmware…, pick Serial port, then the board's port.
  3. Set Chip family to the board's chip and Firmware to ThingStudio custom image. If there is no ThingStudio custom image for the chip, no image for it has been published yet: use official MicroPython.
  4. Pick a Version. Each version listed ran on a board before it was published, and the editor checks the download against its recorded SHA-256 before writing it.
  5. Click Flash. The editor writes the image at the address in the table above.
  6. Connect, then choose Tools → Install runtime…. It writes only the boot script, main.py: the runtime is already in the image.

docs.title: Install by hand
docs.text:
You need esptool and mpremote on the computer: pip install esptool mpremote.

Each image is attached to the ThingStudio release it was published with. On the releases page, open the release whose assets include the image version you want (the versions are the ones the editor lists), and download three files from it: the image for your chip, its .sha256 file and main.py.

  1. Put the three files in one folder and go there. Check the image against its checksum:
IMAGE=$(ls thingstudio-*.bin)   # the image you downloaded
shasum -a 256 -c "$IMAGE.sha256"      # sha256sum -c on Linux
  1. Put the board in download mode if your board needs it, then write the image. Use the chip and address from the table above. For a classic ESP32:
esptool.py --chip esp32 --port /dev/ttyUSB0 write_flash 0x0 "$IMAGE"

For an ESP32-C5, --chip esp32c5 and 0x2000. Written at 0, a C5 does not boot. On macOS the port looks like /dev/cu.usbserial-14420. On Windows it is COM3 or similar.

To write the downloaded image from the editor instead, use Or use your own image file in Tools → Install firmware… and set Address, under Install options, to the one in the table. Without it, a classic ESP32 image goes at the family's 0x1000 and the board does not boot.

  1. If you held BOOT to get into download mode, press RESET now: without it the board stays in its bootloader, and mpremote fails with could not enter raw repl. Then write the boot script, the one file that lives on the filesystem rather than in the image:
mpremote connect /dev/ttyUSB0 fs cp main.py :/main.py

main.py starts the runtime that is frozen into the firmware. A board with the image and no main.py starts at the Python prompt instead. The image carries the list of libraries it froze, so Deploy skips them without a file on the board.

  1. Reset the board. It starts the listener and prints LISTENER_READY.

The repository also has firmware/install.sh, which runs these steps in one command (PORT=/dev/ttyUSB0 firmware/install.sh esp32-c5). Read it before running it: it erases the filesystem partition, and its port name comes from PORT.

docs.title: Connect and deploy
docs.text:
Connect in the editor as usual. Two things confirm the image is running:

  • the console's version line reports the image's runtime version, as listed under Version in the Install firmware dialog
  • [libraries] … already on the board: … names every library the flow imports

Then deploy the flow.

docs.title: Memory and the board
docs.text:
The image does not add RAM. Measured on the CYD (classic ESP32-D0WD, 4 MB, no PSRAM) with a GUI flow, in KB:

Board state MicroPython free Largest block ESP-IDF free ESP-IDF largest Just booted, no flow 142 105 129 108 GUI flow running 108 50 70 52 GUI flow running, after two more deploys 120 27 18 14

Read the third row before leaning on deploys: each deploy over a running flow leaves the heaps more fragmented, and the chip's own heap shrinks as MicroPython takes from it. WiFi and Bluetooth draw from that chip heap, and the console warns when it is low.

The C3 and C5, measured with each flow running after deploying it over itself, in KB:

Board Flow MicroPython free ESP-IDF free ESP-IDF largest ESP32-C3 module MQTT over WiFi 114 36 28 ESP32-C5-340X MQTT over WiFi 94 29 17 ESP32-C5-340X BLE central 113 108 88

WiFi takes the most from the chip's heap.

Keeping frames small and recovering from a MemoryError are covered in Memory and MemoryError or a library that won't load.

docs.title: Back to stock MicroPython
docs.text: Install MicroPython with a standard build for the board, then install the runtime again. Flashing erases the board's flows and settings, as above.

docs.title: Reporting a problem
docs.text: Reports on any board with these chips are welcome, listed or not. Include the board's name and the console's version and [memory] lines from a fresh boot.

docs.title: Writing a custom node for ThingStudio
docs.text: A custom node is two files sharing a base name: <name>.node.json (the descriptor) and <name>.node.py (the behavior), placed in the backend's ~/.thingstudio/custom-nodes/ directory. ThingStudio loads it for you, and you drag it onto the canvas like any built-in node.

docs.title: Loading a custom node
docs.text:
Put both files in ~/.thingstudio/custom-nodes/ on the computer running ThingStudio.

The editor loads every package in that folder when it starts, and again when you switch back to its window. After changing a file, you can also click Reload custom nodes at the bottom of the palette. The console lists what loaded. Each node appears in the palette under its group.

A package with a problem isn't loaded, and the console says which file and why. The others still load. If two packages use the same type, the first one by file name is loaded and the other is reported.

The folder starts with two examples, doubler and dht22, under examples in the palette. Read them, change them or delete them. ThingStudio adds them only the first time it runs, so deleted examples stay deleted.

docs.title: The descriptor: <name>.node.json
docs.text:
Example — a node that doubles a numeric payload:

{
  "type": "custom/doubler",
  "kind": "transform",
  "label": "doubler",
  "color": "#6e3b8a",
  "bgcolor": "#3f1f4a",
  "icon": "×2",
  "ports": {
    "inputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "any" }],
    "outputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "any" }]
  },
  "properties": [
    { "name": "factor", "label": "factor", "kind": "number", "default": 2 }
  ]
}

type (required) — unique id, shaped namespace/name (lowercase letters, digits, underscores). Must not start with thingstudio/ — reserved for built-in nodes.

kind (required) — one of:

  • source — generates messages on its own. 0 input ports, 1 output port. Must declare a numeric intervalMs property (below) — unless eventSource is true (it waits on an event) or runOnce is true (it runs once at flow start).
  • transform — one message in, one or more out. 1 input port, 1+ output ports.
  • sink — consumes a message, produces nothing. 1 input port, 0 output ports.

label (required) — name shown on the canvas and in the palette.

title (optional) — the canvas title, when it should differ from label.

hidden (optional) — hide the node from the palette (a flow file can still use it).

description (optional) — a short line shown at the top of the property panel, like a built-in node's own description.

presetType / screenOutline (optional) — show a save/load-preset control or the screen-layout outline in the property panel, as the relevant built-in nodes do.

color / bgcolor (optional) — CSS colors for the node's outline and fill. Default is gray.

icon (optional) — one or two characters shown in the icon chip.

group (optional) — which palette section the node sorts into. Defaults to "general". Any name works; a new one gets its own section, added after the built-in ones.

priority (optional) — a number controlling order within group, lower first. Omit it and the node sorts after every built-in node in that group.

ports.inputs / ports.outputs — arrays of { name, type }. type is one of int, number, bool, string, bytes, any — the same types built-in nodes use, with the same wire-compatibility checks. Use any when unsure.

A port type can follow a select property instead of being fixed:

{ "name": "msg", "type": { "property": "payloadType", "map": { "bool": "bool", "number": "number" }, "default": "bool" } }

The value of property picks the wire type; an unset or unmapped value uses default. The property must be a select field, and every key in map must be one of its options.

A transform may declare more than one output. Return a list to route messages across them, Node-RED style (e.g. return [msg, None] sends to output 1 only). A source has one output; a sink none.

properties (optional) — fields shown in the property panel when the node is selected:

{ "name": "factor", "label": "factor", "kind": "number", "default": 2 }
  • name — identifier. Your Python reads the value by this key.
  • label — shown in the property panel.
  • kind — text, textarea, number, boolean, select, configRef, pin, or target.
  • default — used when a node instance doesn't set the property. Type must match kind.
  • options — required for select: array of { value, label }. default must be one of the values.
  • configType — required for configRef: the config type the picker offers (e.g. thingstudio/config/i2c-bus). At compile time the picked config's own properties become a dict the node reads — see below.
  • singleton — optional, on a configRef: resolve the flow's one config of configType at compile time instead of an id you store (how a built-in uses the shared WiFi setting). Zero or two such configs is a compile error.
  • pinUse / pinPull — optional, on a pin: input or output, and the pull (none/up/down). Adding pinUse makes the compiler claim the pin, so two nodes can't quietly set the same pin up two ways. A pin without pinUse is just a value (checked to exist on the board) — use that for a bus line like SCL/SDA.
  • target — a kind for a board-specific node. Its value in Python is a dict of the board/processor this flow is compiled for — boardId, boardName, processorId, processorName, label, capabilities — or None if no board is chosen, so guard for that. Use it to identify your exact board (e.g. a XIAO nRF52840's own IMU).
  • nodeId — a kind whose Python value is this node's own id (a string). Use it to report status about yourself: runtime.report_status(properties['id'], 'connected').
  • help / placeholder / min / max / step / optional / rows — optional, the same panel hints a built-in field has. rows sets a textarea's height (default 4). pin fields take a number default; optional marks one where -1/blank means "not wired".
  • visibleWhen — optional: show the field only when another property satisfies a condition, e.g. { "field": "mode", "equals": "deadband" }. Operators: equals, notEquals, in (an array), gt, gte, lt, lte.

A polled source node must declare a numeric property named intervalMs — it sets the poll interval, a whole number of milliseconds, 1 or more. An eventSource or runOnce source does not need one.

requires (optional) — hardware the node needs, as { "capabilities": ["ble"] }. The words are the board definitions' capabilities (wifi, ble, espnow, pio, see Boards). On a board without one, the palette grays the node out and the compile refuses it, naming the missing capability.

docs.title: The behavior: <name>.node.py
docs.text:
Ordinary MicroPython. Define exactly one top-level function, named for your node's kind:

  • transform / sink → async def run(msg, properties):
  • source → async def emit(properties):

msg is a dict with a payload key, a topic key, and room for any extra keys you add. topic is a routing/identification string — the mqtt subscribe built-in node, for instance, fills it with the real MQTT topic a message arrived on. Most nodes have no natural topic of their own; set it to '' rather than a real value. The key is required either way — don't leave it out. properties is a dict of the node instance's configured values.

Transform — return the (possibly modified) msg, or None to stop it propagating:

async def run(msg, properties):
    msg['payload'] = msg['payload'] * properties['factor']
    return msg

Sink — return value is ignored:

async def run(msg, properties):
    print('got:', msg['payload'])

Source — called once per intervalMs, must return a msg:

async def emit(properties):
    return {'payload': 42, 'topic': ''}

Anything else — imports, helper functions, setup code — is ordinary Python.

docs.title: Example: a temperature sensor source
docs.text:
temp_sensor.node.json:

{
  "type": "myproject/temp_sensor",
  "kind": "source",
  "label": "temp sensor",
  "ports": { "outputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "number" }] },
  "properties": [
    { "name": "pin", "label": "data pin", "kind": "number", "default": 4 },
    { "name": "intervalMs", "label": "read interval (ms)", "kind": "number", "default": 5000 }
  ]
}

temp_sensor.node.py:

import dht
import machine

_pin = properties['pin']
_sensor = dht.DHT22(runtime.shared('pin', _pin, ('dht22',), lambda: machine.Pin(_pin)))

async def emit(properties):
    _sensor.measure()
    msg = {'payload': _sensor.temperature(), 'topic': ''}
    msg['humidity'] = _sensor.humidity()
    return msg

The sensor is built once, at setup, not on every emit() call — top-level code and emit share the same properties.

Temperature goes in payload, not humidity, because payload is the field the port's declared type (number, here) checks against, and the field a generic downstream node reads — debug prints msg['payload'] and nothing else, whatever else is in msg. Put whichever value you want wired and type-checked that way in payload. Anything else is a passenger: humidity rides along in the same msg, but only a node written to look for it specifically will ever read it.

docs.title: nonlocal, not global
docs.text:
Your file's top-level code doesn't run at true module scope — each node instance gets its own wrapper function, so two instances of the same custom type never share state. To keep a value across calls, use nonlocal:

_count = 0

async def emit(properties):
    nonlocal _count
    _count += 1
    return {'payload': _count, 'topic': ''}

global raises NameError here — there's no module-level name to find.

docs.title: Pins and buses
docs.text:
Get a pin or bus with runtime.shared(kind, key, settings, make), not by building it yourself. The first node to ask builds it with make(); every later node gets the same object. If a later node asks with different settings, the flow stops with an error naming both, instead of one node quietly changing the pin under another.

_pin = runtime.shared('pin', 5, ('in', 'up'), lambda: machine.Pin(5, machine.Pin.IN, machine.Pin.PULL_UP))
_i2c = runtime.shared('i2c', 0)  # fetch a bus another node in the flow set up

The built-in nodes use these settings: ('in', 'none' | 'up' | 'down') and ('out', 'none') for pins, and () for an ADC (runtime.shared('adc', 26, (), lambda: machine.ADC(machine.Pin(26)))). Pins, ADC, PWM, I2C and SPI all work this way: see Hardware is shared.

docs.title: Sharing a config (I2C bus, touch panel)
docs.text:
A configRef property lets your node pick one of the flow's config nodes. Its value in properties is that config's own properties as a dict (or None if none is picked), so a custom I2C node can join the same bus a built-in i2c/bme280 node uses:

{ "name": "bus", "label": "I2C bus", "kind": "configRef", "configType": "thingstudio/config/i2c-bus", "default": "" }

_i2c = runtime.shared('i2c', properties['bus']['bus'])  # the flow's shared bus, by its number

The bus/pins come from the config; keep the same runtime.shared key a built-in would use so a clash is reported, not silently shared. (Network configs — WiFi, MQTT — expose only the credential's name, not the secret, so a custom node can't make a WiFi connection from one.)

docs.title: Cleanup
docs.text:
If your node opens something that needs closing on redeploy — a socket, typically — register it:

import socket

_sock = socket.socket(socket.AF_INET, socket.SOCK_DGRAM)
runtime.register_cleanup('my_node_socket', lambda: _sock.close())

async def run(msg, properties):
    _sock.sendto(str(msg['payload']).encode(), ('192.168.1.50', 9000))

runtime is already available — no import needed. Without cleanup, a redeployed flow can leave the old socket open and fail with EADDRINUSE on the next deploy.

docs.title: Libraries you can import
docs.text:
When a node imports one of these, ThingStudio sends it to the board with the flow:

Library For ts_ble the board's Bluetooth LE radio, shared with the ble nodes (below) ts_wifi, ts_mqtt, ts_http_server the flow's WiFi, MQTT client and HTTP server, shared with the network nodes threadsafe_event waking a coroutine from a hardware interrupt (see Event-driven sources) events, delay_ms, encoder, aadc Peter Hinch's asyncio switch, button, timer, encoder and ADC drivers ssd1306, st7789py, st7796py display drivers bme280_float, ft6336u the BME280 sensor and FT6336U touch drivers mqtt_as Peter Hinch's asyncio MQTT client

A library of your own can't be sent yet. Code two of your nodes share goes in each .node.py.

For Bluetooth, use ts_ble.radio(), not bluetooth.BLE(): the board has one radio, and the ble nodes use the same one. radio().scan(...) and radio().advertise(...) share it as ble scan and ble advertise do, and ts_ble.decode(adv) and ts_ble.build_adv(...) read and build advertising data. The radio is turned off on each redeploy.

docs.title: Persisting values
docs.text:
runtime.settings keeps a value across reboots and redeploys of the same flow. Use it for an application setting a user changes on the device — units, a colour scheme — not for per-message state, which belongs in a closure local.

async def run(msg, properties):
    units = runtime.settings.get('units', 'kg')   # the default is yours, not the store's
    runtime.settings.set('units', msg['payload'])
    msg['payload'] = units
    return msg

Values are namespaced by the deployed flow's name, so a different flow cannot read or overwrite them. Renaming the flow starts a fresh namespace. A missing key returns your default. set raises SettingsError if the board cannot save (full or read-only flash) — let it surface as a node error rather than assuming the write worked. delete(key) and keys() round out the surface.

The store is a plain key/value; it does not know what a value means. Save only what the user changed, and supply the default at the read. To clear stored values, see debugging.

docs.title: Event-driven sources
docs.text:
A source that reacts to something other than the clock sets "eventSource": true and defines a second function, async def wait(properties), alongside emit. wait is awaited, so it blocks until your event fires; then emit builds the message. No intervalMs is needed.

{
  "type": "custom/button",
  "kind": "source",
  "label": "button",
  "eventSource": true,
  "ports": { "outputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "bool" }] },
  "properties": [{ "name": "pin", "label": "pin", "kind": "pin", "default": 11, "pinUse": "input" }]
}

A hardware interrupt (machine.Pin.irq) is the usual reason to use eventSource. Bridge it into asyncio with the vendored ThreadSafeEvent — its set() is the one call safe in a hard-IRQ handler — and register the handler:

import machine
from threadsafe_event import ThreadSafeEvent   # pushed with the flow because you import it

_evt = ThreadSafeEvent()

def _irq(_pin):
    _evt.set()          # a hard-IRQ handler may only do this: no allocation, no print, nothing else

_pin = runtime.shared('pin', properties['pin'], ('in', 'up'),
                      lambda: machine.Pin(properties['pin'], machine.Pin.IN, machine.Pin.PULL_UP))
_pin.irq(trigger=machine.Pin.IRQ_RISING, handler=_irq)

async def wait(properties):
    await _evt.wait()
    _evt.clear()

async def emit(properties):
    return {'payload': True, 'topic': ''}

runtime.asyncio.Event() is fine when the event is set from other asyncio code; for a real IRQ use ThreadSafeEvent, which survives the hard-IRQ context.

Keep any state the two share at the top of the file (both functions come from one per-instance closure, so nonlocal works across them).

docs.title: Run-once sources
docs.text:
A source that runs once, at flow start, sets "runOnce": true instead. It defines only emit; ThingStudio calls it once, with no intervalMs and no wait.

{
  "type": "custom/boot",
  "kind": "source",
  "label": "boot",
  "runOnce": true,
  "ports": { "outputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "string" }] }
}

docs.title: Two-faced nodes
docs.text:
A sink with "eventSource": true both consumes and produces: one input, one output, and three functions in .node.py. run(msg, properties) handles the input; wait(properties) then emit(properties) produce the output. All three come from the same per-instance closure, so they share state through nonlocal.

{
  "type": "custom/gateway",
  "kind": "sink",
  "label": "gateway",
  "eventSource": true,
  "ports": {
    "inputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "any" }],
    "outputs": [{ "name": "msg", "type": "string" }]
  }
}

Use it when the node has to react to messages and also act on its own (a clock that echoes a message and then ticks, or a subscription you can change at run time). A transform cannot be two-faced.

docs.title: Compile time: <name>.compile.py
docs.text:
A package can also include an optional compile-time hook, <name>.compile.py, defining one function:

def compile(ctx, properties):
    return {"properties": {...}, "errors": [...]}

It runs in the editor when the flow is compiled — never on the board. properties is what the flow file holds for this node; ctx describes the flow:

  • ctx["node"] — this instance: id, type, properties, and wired (a boolean per input/output).
  • ctx["flow"]["nodes"] / ["configs"] — every node and config, with non-secret properties only.
  • ctx["nodesOfType"] — every node of this node's type in the flow, including this one: id, type, and non-secret properties. Use it when the nodes share a decision (for example, a port's set of routes).
  • ctx["referencedConfigs"] — the full properties (including credentials) of the configs this node's configRef fields point at.
  • ctx["target"] — the board/processor being compiled for, or None.

Return a dict (or None). Everything is optional:

Key Meaning properties Extra values merged into what .node.py receives. Keys your descriptor doesn't declare are allowed. claims [{"resource": "GPIO 22", "use": "my device"}], checked like a pin field. warnings Strings shown in the compile warnings. errors Strings that stop the compile, naming the node.

The hook is sandboxed: no files, network, clock or randomness. Its result is data only — it cannot return Python or change the generated code's shape. Limits: 64 KB of properties, 64 claims, 32 warnings and 32 errors, and one second per hook; a hook that runs too long is stopped.

wifi status is an example: its hook derives the flow's WiFi config and whether an MQTT node is present, so its Python never asks you for the network twice.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Load time — a malformed .node.json is rejected immediately, with a message naming what's wrong: bad type, wrong port count, missing intervalMs, and so on.

Compile time — a bad property value on a specific node instance (e.g. a non-numeric number field) errors out naming that node and property.

Without the editor — the check command loads the same folder (or --custom-nodes <dir>). Check a flow that uses your node and it reports load and compile errors the same way:

node dist-cli/thingstudio-compile.mjs --board board:cyd my.flow.json

Deploy time — .node.py is spliced into the flow as-is; ThingStudio doesn't check it. A typo surfaces as a runtime error (e.g. NameError) reported from the device, attributed to your node.

docs.title: Limitations
docs.text:
A polled source node's emit runs on a fixed intervalMs schedule; an eventSource source waits on wait instead.

Two instances of the same custom node get independent setup. For a pin field that declares pinUse, ThingStudio checks it against the board and claims it at compile time; a pin you build in Python yourself (or read from a plain number field) it can't see, so use runtime.shared() for those, and a clash is caught when the flow starts.

Custom node Python runs with the same trust as any other node, including ThingStudio's function node. Loading a package only adds it to the palette; its Python runs on a board only when you place the node and deploy. Only files you place in the folder are loaded — there's no registry and no URL install — so don't put a package there that you haven't read.

docs.title: Console and compiled source
docs.text:
The console shows what the board and ThingStudio report: deploy results, node errors, and what debug nodes and print() send. Clear empties it. Scroll up to read or copy: the console stops following new lines until you scroll back to the bottom.

Its Show menu sets how much it shows:

  • Normal: your flow's output, warnings, errors, and the results of what you do, such as a deploy.
  • Info: adds routine reports: board detected, versions, memory, libraries sent, network status.
  • Debug: adds raw protocol messages and the board's boot output.

Hidden lines are kept, so choosing Info or Debug later shows what was already logged.

The Compiled source panel shows the MicroPython your flow compiles to. Download .py saves it as a file, named after the flow.

The editor's version is next to its name in the toolbar, and in Help → About ThingStudio. A + after it means you built it from uncommitted changes. Include the versions when you report a problem.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
With Show set to Info, the console prints a [memory] line after each connect and deploy. On an ESP32 it looks like this:

[memory] MicroPython 118 KB free · ESP-IDF heap 64 KB free, largest block 31 KB
  • MicroPython … free is the memory your flow and its libraries run in. It is the total free, not the largest piece.
  • ESP-IDF heap … free is the memory the chip's own software uses, including WiFi, MQTT and TLS. largest block is the biggest single piece of it. Only ESP32 boards report this part.

Which figure matters depends on the failure:

  • A deploy or a library failing with MemoryError is about MicroPython's memory. The total can look healthy while no single piece is big enough. See MemoryError or a library that won't load.
  • WiFi failing to start on an ESP32 is about the ESP-IDF heap. Below about 30 KB WiFi may not start, and the console warns before a deploy when less is free. Tools → Reset board (hard) returns that memory; a soft restart doesn't. See Restarting the board.

A real memory failure says MemoryError, memory allocation failed or names memory. A network error with a low figure beside it is still a network error: if the board has joined WiFi and the console says it can't reach a broker or host, memory isn't the cause. For an MQTT broker, see MQTT broker unreachable. The FAQ explains where an ESP32's memory goes.

docs.title: Commands and the Python prompt
docs.text:
The command box under the console runs Python on the board. Type a line and press Enter; the result appears in the console. The up and down arrows bring back earlier commands. The box takes one line: a pasted block of several lines is joined into one, which Python reads as a SyntaxError. Put statements on one line separated by ;, and write a loop as a list comprehension, for example [print(i) for i in range(3)].

gc.mem_free()
import machine; machine.Pin(15).value()
os.listdir()

Commands run alongside your flow, and variables you set stay for the next command. A command that takes time, such as a sleep or a loop, holds up the flow until it finishes.

The stored application values are available as settings:

settings.namespaces()      # each flow's name and how many values it holds
settings.clear()           # clear the current flow's values
settings.clear_all()       # clear every flow's values

Use these if a saved value is wrong, or a flow you no longer deploy left values behind. Clearing takes effect immediately; the next read returns the default. Tools → Clear device settings… does the same from the editor: choose the current flow, or every flow.

For MicroPython's own >>> prompt, click Stop flow & open prompt. The flow and the runtime stop; nothing is deleted. What you type in the box now goes to that prompt, and Deploy is off. Click Restart ThingStudio to start the runtime and the saved flow again.

To use the prompt from another program, such as Thonny or mpremote, click Connected · Disconnect first.

docs.title: Watching a board start up
docs.text:
To see a board's own startup messages, connect with mpremote connect PORT and no further command, or a serial monitor that doesn't send Ctrl-C when it opens. A working runtime prints LISTENER_BOOTING, then LISTENER_READY.

mpremote repl and Thonny's Shell interrupt the board as they connect, which looks like a board that never starts. Close them before connecting from ThingStudio: only one program can use the port at a time.

docs.title: Board won't connect
docs.text:
When Connect, Tools → Check status or Tools → Install runtime… gets no proper reply, the console says what the board sent instead, and what to do:

Console says What to do Nothing came back Usually no MicroPython. Install MicroPython. If it's there, press reset, then Tools → Check status. MicroPython but no ThingStudio runtime Tools → Install runtime…. MicroPython replied but didn't enter install mode Press reset and install again. Board is in its bootloader An ESP32 in download mode. Press reset, not BOOT. If it repeats, install MicroPython. Board runs CircuitPython, or replied but not as MicroPython Install MicroPython. Runtime still starting Wait, then Tools → Check status. Install stalled Replug the board, click ⟳, and try again. If it repeats, restart ThingStudio.

If the port itself won't open, the console says why:

Console says What to do port in use Close other serial monitors, IDEs, or editor tabs using the board. port access refused Replug the board and check port permissions. On Linux, check you're in the dialout group. board gone from that port Check the cable, click ⟳, and connect again.

The raw error stays in the message, in brackets. Include it if you report a problem.

docs.title: Install firmware… fails or lists nothing
docs.text:
Tools → Install firmware… writes MicroPython onto a board in its bootloader. Each refusal names the step:

What the dialog says What to do (no serial ports found), or the board's port is missing Put the board in download mode — hold BOOT, tap RESET, release BOOT — then click ⟳. (no mounted drives found), or the drive you want isn't listed Hold BOOTSEL while plugging the board in, then click ⟳. If it's mounted somewhere the list doesn't look, type the path in the box under the list — on macOS a Pico shows up as /Volumes/RPI-RP2. A port named /dev/ttyS0, /dev/ttyS1… Those are the computer's own serial ports, not the board. USB ports are listed above them, labelled with their path and the adapter's name (/dev/ttyUSB0 -- CH340). (no build for this chip — choose a file) The catalog has no pinned image for that chip family. Under Or use your own image file, pick the .bin or .uf2 from micropython.org/download. The chip family list is empty, or the catalog can't be read This install's firmware/builds.json is missing or malformed; the dialog says which line. A reinstall replaces it. The catalog from docs.thingstudio.net was refused The list on the site didn't carry a valid ThingStudio signature, or is older than one this computer already has. The dialog uses the saved or installed list instead, so flashing still works. Report it (Help → Report a problem) with the reason in the line. … is not a .uf2, or is a .uf2 sent to a serial port A mounted drive takes the .uf2 build, a serial port the .bin. Pick the matching file. choose the chip family, so esptool knows which chip and address to use A file on its own doesn't say which chip it is for. Pick the family; if the image is the reason, the editor reads it out of the file. The board doesn't start after flashing, or its serial output repeats invalid header The address or the family was wrong: 0x1000 for an ESP32 or ESP32-S2, 0x2000 for an ESP32-C5, 0 for an ESP32-S3, C3, C6 or ESP8266, and 0 for a ThingStudio custom image on a classic ESP32. A board maker's manual may give another address for its own demo images; for MicroPython, use these. Thonny can't write a C5 at 0x2000 (Install MicroPython). Flash again with the right family; the board is recoverable. esptool is not installed on this machine The backend's Python has no esptool: pip install esptool, then restart ThingStudio. esptool exited N at … on PORT The write stopped; the dialog's log has the tool's own lines. Check the cable and the bootloader mode, and retry. In Install options, try a slower speed, or tick Disable the stub loader. the flash did not finish within … The tool stopped answering. Unplug and replug the board, then flash again.

Erase all flash first is on by default: a board that had a different layout (a previous MicroPython, or a vendor image) needs it, or the new image can be written and still not boot.

A flash that finishes but leaves the board silent usually means it is waiting for Tools → Install runtime…: a stock MicroPython build has no runtime at all, and the ThingStudio custom image carries one but not the boot script that starts it.

docs.title: A full runtime on a custom-image board
docs.text:
On the ThingStudio custom image, Tools → Install runtime… writes only the boot script, main.py; the runtime is already in the firmware. A full copy of the runtime on the board's filesystem can only come from flashing the image without Erase all flash first over an older install that had one.

To see what is on the filesystem, type this in the command box:

import os; print(os.listdir('/'))

A board with only the boot script lists main.py among a few small files. A full runtime adds a long list of its own files. Flash the image again with Erase all flash first ticked, then install the runtime.

docs.title: Deploy is grayed out
docs.text:
Compile → Deploy is grayed out when:

  • the editor isn't connected to a board;
  • the flow on the board is the one on the canvas, deployed and unchanged since;
  • the flow is stopped at the Python prompt (click Restart ThingStudio);
  • the board is restarting.

docs.title: Module missing on the board
docs.text:
A deploy can fail with ImportError: no module named '...': the flow needs a module the board's MicroPython doesn't have. The board keeps running its previous flow.

The usual cause is networking. MQTT, UDP, HTTP and WiFi nodes need the network and socket modules, which only boards with WiFi or Ethernet have. A Raspberry Pi Pico has neither; a Pico W does. If the board reports no WiFi, the console warns you before the deploy.

Other modules differ between ports and builds. If the import is in your own function node, check the module exists for your board in the MicroPython docs. A board that should have it may need a different MicroPython build.

ThingStudio's own libraries, such as the MQTT client and display drivers, are sent by Deploy. See Libraries.

docs.title: MemoryError or a library that won't load
docs.text:
The [memory] line can show free RAM while a deploy still fails with MemoryError: the free RAM is in pieces, and a flow or a library needs one piece big enough to fit. This is common on ESP32 boards without PSRAM once a display flow has run.

When a deploy fails this way, work through these in order:

  1. Tools → Remove flow… — so nothing is resumed at start-up.
  2. Power cycle the board — unplug its USB cable and plug it back in, or Tools → Reset board (hard).
  3. Deploy again.

Removing the flow alone doesn't help: the running flow keeps its memory until the chip restarts. A soft restart doesn't either: it restarts the interpreter over the same heap regions and returns no chip memory. Only a power cycle gives the board a clean heap.

If it still fails after the power cycle, the flow may be too big for this board. Then do one of these:

  • Make the flow smaller. Use fewer GUI pages, import fewer libraries, pick a smaller frame. The gui screen node sends a frame in strips for this reason; a function node that builds a whole frame at once still needs one big block.
  • Use a board with more memory. A board with PSRAM can start flows that a board without it cannot.
  • Run a firmware image with the libraries built in. The classic ESP32, ESP32-C3 and ESP32-C5 have ready-made ones: Custom firmware. On other boards, build your own by freezing the runtime and the flow libraries into MicroPython.

Deploy stops here on purpose; freeing or restarting is yours to invoke. When the board looks short of memory before a deploy starts, the console says so in one line (only 19 KB free on the board, this flow is 10 KB -- it may not fit) and deploys anyway. The figure is total free memory, not the largest block, so it is a hint, not a verdict.

docs.title: WiFi Internal State Error on deploy
docs.text: On an ESP32, deploying a flow with MQTT nodes can fail with "Wifi Internal State Error". The board is still reconnecting to the network the previous flow used, and refuses a new connection until that finishes. The MQTT nodes retry up to three times. If it still fails, deploy again.

docs.title: MQTT broker unreachable
docs.text:
An mqtt publish or mqtt subscribe node shows a red dot, and the console says:

mqtt connect to HOST:1883 failed after 3 attempts (… 'Timeout on socket write' …, wifi status 1010)

The editor adds a line after it, read from the board's WiFi status, such as [mqtt] Board is on WiFi but can't reach the broker HOST:1883 from its network.

The raw line ends with the board's WiFi status. wifi status 1010 means the board has joined WiFi and has an address but can't reach the broker from its network: the cause is the network between the board and the broker, not the board's memory. 201 or 202 means the board never joined WiFi; see The board hasn't joined WiFi.

With 1010, check in order:

  • The host and port in the flow's MQTT broker. The board connects to exactly what the flow says.
  • That the board's network can reach the broker. Your computer reaching it proves nothing: a laptop can reach a home broker over a VPN the board isn't on, and a board on a phone hotspot isn't on the home network.
  • That the network lets port 1883 through. Some mobile networks block it.
  • That the broker listens beyond localhost. Mosquitto 2 listens on localhost only, unless its configuration has listener 1883 and either allow_anonymous true or a password file.

Then do one of these:

  • Put the board on the broker's network.
  • Use the public test broker test.mosquitto.org, port 1883. It is public: anyone can read what you publish, so use a topic nobody else will, such as one with a random number in it (thingstudio/4821937/temperature). A broker on your own network is better if you have one.
  • Relay through a computer the board can reach. With Remote Login on, run ssh -g -N -L 0.0.0.0:1883:BROKER:1883 localhost on that computer, and set the flow's broker to that computer's address.

docs.title: The board hasn't joined WiFi
docs.text:
On an ESP32, status 201 means the network wasn't found, and 202 means joining failed authentication, usually a wrong password. Check, in order:

  • The network name and password in the flow's WiFi credential: ✎ next to the WiFi field.
  • Whether the flow has both MQTT nodes and a wifi status node. In a flow with MQTT nodes, MQTT manages the WiFi connection and wifi status only reports on it. If the join fails, remove the wifi status node and deploy again.
  • The ESP-IDF figure on the [memory] line. Below about 30 KB WiFi may not start; use Tools → Reset board (hard). See Memory.

The console can also show "Wifi Internal State Error". For that error at deploy time, see WiFi Internal State Error on deploy.

docs.title: Deploy resends a piece, or fails part-way
docs.text:
Deploy sends the flow, and each library it uses, in pieces, and waits for the board to confirm each one. Over a USB-serial chip such as the CYD's, a piece can arrive damaged or its confirmation can get lost. The console then shows resending (1/2), and Deploy carries on.

If a piece still fails after three tries, Deploy stops and says so, and the flow on the board is unchanged. Deploy again. If it keeps happening, try another USB cable or port, close anything else using the serial port, or connect over WiFi.

docs.title: The console shows [protocol] illegal or PROTOCOL_ILLEGAL
docs.text: The editor and the board follow a fixed set of moves when they talk. A line starting [protocol] illegal (from the editor) or PROTOCOL_ILLEGAL (from the board) means one of them made a move that isn't in that set. It is a bug in ThingStudio, not something you did. Deploy carries on or fails cleanly either way. Please report it with the console lines around it.

docs.title: Reading a node error
docs.text:
When a node fails on the board, the console shows a [NODE_ERROR] line naming the node and the error, and the node is highlighted on the canvas. Network nodes (udp send, udp receive, http request, mqtt publish, mqtt subscribe) also name the operation and the host and port. A network node error without them is worth reporting.

A node error stops the chain the node is in, from its source onward, until the next deploy: a timer sends nothing more, an inject ignores clicks. The flow's other chains keep running.

docs.title: I2C device not answering
docs.text:
A sensor node's status dot shows disconnected, with "no reply at 0x76", when nothing answers at its address. Scan the bus to see what is there. Type these two lines in the command box, one at a time, with your bus and pins:

i2c = machine.I2C(0, scl=machine.Pin(5), sda=machine.Pin(4))
[hex(a) for a in i2c.scan()]

An i2c device node set to scan does the same from a flow.

An empty list means nothing answered. Check these, in order:

  • The pin numbers. On a Pico, GP4 and GP5 are physical pins 6 and 7.
  • SDA and SCL swapped.
  • Power (3.3 V) and ground to the device.
  • Solder joints on the header pins.

An address different from the node's means the address is wrong, not the wiring.

docs.title: A toggle button goes back
docs.text:
A gui toggle with its input wired shows the state you asked for until the input confirms it. If nothing arrives within wait for confirmation (5 s by default), it goes back to its last state, shows a cross for a moment, and the console shows NODE_ERROR ... NoConfirmation: no confirmation within 5 s.

Check these, in order:

  • The device is reachable and the command reached it. Watch the command topic with a debug node.
  • The input is wired to the device's state topic, not the command topic.
  • The state is sent in a form the toggle matches. A toggle set to true and false ignores ON and OFF: set its value type to text.

docs.title: Deploy fails with an architecture or native-module error
docs.text:
The gs4, gs2 and mono frame formats of display spi compile part of their code to native machine code, which needs the right architecture for the board's chip.

Tools → Native code defaults to Arch: Auto, which uses the processor of the board in the Board menu. If Deploy fails with an architecture or native-module error, pick your board's chip from the list and deploy again.

docs.title: Restarting the board
docs.text:
A board can run short of memory after several deploys, or after a flow that uses a lot of it, such as a display. The console suggests a restart when a deploy fails with MemoryError, when the board restarts while starting a flow, or when an ESP32 has too little memory left for WiFi.

The Tools menu has two restarts:

  • Tools → Restart board (soft) restarts MicroPython. The saved flow starts again with a clean interpreter and the flow's own objects are gone; the heap stays as it was. USB stays connected.
  • Tools → Reset board (hard) resets the whole chip, like its reset button, and frees all memory. A board with native USB (Pico, ESP32-S2, S3 and C3) disconnects; click Connect when it's back.

A soft restart clears a flow's own leftovers, such as a big buffer a faulty node left behind. A deploy that doesn't fit needs the steps under MemoryError or a library that won't load, and an ESP32 short of memory for WiFi needs the hard reset. The console says which. Deploy is off until the board is back, which can take several seconds.

docs.title: Board stuck restarting
docs.text:
A flow that crashes the board as it starts would crash it on every restart. If the saved flow doesn't stay up for 10 seconds on three restarts in a row, the board starts without it, and the console shows [safe mode]. Fix the flow and deploy it again, or remove it.

Tools → Remove flow… deletes the saved flow from the board, for any flow that stops the board answering:

  1. Select the board's port and choose Tools → Remove flow….
  2. If the console asks, press the board's reset button. ThingStudio keeps trying for a minute.
  3. When it's done, click Connect.

The board then starts with the runtime only, as after a fresh install. The flow on your canvas isn't affected.

docs.title: Step 2: Tour the editor
docs.text:
Start ThingStudio if it isn't running: see step 1.

The parts of the editor. Click to see it full size.

docs.title: Toolbar
docs.text:
The toolbar runs left to right in the order you work: the flow, the board, then deploy.

  • New, open, save: the File menu.
  • This flow's name: saved with the flow. The board reports it, so you can tell which flow it's running.
  • Connect to a board: pick the board's port from the list, then click Connect. ⟳ looks for boards again.
  • Board type, pin map: the Board menu sets the board the flow is for; Auto uses the connected board. Pins… opens a page listing that board's pins.
  • Deploy flow to board: Compile → Deploy turns the flow into MicroPython and sends it to the board.
  • Board tools, user guide: the Tools menu has board jobs, such as installing the runtime or removing a flow. The Help menu opens this user guide.

docs.title: Palette
docs.text:
Nodes to add: every node, in groups such as General, Network and Hardware. Drag a node onto the canvas, or click it. Type in the filter box to find one. Custom nodes appear in the group they name, or in General.

Click a group's name to fold or open it. Only General starts open. The editor remembers which groups you opened, in this browser. While you type in the filter box, every group with a match opens.

docs.title: Canvas
docs.text:
The canvas is where you build the flow. The tabs above it, Sheets of this flow, spread one flow across several sheets.

The canvas works like this:

  • Wire two nodes: drag from one node's output, on its right, to another node's input, on its left.
  • Select: click a node or a wire. Ctrl-click to select several nodes.
  • Delete: select, then press Delete or Backspace. Deleting a node removes its wires too.

The editor refuses a wire between ports whose types don't fit. See Wiring.

docs.title: Properties, notes and console
docs.text:
The right-hand side holds the selected node's settings and what the board sends back:

  • Selected node's settings: the properties panel.
  • Notes on this flow: the Notes panel, free text saved with the flow.
  • Generated MicroPython: the Compiled source panel. Click it to open it. Download .py saves it as a file. Like the panel, the file holds your WiFi password and broker login.
  • Messages from the board: the Device console, with messages from ThingStudio and the board, including your flow's output. Its Show menu sets how much it shows: Normal for your flow's output, results and errors, Info to add routine reports such as memory, Debug for everything.
  • Run Python on the board: type a line of Python and click Send. It runs on the board alongside the flow. See Commands and the Python prompt.
  • Escape to REPL: Stop flow & open prompt stops the flow and gives you MicroPython's own >>> prompt. Restart ThingStudio starts the flow again.

To make the notes, compiled source and console column wider or narrower, drag its left edge. Double-click the edge to reset it.

Editor in depth covers wire types, node labels, presets, config nodes and node status.
