docs.title: Where do I ask a question or report a problem?
docs.text: Ask questions, and show what you've built, in GitHub Discussions. Report a bug or a missing feature on the issue tracker, or with Help → Report a problem. Include the editor's version (Help → About ThingStudio), your board, and the console lines around the problem. Share the flow file, not compiled output; see the next question.

docs.title: How do I share a flow when I ask for help?
docs.text: Share the flow file: File → Save, then attach or paste the .flow.json. It holds the nodes and wiring and no passwords: the WiFi and broker logins stay on your computer (The ThingStudio folder). Don't paste the Compiled source panel, a downloaded .py or the console's compiled output: they contain the resolved WiFi password and broker login. If you pasted it somewhere public, change the password.

docs.title: Why does my ESP32 have so little free memory?
docs.text:
An ESP32's RAM is shared between MicroPython and the chip's own software: ESP-IDF, its FreeRTOS scheduler, and the WiFi stack. About half of a classic ESP32's 520 KB is taken before anything runs, by code that has to run from RAM, the flash cache and fixed buffers. WiFi and the rest of ESP-IDF then take more as they run.

Measured on a CYD (classic ESP32, no external RAM) with a flow running:

KB Used before the heap starts ~287 MicroPython's heap 109 ESP-IDF, FreeRTOS and WiFi, allocated while running ~85 Free 33

So MicroPython gets about a fifth of the chip's RAM. The [memory] line in the console (shown at the Info level) shows the current figures.

docs.title: Why does a Pico W have more room than an ESP32-C3, when the C3 has more RAM?
docs.text: The Pico W's WiFi chip has its own processor and memory. On an ESP32 the whole WiFi stack runs on the main chip and uses its RAM. So a 264 KB Pico W leaves more for your flow than a 400 KB ESP32-C3.

docs.title: Deploy failed with "MemoryError ... allocating 38400 bytes". Why, when there's more free memory than that?
docs.text: Free memory is in pieces, and a big buffer needs one piece that size. A 240x320 frame in 16 grays is 38,400 bytes. The GUI nodes draw in strips to avoid this; a function node that builds a full frame should too. See MemoryError or a library that won't load.

docs.title: Why isn't a soft restart enough after "too full to receive the flow"?
docs.text: A soft restart reuses the same heap; only a power cycle rebuilds it. See MemoryError or a library that won't load.

docs.title: Deploy failed a second time. Is the flow too big for my board?
docs.text: Possibly. If a deploy still fails after Tools → Remove flow… and a power cycle, the flow may be too big for the board. See MemoryError or a library that won't load for what to do.

docs.title: Redeploying a BLE flow on an ESP32-C5 fails with "MemoryError". Why?
docs.text: On stock MicroPython, the Bluetooth stack keeps its memory between flows, and the runtime, libraries and new flow have to fit in what is left. Install the ThingStudio custom image: it redeploys the same flow with room to spare. Or choose Tools → Remove flow…, power cycle the board, then deploy.

docs.title: Why does http request fail with "MemoryError" fetching a page?
docs.text: The node reads the whole response body into memory at once. A page larger than the largest free block fails, even when the console shows more free memory than the page size. A 56 KB page on an ESP32-C3 failed with MemoryError allocating 56722 bytes; a 48-byte page worked. Point the node at a smaller response, or use a board with PSRAM for large pages.

docs.title: Which MicroPython build does my ESP32-S3 need for its PSRAM?
docs.text: The kind of PSRAM decides, not the flash size. Quad PSRAM, usually 2 MB (modules such as N8R2), works with the generic build: it finds the PSRAM at startup. Octal PSRAM, usually 8 MB (modules such as N16R8), needs the octal build (SPIRAM_OCT). On the generic build an octal board's PSRAM stays unused and the console shows only about 120 KB free. Freenove's S3 display boards are octal: 121 KB free before, 7.8 MB after.

docs.title: My ESP32-C5 prints "PSRAM chip is not connected" at boot. Is it broken?
docs.text: No. The generic ESP32-C5 build looks for PSRAM, and many C5 modules have none. It reports the failure, says "continuing without it", and starts MicroPython with the chip's own RAM. The ThingStudio C5 image doesn't look for PSRAM, so it doesn't print this.

docs.title: Why does GPIO 10 pulse when my flow doesn't use it?
docs.text: Runtime 15.0.0 and earlier toggle GPIO 10 every 200 ms on every board, a signal meant only for Thingstudio's own test rig. It runs with no flow deployed, so changing your flow doesn't stop it. Install the runtime again with Tools → Install runtime… to get one that leaves GPIO 10 alone.

docs.title: Which board should I use for a display and WiFi together?
docs.text: An ESP32 with external RAM (PSRAM), such as many ESP32-S3 boards. MicroPython puts its heap in the external RAM, leaving the chip's own RAM for WiFi. A classic ESP32 or ESP32-C3 without PSRAM can run a display and WiFi, but only at lower color depths and with little to spare.

docs.title: My WiFi flow worked before, but now the board crashes or won't join. Why?
docs.text: On an ESP32, MicroPython's heap grows by taking memory from ESP-IDF, and keeps it until the chip is reset. After a flow that uses a lot of memory, such as a display, WiFi may have too little left to start. Use Tools → Reset board (hard): a soft restart doesn't give that memory back. See Memory and Restarting the board.

docs.title: Why does opening a flow ask "Save changes to …?" even though I changed nothing?
docs.text: That is the browser's file-permission dialog, not the editor. A page may read a file you pick, but to write it back (Save) it needs your permission, and the browser asks with that wording: "Save changes to gui-hero-cyd.flow.json? https://127.0.0.1:8765 will be able to edit it." Accept it to let the editor save back to that file. It is not about unsaved changes on the canvas, and it comes back after a page refresh because browsers grant file access per page session. Opening from Open… or Recent is the same file; nothing is written until you press Save.

docs.title: Why does Deploy say the board needs the runtime installed again?
docs.text: The editor and the runtime on the board talk a shared protocol. When an update changes it, a board with the older runtime can't run flows from the newer editor, so Deploy stops and says so. Use Tools → Install runtime…, then Connect and deploy again.

docs.title: How do I tell which version of the editor I'm running?
docs.text: It's next to ThingStudio in the toolbar, and in Help → About ThingStudio. A + after it means you built the editor from uncommitted changes.

docs.title: My clock shows -- and never the time. Why?
docs.text: The ntp node hasn't synced yet. Its status says why: waiting for WiFi, or NTP from server failed when the board can't reach the server. It tries again every 30 seconds. See ntp.

docs.title: My gui toggle shows --. Why?
docs.text: A toggle with its input wired shows -- until the input sends a value it recognizes. It matches the input against its on sends and off sends values, true and false unless you changed them. A Tasmota plug reports ON and OFF as text: set the toggle's value type to text. See a toggle that follows the real device.

docs.title: Why can't I use a touch node and a gui screen on the same panel?
docs.text: Both would poll the same chip, and each would take touches from the other. A gui screen reads its panel itself. Use the touch node only when you aren't using the GUI. Deploy stops and names both nodes if a panel is picked twice.

docs.title: Why can't a page resize, or a text element take a percentage width?
docs.text: There is nothing to resize to: a page fills a display of one fixed size, and the layout is resolved when the flow compiles, not by a browser at runtime. An element's cells, its font and its position are fixed numbers on the board. See Laying out pages.

docs.title: Why won't a function node's output wire into pwm out?
docs.text: A function node's output has the type any, and pwm out's input takes a number. The editor refuses a wire from any to number, int or string inputs. See Wiring.

docs.title: Why does compile fail with "needs a WiFi network"?
docs.text: An mqtt publish or mqtt subscribe node talks to its broker over WiFi, and it manages that connection itself, so it needs real credentials: a WiFi config in the flow and a broker. Compile stops with one line naming what's missing — "needs a WiFi network" or "needs an MQTT broker". Set the node's WiFi (or MQTT Broker) field; every MQTT node in a flow shares that one setting. See Config nodes.

docs.title: Why do http in requests take a second to answer?
docs.text: The flow answers immediately; the wait is the board's WiFi waking up. An idle board's radio sleeps (modem-sleep), and a new request pays the wake and the connection set-up before anything the flow does. On a classic ESP32 behind a VPN tunnel, requests took up to 1.2 s with the radio asleep and 0.15–0.20 s once it was warm. If the board has steady network traffic, a flow that talks or sits connected, the wake cost goes away on its own.

docs.title: Why is Compile → Deploy grayed out after a deploy?
docs.text: The board already runs the flow on the canvas. Deploy comes back when you change the flow. See Deploy is grayed out.

docs.title: Why are the pin fields dropdowns?
docs.text: Your processor names its pins instead of numbering them. The STM32 on a pyboard uses X1, A13 and so on. Pin fields then list the chip's own pins rather than take a number. See Pins that aren't numbers.

docs.title: Why can't I use SPI bus 0 or 1 on an nRF52840?
docs.text: On the nRF52840, SPI 0 and 1 share hardware with I2C 0 and 1, so a flow using both would fail on the board. ThingStudio offers SPI on buses 2 and 3 only. See Boards and processors.

docs.title: Why did my saved settings reset after I renamed the flow?
docs.text: Saved values are kept per flow name. Renaming the flow makes it a new name to the board, so its values start from the defaults. The old values are still on the board: rename the flow back to use them again, or clear them from the command box.

docs.title: Why doesn't my Uno TFT shield work on a Wemos D1 R32?
docs.text: The D1 R32 puts the shield's A2, A3 and A4 on GPIO 35, 34 and 36, which are input only on an ESP32. A parallel TFT shield drives its RS, CS and RST lines from those pins, so it can't start. Wire GPIO 15 to A2 (RS), GPIO 33 to A3 (CS) and GPIO 32 to A4 (RST), then set those pins in the display node.

docs.title: Do I need a terminal to install MicroPython?
docs.text: No, for boards ThingStudio can flash: the ESP32 family over a serial port, and a board whose bootloader mounts as a drive (RP2040, RP2350, nRF52). Put the board in its bootloader and use Tools → Install firmware…. Other chips have their own installation routes; see Install MicroPython.

docs.title: Why are the ble nodes grayed out?
docs.text: The chosen board has no Bluetooth LE that MicroPython's bluetooth module drives. The ESP32, S3, C3 and C5 have it. The ESP32-S2 has no Bluetooth, and an nRF52840's MicroPython reaches its radio through a different module (ubluepy), which these nodes don't use yet. Pick your board in the Board menu; see boards.

docs.title: Why doesn't ble scan show my device's name?
docs.text: Many devices put their name only in the scan response, which a passive scan doesn't ask for. Turn on active scan. Some never advertise a name: filter them by address or manufacturer id instead.

docs.title: Why did WiFi get slower when I added a ble scan?
docs.text: On an ESP32 the WiFi and Bluetooth share one radio, taking turns. The longer the scan window against the scan interval, the less time WiFi gets. The default listens 30 ms in every 320 ms; lower the window, or raise the interval, if MQTT or HTTP become slow. See ble scan.

docs.title: A phone or computer still shows the old characteristics after I changed the flow. Why?
docs.text: Phones and computers remember a device's services between connections. After a deploy that changes the characteristics, turn Bluetooth off and on, or forget the board in the Bluetooth settings, then connect again. In nRF Connect, Refresh services in the device's menu does it too.

docs.title: A device connects, but no new values arrive. Why?
docs.text: Reading shows the value once; to get each new one, the connected device has to subscribe. In nRF Connect, tap the characteristic's arrow icon (notify). The ble characteristic out node's notify must be on.

docs.title: Why does a ble peer stay on "finding"?
docs.text: The board hasn't seen the device advertise. Check that it's on, in range, and not already connected to something else, such as a phone app: most devices stop advertising while connected. A phone changes its address, so find a phone by name. A ble scan node into a debug node shows what the board can see.

docs.title: After a Bluetooth flow, why does the board have less memory for the next one?
docs.text: The Bluetooth radio stays on between flows once a ble node has started it: switching it off and on again can leave the ESP32-C5's radio unable to scan until a power cycle. The radio keeps its share of ESP-IDF memory, the memory WiFi and displays also use, even if the next flow has no ble nodes. Tools → Reset board (hard) gives it back. See Memory.

docs.title: Step 6: Blink an LED
docs.text:
Your first flow: make an LED blink once a second, using three nodes.

Your board should be connected, with the runtime installed: steps 4 and 5.

docs.title: Find your LED's pin
docs.text:
Many boards have an LED wired to a GPIO pin. To find it, click Pins… next to the Board menu. Pins that the board names, such as LED, are listed first. Supported hardware lists the boards ThingStudio has definitions for. For any other board, check its documentation.

The Pico W and Pico 2 W LEDs are wired through the WiFi chip, not a GPIO pin, so gpio out can't reach them. On those boards, or any board without an LED, wire an LED and a 330 Ω resistor from a free GPIO pin to GND. The LED's longer leg goes towards the GPIO pin.

Don't leave out the resistor. Without it, the LED draws too much current and can damage the board.

docs.title: Build the flow
docs.text:
1. Drag a timer onto the canvas. Set interval (ms) to 500.

  2. Drag a function onto the canvas. Replace its code with:

    msg['payload'] = msg['payload'] % 2
return msg

  3. Drag a gpio out onto the canvas. Set pin to your LED's GPIO number.

  4. Wire timer → function → gpio out.

This flow is tutorials/blink.flow.json, in the tutorials folder. Opened from there, it needs only pin set to your LED's GPIO number.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
Click Compile → Deploy. A successful deploy ends like this in the console:

[deploying "my flow" as 3f2a…]
[deploy OK -- flow is running on the device]

The flow name and ID will differ. Set the console's Show menu to Info or Debug to see each stage, including the board's free memory.

The LED now blinks: on for half a second, off for half a second.

The flow keeps running on the board after you unplug it from your computer and power it another way.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The timer sends a message every 500 ms. Its payload is a count: 1, 2, 3, and so on.

gpio out turns the pin on for any payload that isn't zero. Wired straight to the timer, the LED would switch on and stay on.

The function node turns the count into 1, 0, 1, 0 with % 2. That gives on, off, on, off.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
Two tutorials take the flow further:

  • Two more blinks — the blink again, two more ways: the LED's state on the hardware, read and written back in code, or kept in the node with context.
  • A sensor display — the next job past blinking: read a sensor and show it on a screen.

docs.title: Tell us how it went
docs.text: Started from a blank board? Tell us how it went: where the guide or the tool let you down is the most useful part. To keep it private, email mike@minus1.com.

docs.title: If it doesn't blink
docs.text:
Each symptom below has its own fix:

  • Deploy is grayed out: you aren't connected, so click Connect. Deploy is also grayed out after a deploy until you change the flow, while the flow is stopped at the Python prompt (Stop flow & open prompt), and while the board restarts.
  • Compile fails: usually a mistake in the function node's code, such as a missing quote or wrong indentation. The console shows the Python error in red, with its line, and highlights the node. Fix the code and deploy again.
  • Deploy works, then the console shows [NODE_ERROR]: the code ran on the board and failed, for example on a misspelt name. The message names the error, and the node is highlighted.
  • Deploy fails: the console says why. See Board won't connect.
  • Deploy works but the LED stays dark: check the pin number against Pins…. Some boards' LEDs light when the pin is off; the LED still blinks, the other way round.

For anything else, see Debugging & troubleshooting.

docs.title: Flow lifecycle
docs.text: How a flow is saved, opened, deployed and disconnected.

docs.title: Save and open
docs.text:
A flow is saved in a .flow.json file you choose, so it can live in a project's git repo like any other file. The file holds the nodes and their properties, the wiring, the canvas layout and the config nodes.

  • File → Save (⌘S, or Ctrl+S on Windows and Linux) writes to the flow's file. A new flow has no file yet, so the first Save asks where, like Save As. The file's name shows next to the flow name.
  • File → Save As… (⇧⌘S, or Ctrl+Shift+S) always asks where, and that file becomes the flow's file.
  • File → Open… (⌘O, or Ctrl+O) loads a flow file. Save then writes back to it.
  • Open recent, in the File menu, lists the last 8 files you opened or saved, newest first, with each one's flow name. After a reload the browser asks once for permission to use the file again. A file that has moved or been deleted is taken off the list. Clear recent files forgets the list, not the files.
  • File → New flow starts an empty flow with no file.

If the file has changed on disk since you opened or last saved it, for example after a git checkout, Save asks before overwriting it. Say no and use Save As to keep both.

The recent list is kept in your browser, so another browser or a private window has its own. Safari and Firefox can't save back to a file: there, Save and Save As download the flow, Open uploads one, and there's no recent list.

The flow name field is saved inside the file itself and is sent with every deploy, so a connected board's identity is visible in the console instead of a bare deployment id. It also suggests a filename for Save As (spaces and punctuation become dashes), but you can type over that suggestion freely.

Custom node packages and saved credentials live in ~/.thingstudio/custom-nodes/ and ~/.thingstudio/credentials/. They're shared across flows rather than tied to one project, unlike a flow itself — a saved credential referenced by name from a config node is never written into the .flow.json file. See The ThingStudio folder.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text:
Compile → Deploy compiles the current canvas to MicroPython bytecode and sends it to the connected board, replacing whatever flow is currently running there.

A successful deploy shows a confirmation in the console and the new flow starts running immediately. The board keeps the deployed flow and starts it again each time the board starts, with or without the editor. Each start begins every node afresh: counts, filters, journals, flow variables and a function node's context start empty. Only settings keeps its values (see function).

A failed deploy leaves the board's current flow running and shows a specific error:

  • a compile error — something in the flow itself, such as a missing required property
  • a space error — the compiled flow doesn't fit in the board's available flash/RAM
  • a library error — see below

After a successful deploy the button grays out: the board is already running exactly what's on the canvas. It re-enables the moment you change anything (a property, a node, a wire). A change reaches the board only with the next deploy. A failed deploy leaves it enabled so you can fix the problem and retry.

docs.title: Libraries
docs.text:
Some nodes need a library on the board, such as MQTT or a display driver. Deploy installs the libraries your flow uses and removes ones it no longer uses, so a board holds only what its flow needs. The console lists them on each deploy. A library already on the board isn't sent again.

A function node that imports one of these libraries, such as import mqtt_as, gets it the same way. If the board can't take a library, for example because its flash is full, the console names the library and says why.

Tools → Check status re-requests the board's identity — chip type, runtime version, and whichever flow is currently running — without resetting the board or redeploying anything. Useful for confirming what's actually on the board after reconnecting to a session already in progress.

Disconnect closes the serial connection. The board keeps running whatever flow was last deployed; disconnecting the editor doesn't stop it.

docs.title: Getting started
docs.text:
Want a look first? Try the editor in your browser before you install anything. The demo doesn't connect to a board, but you can build a flow and read the MicroPython it makes.

From a new board to a blinking LED, in six steps:

  1. Install ThingStudio on your computer.
  2. Tour the editor: what each part of the screen does.
  3. Install MicroPython on your board. A standard ESP32 takes the advised custom image.
  4. Connect your board to ThingStudio.
  5. Install the runtime, the part of ThingStudio that runs on the board.
  6. Blink an LED: build your first flow and deploy it. Or open tutorials/blink.flow.json (the tutorials folder) with File → Open…, point the pin at your board's own LED, and deploy.

When something doesn't work, Debugging and the FAQ go by what you see on screen.

You need a board with one of the processors in Supported hardware, and a USB cable that carries data, not only power. Installing uses a terminal, or PowerShell on Windows.

docs.title: Step 1: Install ThingStudio
docs.text:
ThingStudio is a program you run on your computer. It opens its editor in your web browser: Chrome or Edge 137, Firefox 131 or Safari 18.4, or later. It brings its own Python, so nothing else needs installing to run it.

There are two ways to install it. Both give you the same program.

  • Download a package and unpack it. Nothing runs until you start it.
  • Run the installer script. It picks the right package, checks its checksum, and adds a thingstudio command. Run it again to upgrade.

docs.title: Download a package
docs.text:
Download the package for your computer from the releases page. Installation details lists the package for each platform.

macOS and Linux: unpack it with tar -xzf thingstudio-VERSION-PLATFORM.tar.gz. ThingStudio is the thingstudio file in the unpacked folder.

Windows: unzip it anywhere, for example into your Documents folder. ThingStudio is thingstudio.cmd in the unzipped folder. If Windows says "Windows protected your PC", click More info, then Run anyway. The Windows package isn't signed.

docs.title: Run the installer script
docs.text:
The commands below download the installer script and pipe it straight into a shell. To read the script before running it, download install.sh or install.ps1 and open it in a text editor.

macOS and Linux: run this in a terminal. On a Mac, that's the Terminal app, in Applications → Utilities.

curl -fsSL https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh

If the installer says ~/.local/bin isn't on your PATH, run the command it prints, then open a new terminal.

On Linux, your account must be in the dialout group (uucp on Arch) to use USB boards. The installer reports this if your account isn't in the group, and prints the command to fix it.

Windows: open PowerShell from the Start menu and run this. It doesn't need administrator rights.

irm https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases/latest/download/install.ps1 | iex

To upgrade or remove ThingStudio, or build it from source, see Installation details.

docs.title: Start ThingStudio
docs.text:
How you start ThingStudio depends on how you installed it:

  • Installer script: run thingstudio in a terminal. If the command isn't found, see If the command isn't found.
  • Package on macOS or Linux: run ./thingstudio in the unpacked folder.
  • Package on Windows: run thingstudio.cmd in the unzipped folder.

The editor opens in your browser at http://127.0.0.1:8765/. Leave the terminal open while you work. Press Ctrl-C there to stop ThingStudio.

ThingStudio also serves this user guide, so it works offline. Help → User guide opens it.

docs.title: Where it is installed
docs.text:
• Installer script, macOS and Linux: the program is in ~/.local/share/thingstudio, and the thingstudio command is ~/.local/bin/thingstudio.
  • Installer script, Windows: %LOCALAPPDATA%\Thingstudio. The thingstudio command is in its bin folder.
  • Package: the folder you unpacked it into.

To see which copy your terminal runs, use command -v thingstudio in a macOS or Linux shell, or Get-Command thingstudio in PowerShell.

docs.title: If the command isn't found
docs.text:
The shell looks for commands in the folders listed in your PATH, and remembers what it found. After an install it can be out of date in two ways.

The command's folder isn't on your PATH. To check, run echo "$PATH" and look for .local/bin. When it's missing, the installer prints the line that adds it to your shell's startup file; it prints nothing when the folder is already on your PATH. Run that line, or add the line export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" to the startup file yourself. Then make the current terminal read the file, or open a new terminal:

Shell Run zsh (macOS default) source ~/.zshrc bash on Linux source ~/.bashrc bash on macOS source ~/.bash_profile PowerShell Open a new window.

The folder is on your PATH, but the shell hasn't noticed the new command. In zsh, run rehash. In bash, run hash -r.

On Windows, the installer adds the command to the PowerShell window that ran it and to your saved PATH. A PowerShell window that was already open doesn't see it. Open a new window, or run this in the old one:

$env:Path = [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','User') + ';' + [Environment]::GetEnvironmentVariable('Path','Machine')

If the command still isn't found, start ThingStudio by its full path, from the list above.

docs.title: Remove ThingStudio
docs.text: Installation details has the commands for the installer script. To remove a package, delete its folder. Removing never touches your flows or your settings in .thingstudio.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text: When something goes wrong, Debugging & troubleshooting and the FAQ go by what you see on screen. Questions, and what you've built, go in GitHub Discussions. Bugs go on the issue tracker, or use Help → Report a problem.

docs.text: Step 2: tour the editor.

docs.title: Installation details
docs.text: How ThingStudio is packaged, where it puts its files, how to upgrade and remove it, and how to build it from source. Getting started has the install steps.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
Each release has a package for each platform:

Platform Package macOS, Apple Silicon (M1 and later) thingstudio-VERSION-macos-arm64.tar.gz macOS, Intel thingstudio-VERSION-macos-x86_64.tar.gz Linux, x86_64 thingstudio-VERSION-linux-x86_64.tar.gz Linux, ARM 64-bit (Raspberry Pi 4 and 5 on a 64-bit OS) thingstudio-VERSION-linux-aarch64.tar.gz Windows, x86_64 thingstudio-VERSION-windows-x86_64.zip

SHA256SUMS lists each package's checksum. The macOS packages are signed and notarized by Apple. For a version other than the latest, open that release from the releases page.

A package doesn't add a thingstudio command; start it from its folder, or by its full path. To upgrade, replace the folder with a newer one. To remove it, delete the folder. On Linux, add your account to the dialout group (uucp on Arch) yourself to use USB boards.

docs.title: Installer script
docs.text:
On macOS and Linux, the installer puts ThingStudio in ~/.local/share/thingstudio and the thingstudio command in ~/.local/bin. Your settings live in ~/.thingstudio (see The ThingStudio folder).

On Windows, it puts ThingStudio in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Thingstudio and adds the thingstudio command to your PATH. Your settings live in %USERPROFILE%\.thingstudio.

To upgrade, run the installer script again.

docs.title: Remove
docs.text:
To remove ThingStudio on macOS and Linux:

curl -fsSL https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases/latest/download/install.sh | sh -s -- --uninstall

On Windows:

& ([scriptblock]::Create((irm https://github.com/mkarliner/ThingStudio/releases/latest/download/install.ps1))) -Uninstall

Upgrading and removing never touch ~/.thingstudio (%USERPROFILE%\.thingstudio on Windows), or your flows, which are saved wherever you chose. To start again as a new user, move that folder aside as well: it holds your credentials, presets, custom nodes and board definitions.

docs.title: Tutorial flows
docs.text: Every install has a tutorials folder. Tutorial flows says where it is for each route.

docs.title: From source
docs.text:
For working on ThingStudio itself. You need Python 3.10 or later, Node.js 22 (22.23 is known to work, 24.13 isn't), and make. make checks your Node.js before it builds. On a Mac, make comes with the Xcode command line tools (xcode-select --install).

In the repository folder, run make. This builds the editor and the user guide, installs ThingStudio into a .venv folder, and puts the thingstudio-backend command on your PATH. Run make again after updating the repository. It only rebuilds what changed. If your python3 is older than 3.10, name a newer one: make PYTHON=python3.12.

Start it with thingstudio-backend, or make run. On a Mac, start it from Apple's Terminal app. macOS blocks WiFi connections from a copy run from source in other terminals, such as iTerm.

docs.title: Step 3: Install MicroPython
docs.text:
ThingStudio runs on top of MicroPython, so the board needs it first. You install it once per board.

A new board usually doesn't have MicroPython. If yours already has it, or you're not sure, go to step 4. If MicroPython is missing, the console says so when you connect, and links back here.

ThingStudio can install it for you, on the chips it can write.

docs.title: Install from ThingStudio
docs.text:
ThingStudio writes the firmware itself: over a serial port for the ESP32 family, and onto a mounted drive for RP2040, RP2350 and nRF52 boards.

ESP32 without PSRAM? Use a custom image

ESP32 boards without PSRAM can be very tight on memory, as the ESP32's WiFi stack and FreeRTOS take quite a bit of RAM. We strongly suggest that you flash these boards with one of our custom MicroPython images. They include the runtime and the common libraries, and so release significant memory for your flow.

On a classic ESP32 with 4 MB of flash and no PSRAM, an ESP32-C3 or an ESP32-C5, pick ThingStudio custom image as the Firmware when the dialog lists one for the chip. Its Version list holds the published releases. After flashing it, Install runtime writes only the boot script.

The list of builds comes from docs.thingstudio.net, so a new image appears without updating ThingStudio. ThingStudio uses that list only when it carries ThingStudio's signature; offline, it uses the last list it saved, or the one it was installed with. The line under Version says which.

  1. Plug the board into USB. A Pico needs BOOTSEL held while you plug it in.
  2. Choose Tools → Install firmware….
  3. Pick Serial port or Mounted drive, then the port or drive from the list. USB ports come first, shown as the path and the adapter's name (for example /dev/ttyUSB0 -- CH340). If an ESP32 isn't listed, hold BOOT, tap RESET and click ⟳; the line under the list says how many it found. If it still isn't listed, type the path in the box (on macOS a mounted Pico is /Volumes/RPI-RP2).
  4. Pick the Chip family, the Firmware (Official MicroPython (micropython.org) or ThingStudio custom image), the Build and the Version. A board that names its own build is preselected.
  5. Click Flash. Erase all flash first is ticked: it clears an old partition table, which is the usual reason a board doesn't boot after a successful install. The dialog shows each line the tool prints; a failure says what to fix.

The Build matters for the heap as much as for compatibility: an ESP32 with extra PSRAM wants ESP32 with PSRAM (WROVER / SPIRAM), and a single-core SOLO wants ESP32 single-core (SOLO / UNICORE). Only the chip families the editor can write are listed, and only builds whose hash is pinned, so what you flash is what was tested.

The list covers every build ThingStudio pins, so Or use your own image file is only for the rest: a build for a board ThingStudio doesn't list, a chip with no pinned build yet (the ESP32-C5), or an image you downloaded yourself. Pick the .bin or .uf2; the chip family you choose decides the address, and the file's own header usually decides the family. Address, under Install options, overrides the family's address. A ThingStudio custom image for a classic ESP32 needs 0x0 there: see Custom firmware.

Flashing erases the flow and all settings on the board. Afterwards, connect it and install the runtime.

docs.title: Doing it yourself
docs.text: For a chip ThingStudio can't write, or a build it doesn't pin, install MicroPython without the editor.

docs.title: Get the firmware
docs.text:
Download the firmware for your board from micropython.org/download. Pick your exact board if it's listed, or the generic build for your chip:

Chip Generic build File type ESP32 ESP32_GENERIC .bin ESP32-S2 ESP32_GENERIC_S2 .bin ESP32-S3 ESP32_GENERIC_S3 .bin ESP32-C3 ESP32_GENERIC_C3 .bin ESP32-C5 ESP32_GENERIC_C5 .bin RP2040 (Pico, Pico W) RPI_PICO, RPI_PICO_W .uf2 RP2350 (Pico 2, Pico 2 W) RPI_PICO2, RPI_PICO2_W .uf2

For any other chip, see Other microcontrollers.

docs.title: RP2040 and RP2350: drag and drop
docs.text:
Copy the firmware onto the board as a file:

  1. Hold the BOOTSEL button while you plug the board into USB.
  2. A drive called RPI-RP2 (or RP2350) appears.
  3. Copy the .uf2 file onto it.

The board restarts into MicroPython by itself.

docs.title: ESP32 family: esptool
docs.text:
If ThingStudio is connected to the board, click Disconnect first. Only one program can use the board's port at a time. If another program has it open, esptool reports Resource busy or could not open port.

Install esptool once:

pip install esptool

Erase the flash, then write the firmware. ADDRESS depends on the chip:

esptool.py --port PORT erase_flash
esptool.py --port PORT --baud 460800 write_flash ADDRESS firmware.bin
Chip ADDRESS ESP32, ESP32-S2 0x1000 ESP32-S3, ESP32-C3 0 ESP32-C5 0x2000

PORT is the board's serial port. On macOS and Linux it starts with /dev/, on Windows it's COM followed by a number. To find it, run esptool.py flash_id with no --port: esptool searches for the board and prints the port it found.

If esptool can't talk to the board, put it into download mode and try again: hold BOOT, press and release RESET, then release BOOT. Boards with a separate USB-serial chip usually do this by themselves. If writing fails partway, leave out --baud 460800.

Press RESET when it finishes. A board that uses the chip's own USB (most ESP32-S2 and S3 boards) may show up on a different port afterwards.

docs.title: Without a terminal: Thonny
docs.text:
Thonny installs MicroPython on the board through a GUI. Open Tools → Options → Interpreter and use Install or update MicroPython.

When it's done, close Thonny. Like esptool, it needs the board's port to itself.

Thonny can't install MicroPython on an ESP32-C5. It writes the image at 0, but a C5 needs 0x2000, and Thonny doesn't offer that address. The board then restarts in a loop printing invalid header. Use ThingStudio or esptool instead. (Thonny issue #3963)

docs.title: Other microcontrollers
docs.text:
Other chips, such as STM32, nRF or SAMD, each have their own way of installing MicroPython. See your board's page on micropython.org/download and the MicroPython documentation.

Supported hardware lists the chips ThingStudio is tested on. Another chip needs a processor definition: see Other boards.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Step 4: connect your board to ThingStudio.

docs.title: Step 5: Install the runtime
docs.text:
The runtime is the part of ThingStudio that runs on the board: it receives your flows and runs them. Each board needs it once. Libraries that a flow's nodes need are installed later, by Deploy.

  1. Check the board's port is selected in the port list, as in step 4.
  2. Choose Tools → Install runtime…. If you're connected, ThingStudio disconnects first. The console shows progress; set the console's Show menu to Info to see each file.
  3. If the board is busy and doesn't stop, the console asks you to press its reset button. On a board without one, such as a Pico, unplug it and plug it back in.
  4. The board restarts when the install is done. Click Connect. If the port has gone from the list, click ⟳ first.

After upgrading ThingStudio, the board's runtime may no longer match the editor. Deploy then stops, and the console says to install the runtime again.

If the install fails, the console says what the board sent back and what to do. See Board won't connect.

To install the runtime from the command line instead, see Command line.

docs.title: Next
docs.text: Step 6: blink an LED, your first flow.

docs.title: Kitchen-sink board
docs.text: How to wire a test board for the input and output nodes: a potentiometer, a push button and a NeoPixel on a LuatOS ESP32C3-CORE. Tutorials that need hardware beyond an LED use these parts on these pins, so a flow from one tutorial runs on a board wired for another. Wire all of it, or only the parts a tutorial needs.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A LuatOS ESP32C3-CORE, the version with a USB-serial chip (CH343). The version with native USB works too, but needs GPIO 18 and 19 left free.
  • A 10 kΩ potentiometer. Any value from 1 kΩ to 100 kΩ works.
  • A push button.
  • One WS2812 (NeoPixel) LED, on a breakout or as part of a strip.
  • Hookup wire, and a breadboard or stripboard.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
The parts connect to these pins. The header pin is the number on the board's pin list; Pins… in the editor shows where each one is.

Part Connection GPIO Header pin Name in the editor Potentiometer one end — 13 (3V3) wiper (middle) 0 2 POT other end — 1 (GND) Push button one side 3 20 BUTTON other side — 17 (GND) WS2812 DIN 6 22 PIXEL 5V — 16 or 31 (5V) GND — 14 or 32 (GND)

The button needs no resistor: set the ebutton node's pull to up. The board also has two LEDs of its own, LED_D4 (GPIO 12) and LED_D5 (GPIO 13), and the BOOT button (GPIO 9), so a flow can use those with nothing wired.

docs.title: Pick the board
docs.text: Choose Kitchen sink (LuatOS ESP32C3-CORE) from the Board menu. The board reports itself as a generic ESP32-C3, so Auto can't find it. Pin fields then show POT, BUTTON and PIXEL next to their numbers.

docs.title: Check each part
docs.text:
Wire one node to a debug node, or to a neopixel node, and deploy:

  • Potentiometer: an adc node on pin 0. Turning the knob sends readings to the console.
  • Button: an ebutton node on pin 3, pull up. Pressing it sends press and release.
  • NeoPixel: a startup node with payload type number and value 8192 (0x002000), into a neopixel node on pin 6 with count 1. The LED lights dim green.

docs.title: Other pins
docs.text:
To put the parts on other pins, keep these points in mind:

  • Potentiometer: GPIO 0–4 can read a voltage. GPIO 5 can too, but not while WiFi is on.
  • Avoid GPIO 2, 8 and 9: they decide how the board starts. GPIO 11 powers the flash chip.
  • Rename pins by saving a copy of the board's file under a new name: see Adding a board.

docs.title: Node conventions
docs.text: A node moves a message from one point in a flow to the next. These are the rules a custom node follows; the file format itself is in Writing custom nodes.

docs.title: The message
docs.text:
A message is a dict: msg = {'payload': ..., 'topic': ..., <anything else>}.

  • payload is the node's value. It is what the output port's declared type checks against and the one key a generic downstream node reads — debug prints only payload. Put the value you want wired and checked here.
  • topic is a routing string. Set it to a real protocol topic when the node has one, otherwise ''. Don't put the node's own event or state in topic; use a named field instead.
  • anything else rides along under its own name, and only a node written to read that name sees it.

Put one value in payload and leave the rest as named fields. The DHT22 example sends the temperature in payload and the humidity in msg['humidity'].

docs.title: Ports
docs.text: Port types are int, number, bool, string, bytes and any, the same as built-in nodes, with the same wire checks. A declared output type must match what the node puts in payload. Use any when unsure. The ports follow the kind: a source has one output, a transform one input and one or more outputs, and a sink one input. A sink with eventSource set also has one output; see Two-faced nodes.

docs.title: Kind
docs.text:
Every node is one of three kinds:

  • source — makes its own messages: on the intervalMs schedule, when an event fires (eventSource), or once when the flow starts (runOnce).
  • transform — one message in, one or more out. Return the message, or None to stop it.
  • sink — consumes a message and produces nothing, unless it is two-faced.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: A runtime error in your Python is reported from the board, attributed to your node. A transform that returns None stops that message; anything it passes on continues. The full list is under Errors in Writing custom nodes.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
A custom node has the following limits:

  • A polled source's emit runs on a timer. To react to an external event, use an event-driven source: see Event-driven sources.
  • Two instances of the same custom node get independent setup, so don't put two on the same physical resource, such as the same pin.
  • Your Python runs with the same trust as the function node. Read a package before you put it in the folder.

It does not explain how to use a node. Each entry links to the node's page, which says what the node does and what each property means. To build a flow in the editor, start from the node reference. To write or check a flow file without the editor, see Check a flow without the editor and AI authoring.

In a flow file a node's type is thingstudio/ followed by the type shown here: wifi_status is written thingstudio/wifi_status. A property's editor label is the name the node's page uses for it. A port described as "message, payload bool" carries a message whose payload is a bool.

Ports are numbered from 0 in a flow file's edges: [fromNodeId, outputNumber, toNodeId, inputNumber], in the order listed here.

docs.title: A sensor display
docs.text:
Work in progress

This tutorial is being reworked. The example flow runs, but some steps may not match the editor. The GUI nodes it uses are provisional; see GUI nodes.

If you've followed Getting started, you've driven an LED from a flow. This tutorial moves on to a sensor and a screen. You'll read temperature, humidity and pressure from an I2C sensor, show them with their recent history on a three-page touch display, and publish them over MQTT. It's a separate project from the blink tutorials, with its own parts, listed under What you need.

The flow is a bme280 sensor feeding GUI nodes that draw the readings, with an mqtt publish that sends them on.

The finished flow is in the ThingStudio repository: test-flows/gui-headliner-sensor-freenove-s3-4in.flow.json. Open it in one of two ways:

  • Open the finished flow. Download it and open it with File → Open…, then set your own WiFi and MQTT credentials in its config nodes.
  • Build it yourself. Follow the steps below.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
The steps use this hardware and setup:

  • A Freenove ESP32-S3 4.0" touch display (FNK0104S), with MicroPython and the runtime installed (Getting started steps 3 to 5). Pick it by hand in the Board menu. Other boards work too; the pins below are this board's.
  • A BME280 sensor board. A BMP280 also works, without humidity. Wire it to 3V3, GND, SCL 15 and SDA 16, the touch panel's I2C bus.
  • A WiFi network for the clock and MQTT, and an MQTT broker. See Connecting over WiFi.

docs.title: 1. Read the sensor
docs.text:
1. Drag a bme280 onto the canvas. In its I2C bus field, click + and make a bus: bus 0, SCL 15, SDA 16.
  2. Set the bme280's address to 0x76, or 0x77 if your sensor board ties SDO high, and interval (ms) to 5000.

  3. Drag a function node, set outputs to 5, wire the bme280 to it, and use this code:

    p = msg['payload']
t = {'topic': 'temperature', 'payload': p['temperature']}
h = None
if p['humidity'] is not None:   # a BMP280 has no humidity
    h = {'topic': 'humidity', 'payload': p['humidity']}
pr = {'topic': 'pressure', 'payload': p['pressure']}
ok = {'topic': 'sensor', 'payload': True}
return [t, h, pr, pr, ok]

    Each reading goes out on its own output, so each widget gets only its own number. Output 4 is a second copy of the pressure, for its journal. Output 5 says the sensor is alive.

To test the sensor first, wire the bme280 to a debug node and deploy. A reading appears every 5 seconds. See bme280.

docs.title: 2. Show it on the display
docs.text:
1. Drag a display spi onto the canvas and set it for the Freenove panel:

    Property Value controller st7796 frame format rgb565 SPI bus 1 baudrate 40000000 sck, mosi, dc, cs pin 12, 11, 46, 10 reset pin -1 backlight pin 45 width, height 320, 480 rotation 1 orientation 90° clockwise color order BGR invert colors, data latch order on

    Click 💾 to save these as a preset for next time. 2. Drag a gui screen and wire it to the display spi. It takes its width, height and frame format from the display, so the panel's size is set in one place. 3. In the gui screen's touch panel field, click + and make a Touch panel: controller FT6336U, the same I2C bus, address 0x38, width 320, height 480. 4. Drag three gui readout nodes (temperature, humidity, pressure) and a gui light for the sensor. Wire the function's outputs 1, 2, 3 and 5 to them. In each readout, set units, decimals, lowest value and highest value. 5. Lay out the pages: select the gui screen and use the page outline in its properties to add rows of text and readouts. See Laying out pages, which also says why the layout is fixed when the flow compiles.

Set stale after on the readouts and the light. A reading that stops arriving is then dimmed, so a dead sensor looks different from a steady room.

docs.title: 3. Add the history
docs.text:
A journal keeps the recent readings, and a gui histogram draws them.

  1. Wire the temperature output to a journal with seconds per row 10, rows kept 156 and rows per roll-up 6. Wire its first output to a gui histogram. That histogram shows the last 26 minutes.
  2. Wire the journal's second output, one summary per minute, to a second journal with seconds per row 0. Wire that journal to a second gui histogram, which shows the last 2.6 hours.
  3. Wire output 4, the pressure copy, to a journal with seconds per row 60, and that to a third gui histogram.

Each bar is the average of its row, and the thin line runs from the row's min to its max. Set each histogram's bottom at and top at to the range you expect, for example 15 to 30 for temperature. A histograms shows only the rows its journal kept: give the journal at least as many rows kept as the histogram has columns, or the bars fill the right of the card and leave the rest empty — the compiler warns with the number to raise. See Histogram.

docs.title: 4. Add the clock
docs.text:
1. Drag a timer with interval (ms) 1000, and two ntp nodes. Wire the timer to both.
  2. Set one ntp node's format to time and the other's to date. In both, set UTC offset (hours) for your zone's standard time, and daylight saving to UK / EU: automatic if that's where you are, otherwise none. See ntp.
  3. Add two gui label nodes, one for the time with room for (characters) 5, and one for the date with 10. Wire the time ntp node to the first and the date one to the second.
  4. On a new page, give the time label the font font_seg764 (seven-segment digits) and the date font_body24.

Until the board has the time, the labels show --.

docs.title: 5. Turn the pages
docs.text:
Add a gui button with mode navigate to each page, so you can turn the pages by touch. See Buttons.

The finished flow also turns the pages by itself every 8 seconds, with a node that isn't in the palette. Skip it when you build the flow: the buttons turn the pages by touch.

docs.title: 6. Publish the readings
docs.text: Drag three mqtt publish nodes, one per reading, with topics such as thingstudio/headliner/temperature. Wire outputs 1 to 3 of the function to them, and pick your MQTT broker and WiFi. See mqtt publish.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text: Click Compile → Deploy. The display lights, the readings appear within 5 seconds, the histograms fill as the minutes pass, and the clock starts once the board has the time.

docs.title: If it doesn't work
docs.text:
Each symptom below has its own fix:

  • The picture is scrambled: the width and height on the display spi must be the panel's own size, 320 and 480, even when the picture is turned; the gui screen follows them. Deploy checks this and says so.
  • Touches land in the wrong place: see Touch panels.
  • No readings: check the wiring and the address (0x76 or 0x77), and test with a debug node.
  • The clock stays at --: the ntp node's status says why: no WiFi yet, or the NTP server can't be reached. It tries again every 30 seconds.
  • Compile says a node is "disconnected from any source": a widget has nothing wired to it. Wire it, or reload the editor if the wires are there.

docs.title: Supported hardware
docs.text: The boards, processors, displays, touch panels, sensors and other hardware below have built-in support. "Tested" means flows have been deployed and run on that hardware. Pin details for boards and processors are in Boards and processors.

docs.text:
Each board below has a definition: a pin cheat sheet that names the board's own pins, such as its LED, marks the pins that are reserved and why, and lists the pins each SPI and I2C bus can use. Pins… in the editor shows it. See Seeing a board's pins.

The Pyboard is the exception: it installs over DFU, which the editor doesn't offer; see Install MicroPython.

docs.title: Processors without a board definition
docs.text:
Any board with one of these processors can be used by picking the processor from the Board menu, for example ESP32-C3 (any board). Its board-specific pins, such as an LED, aren't labelled.

Processor Tested ESP32 Yes, on the CYD ESP32-S2 Yes, on the LOLIN S2 Mini ESP32-S3 Yes, on the Freenove board ESP32-C3 Yes, on a generic ESP32-C3 board, over USB and WiFi; also on the custom image ESP32-C5 Yes, on the ESP32-C5-340X, over USB; also on the custom image RP2040 Yes, on the Pico and Pico W RP2350 Yes, on the Pico 2 nRF52840 Smoke tested on the Seeed XIAO nRF52840 (Sense)

The ble nodes run on the ESP32, ESP32-S3, ESP32-C3 and ESP32-C5. On other processors Deploy refuses them.

The GUI nodes that draw on these displays are provisional.

Chip Panel sizes Node Tested ST7789 240x240, 135x240, 240x320 display spi Yes, on the CYD ST7796 320x480 display spi Yes, on the Freenove ESP32-S3 4.0" SSD1306 (I2C only) 128x64, or set width and height display i2c Untested

docs.text:
Touch in the GUI nodes is provisional.

Chip Node Tested FT6336U touch Yes, on the Freenove ESP32-S3 4.0"

docs.text:
Chip Node Tested BME280 bme280 Yes, on a Pico BMP280 bme280 Untested

Other I2C devices can be read with a function node and the chip's datasheet.

docs.text: Hardware Node Tested Analog input (the chip's ADC) adc Yes, on the LuatOS ESP32C3-CORE WS2812 / NeoPixel LEDs neopixel Yes, on the LuatOS ESP32C3-CORE

docs.title: Other boards
docs.text:
Other boards that run MicroPython may work. ThingStudio needs a processor definition for the chip, and a board definition if you want the board's own pins labelled.

You can write definition files yourself: Adding a board and Adding a processor describe every field of the JSON. Or an AI assistant can draft one. Point it at the board maker's web page for the board, and it can usually write the file in seconds. For a processor, give it the chip's datasheet. One of the existing files in ~/.thingstudio/boards/ or ~/.thingstudio/processors/ makes a good example to include. Check the result against the datasheet. A missing reserved pin means the compile won't stop a flow that crashes the board.

docs.title: Reporting hardware
docs.text:
Reports on any board, display or sensor, listed or not, are welcome. Open an issue on GitHub with:

  • the board, processor and any display or sensor
  • the MicroPython version
  • what worked and what didn't

A definition file for a new board can be attached to the issue.

docs.title: The ThingStudio folder
docs.text:
ThingStudio keeps its own files in one folder on your computer:

  • macOS and Linux: ~/.thingstudio
  • Windows: %USERPROFILE%\.thingstudio

ThingStudio creates the folder the first time it starts. Your flows are not kept here. They are saved wherever you choose (see Flow lifecycle).

docs.title: What's in it
docs.text:
Folder Holds Edit by hand? credentials/ WiFi and MQTT broker logins, saved by name No, use the editor presets/ Saved node settings, one folder per node type Yes custom-nodes/ Your own node types Yes boards/ Board definitions Yes processors/ Processor definitions Yes

Every file is plain JSON, except the .node.py file of a custom node. The editor reads these folders through the ThingStudio backend, so they aren't available when the editor talks to the board directly over USB.

docs.title: Credentials
docs.text:
A WiFi or MQTT broker config node holds only the name of a credential. The SSID, password, broker address and login are stored in credentials/wifi/<name>.json or credentials/mqtt-broker/<name>.json. This keeps secrets out of flow files you share or commit. Create and edit credentials from the config node (see Config nodes).

The files are not encrypted. Anyone who can read your home folder can read them. Don't commit this folder or copy it to shared storage.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text: A preset is a named set of property values for one node type, such as the pins and size of a display panel. You save and load presets from a node's property panel (see Presets). Each one is a file at presets/<node type>/<name>.json. A file that isn't valid JSON appears in the list disabled, with the file named.

docs.title: Custom nodes
docs.text: A custom node is two files with the same base name: <name>.node.json and <name>.node.py. The first time ThingStudio starts, it puts two examples here. Deleted examples don't come back. See Custom nodes.

docs.title: Boards and processors
docs.text:
At every start, ThingStudio writes the built-in definitions into boards/ and processors/, replacing files of the same name. An upgrade's changes therefore arrive on the next start.

  • To keep your own version of a built-in, save it under a different name (for example my-cyd.json). It is then a board or processor of its own, and is never overwritten.
  • Editing a built-in file in place works until the next start, when the built-in replaces it.

See Boards and processors.

docs.title: Using a different folder
docs.text:
Start ThingStudio with --data-dir:

thingstudio --data-dir ~/projects/greenhouse/thingstudio-data

This keeps separate sets of credentials, presets and custom nodes, for example one per project.

docs.title: Tutorial flows
docs.text:
If you'd rather not build the tutorial flows from scratch, or you get stuck, their finished flow files are in the tutorials folder, below. Open one with File → Open…. Each entry below says what the flow shows and what to change first.

You'll need to change the flow to match your WiFi setup, and the actual pins that devices, like LEDs, are connected to on your board. If your board is one of those that already have a definition file made for it, you can set it in the Board drop-down (Boards and processors).

docs.title: Where the folder is
docs.text:
Every install has a tutorials folder. Where it is depends on how you installed:

Install Examples folder Installer script, macOS and Linux ~/.local/share/thingstudio/current/tutorials Installer script, Windows %LOCALAPPDATA%\Thingstudio\versions\thingstudio-VERSION-windows-x86_64\tutorials Package tutorials, inside the folder you unpacked From source tutorials, in the repository folder

The Windows path contains the version, so it changes when you upgrade.

docs.title: Before you deploy
docs.text:
• Pins are examples. Set your board's pin in the property panel. Pins… next to the Board menu lists the pins your board has.
  • A flow with a WiFi or MQTT node holds no passwords. The network name, password and broker address are kept in a saved credential on your computer, never in the flow file. Open the node's WiFi or MQTT Broker field and click ✎: fill in your own details and save, or pick one you have already saved from the drop-down. See The ThingStudio folder.

docs.title: The flows
docs.text: In the order that builds up. Each entry lists what to try changing first, and where to read about the node.

docs.title: blink.flow.json
docs.text:
A timer counts, a function turns the count into on and off, and gpio out drives the LED. Walked by Blink an LED.

  • pin on gpio out: your LED's GPIO number. The file has 15.
  • interval (ms) on timer: each tick toggles the LED, so the blink rate follows.
  • The function node's code, which keeps the count's parity with % 2.

docs.title: two-more-blinks.flow.json
docs.text:
The same blink with the state kept elsewhere. This file reads the LED's pin back with machine.Pin to decide the next level. Walked by Two more blinks, which also swaps in the context version.

  • The pin number, in two places: the gpio out node's pin and the function's machine.Pin(15). They have to agree.
  • The function node's code: replace it with the context version from the tutorial.

docs.title: http-blink.flow.json
docs.text:
The same LED, toggled from a browser. An http in node serves /toggle on port 9999, a function flips the LED and builds the reply, and http response answers the browser. wifi status and debug show the connection. It needs a WiFi network of yours. Walked by Web Blink.

  • path and port on http in.
  • The reply text in the function's code ('LED on' and 'LED off').
  • poll interval (ms) on wifi status.

docs.title: blink-from-anywhere.flow.json
docs.text:
The same LED through an MQTT broker. Clicking inject publishes pressed to a button topic, and mqtt subscribe on an led topic feeds a function that turns on, 1 or true into true for gpio out; debug prints what arrives. It needs a WiFi network and a broker of yours. Its topics start thingstudio/change-this-number/: replace that number in both before you deploy, because the broker is public. Walked by Blink from anywhere.

  • The number in both topic fields, on mqtt publish and mqtt subscribe.
  • host and port in the broker form, to use a broker on your own network.
  • The function node's code, which decides which messages count as on.

The repository's test-flows/ folder holds more flows, written for trying one node at a time on a board. They aren't installed.

docs.title: Flows written by an AI assistant
docs.text: An assistant can write a flow file for you to open the same way. See Writing flows with an AI assistant.

docs.title: Connecting over WiFi
docs.text: The editor can connect to a board over WiFi instead of USB. Once connected over WiFi, everything works the same as over USB: deploy, the console, Tools → Check status, and clicking an inject node.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text:
• A board with WiFi and the ThingStudio runtime. Plain Raspberry Pi Pico and Pico 2 boards have no WiFi.
  • A flow on the board that uses WiFi and has joined your network. The board is only reachable while that flow is running. It starts again by itself after a reset.
  • A board password, set over USB.
  • This computer on the same network as the board.
  • On a Mac, ThingStudio started from Apple's Terminal app. See If it doesn't connect.

docs.title: Set the password and name
docs.text:
1. Connect the board over USB.
  2. Choose Tools → Board settings…. The top line names the board these settings apply to: its chip, USB port and current name.
  3. Enter a network name and a password of 8 to 64 characters, then click Save to board.

The name and password are stored on the board, not in the flow. The editor also remembers the password on this computer. A board with no password only accepts USB.

A new name is used from the next time the board joins WiFi. Reset the board to use it straight away.

docs.title: Connect
docs.text:
Click ⟳ next to the port list. Boards on your network appear in the port menu under WiFi. Pick one and click Connect.

If the board isn't listed, choose WiFi address… and type its name (for example kitchen or kitchen.local) or its IP address.

If this computer has no saved password for the board, the editor asks for it.

A board with no password is listed as no password set. It won't accept a WiFi connection until you set one.

Connected over USB, the console says whether the board can take a WiFi connection now:

[wifi] kitchen is on a network at 192.168.1.42 (kitchen.local): you can connect over WiFi
[wifi] kitchen is not on a network: WiFi connects need a running flow that joins one

docs.title: Good to know
docs.text:
• Only one editor can connect over WiFi at a time.
  • Board settings can only be changed over USB.
  • Installing the runtime and Tools → Remove flow… need USB.
  • If the board loses power or leaves WiFi range, the editor shows it disconnected within about 30 seconds.
  • Deploying a flow that doesn't use WiFi takes the board off the network at its next reset.
  • The password is never sent over the network, but the connection isn't encrypted. Use it on a network you trust.

docs.title: If it doesn't connect
docs.text:
The console says what went wrong:

  • No route to host (Mac): macOS is blocking local network access. The first time ThingStudio reaches for the network, macOS asks whether it may find devices on your local network; choose Allow, then click Connect again (the attempt that raised the question can fail). If you chose Don't Allow, turn thingstudio-python on in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Local Network, then restart ThingStudio. When running from source (thingstudio-backend), macOS may block it without asking: start it from Apple's Terminal app instead, which macOS always allows.
  • No answer: check the board is on, its flow has joined WiFi, and this computer is on the same network. If a .local name doesn't work, try the IP address, shown in the console when you connect over USB.
  • Wrong password: the editor asks again. To change it, connect over USB and use Tools → Board settings….
  • Already has a network session: another editor is connected. Disconnect it first.
  • No password set or Connection refused: the board has no password, so it only accepts USB. Set one over USB in Tools → Board settings…, then click ⟳.
  • Board not listed: click ⟳ again. If it's still missing, check its flow has joined WiFi, or use WiFi address…. If the console says the WiFi scan didn't run, the reason follows; on a Mac it's usually the Local Network permission (see No route to host above).

docs.title: WiFi provisioning
docs.text: You can leave a flow's WiFi network and password out, and enter them on the board when it first starts. Use this for a board you hand to someone else, or one that goes on a network you don't have the password for.

docs.title: Turning it on
docs.text:
In the flow's WiFi config, set security to Unmanaged and leave the credential blank. See Config nodes. Deploy as usual.

A flow with MQTT nodes can't use Unmanaged: an MQTT node connects to the network itself, so the network's name and password must be in the flow.

docs.title: Entering the network on the board
docs.text:
When the board starts with no saved network, it opens its own WiFi network, Thingstudio-Setup-XXXX, with the password thingstudio:

  1. Connect a phone or laptop to Thingstudio-Setup-XXXX. Most phones open the setup page by themselves. If not, browse to http://192.168.4.1/.
  2. Pick your network from the list, or type its name. Some boards' scans miss nearby networks, so typing always works.
  3. Enter the password and submit.

Once the board connects, it saves the network and joins it on every later start. If nobody enters a network within 10 minutes, the board carries on starting without WiFi.

docs.title: Reopening setup when WiFi fails
docs.text:
By default, setup only runs while no network is saved. If the saved network later becomes unreachable, the board stays disconnected.

Tick Allow reprovisioning on connect failure in the WiFi config to reopen the setup network whenever the saved network fails. Only do this on a network you control: while the setup network is open, anyone in range who knows its password can point the board at a different network.

docs.title: Changing the setup network's password
docs.text:
There's no field for it in the editor. Connect to the board and type this in the command box under the console (see Commands and the Python prompt):

import wifi_provision; wifi_provision.set_ap_password('yournewpassword')

Then choose Tools → Reset board (hard). Use at least 8 characters: with fewer, the setup network doesn't open. Set it to 'thingstudio' to go back to the default.

docs.title: Starting over
docs.text:
To make the board forget its saved network and run setup again, type this in the command box, then reset the board:

import os; os.remove('/_wifi_provision.json')

This also clears a changed setup password.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Every port has a type: int, number, bool, string, bytes or any. The editor refuses a wire between types that don't fit. What each input type accepts:

Input Accepts wires from any any output bool any output. The value is tested with Python's bool(). number number, int, string int int, string string string bytes bytes, any

A string that isn't a number fails on the board when it reaches a number or int input, with a NODE_ERROR. An any output, such as the output of a function node, connects only to any, bool and bytes inputs.

An input can take any number of wires. The node runs once for each message that arrives, whichever wire it came on. An output can feed any number of inputs.

When an output feeds more than one wire, the first wire gets the message itself and each other wire gets a copy, made before any of them runs. The wires then run one after another, in the order they were drawn. The copy is shallow: a list or dict inside the message is shared, so a node that changes msg['payload'] in place, rather than replacing it, changes it for the other wires too.

docs.title: Typed values
docs.text:
Some nodes take a value you type next to a type you pick: inject and startup (payload type and value), and change (literal type and value / source property). The value is read as that type:

  • bool: true is True. Anything else is False, including True and 1.
  • number: a whole number becomes an int, any other number a float. An empty value is 0. Write numbers in decimal: 0x2000 is not a number.
  • string: sent as typed.

With type number, a value that isn't a number stops the deploy for change. For inject and startup it fails on the board when the node fires, with a [NODE_ERROR].

docs.title: Giving a node a flow label
docs.text:
Every node has a flow label field at the top of its property panel. Type something, say Fire!, and the canvas shows it instead of the node's name. Leave it blank to show the name again. Console messages and errors that name the node use the flow label too.

A gui button also has a board label, the text drawn on the button. If the board label is blank, the button shows the flow label.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text:
A preset is a named set of property values, such as the pins and size of one display panel. display spi, display i2c and the Touch panel config have a preset menu at the top of their property panel:

  • Pick a preset to copy its values into the node's properties.
  • Click 💾 to save the current values as a preset, under a name you choose.
  • Click ↻ to read the preset files again.

Applying a preset copies the values once. Later changes to the node or the preset don't affect each other.

Each preset is a JSON file in ~/.thingstudio/presets/<node type>/, which you can also write by hand. A file that isn't valid JSON appears in the menu disabled, with the file named. See The ThingStudio folder.

docs.title: Config nodes
docs.text:
A config node holds settings that several nodes share. A node's property panel has a field to pick one; ✎ edits it and + makes a new one. The config nodes are:

  • WiFi: a saved credential and a security mode: password, open, or unmanaged.
  • MQTT Broker: a saved credential holding the host, port and optional username and password. One per flow.
  • I2C bus: the bus number, SCL and SDA pins, and frequency. See I2C bus.
  • BLE: the board's Bluetooth name. Optional; one per flow. See BLE.
  • BLE peer: a Bluetooth LE device the board connects to, by address or name. One per device. See BLE peer.
  • Touch panel: the touch controller, its I2C bus and address, and its size and orientation. See Touch panels.

The WiFi and MQTT Broker configs hold only the name of a saved credential. The SSID, passwords and broker address are saved by name in ~/.thingstudio/credentials/, not in the flow file, so a flow you share or commit holds no secrets. Two flows that use the same credential share its values: edit it once and both change.

Pick a saved WiFi network or broker from the field's list. ✎ opens the saved values, such as a broker's host, port and login, with the config's other settings; Save stores them and Cancel discards the changes. + makes a new one: give it a name, fill it in and save. If a flow names a credential that isn't saved on this computer, ✎ says so, and saving creates it. See The ThingStudio folder.

A flow has one WiFi network and one MQTT broker. Every node that uses WiFi has a WiFi field, and every MQTT node an MQTT Broker field. They all show the flow's one setting: change it on one node and it changes on all. A flow doesn't need a wifi status node to use the network.

docs.title: Node status
docs.text:
Some nodes show a colored dot and a line of text under the node while the editor is connected to the board:

Dot Meaning Green connected Amber connecting Gray disconnected Red error

The dot shows what the board reports, not the editor's guess. It appears once the running flow first reports, and clears on every deploy until the new flow reports.

These nodes report a status: wifi status, mqtt publish, mqtt subscribe, ntp, i2c device, bme280, touch and a gui screen with a touch panel. adc and neopixel report only a failed read or write, as a red dot. A custom node reports one if its code does.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: The Notes panel on the right is free text about the flow: what it does, what to wire up, how to use it. It's saved in the flow file, and opens by itself when you open a flow that has notes. File → New flow clears it.

docs.title: Event-driven programming
docs.text: An event-driven program waits for things to happen, and runs a piece of code for each one. A button press, a timer tick and an incoming network message are all events. The code that handles one is often called a handler.

docs.title: The loop you may know
docs.text:
Most microcontroller programs start as a loop:

while True:
    if button.value() == 0:
        led.on()
    temperature = sensor.read()
    time.sleep(0.1)

Every job lives inside the loop, and each one waits for the others. A slow sensor read delays the button check. A sleep long enough to pace one job stalls all of them. Adding a job means reworking the timing of the rest.

docs.title: The same program, as events
docs.text:
Written as events, each job stands on its own:

  • when the button pin falls, turn the LED on
  • every 10 seconds, read the sensor

Nothing is checked in a loop. The board sleeps until an event arrives, runs its handler, and waits again. Jobs with different timing don't get in each other's way.

docs.title: How ThingStudio does it
docs.text:
ThingStudio is built on asyncio, MicroPython's built-in module for event-driven programming. It provides an event loop: one scheduler that runs many tasks, switching between them whenever one is waiting.

In ThingStudio, each chain of nodes that starts at a source (a timer, an interrupt, an mqtt subscribe) is one handler. When you deploy, the flow is turned into MicroPython code in which each source becomes an asyncio task. While one task waits, for a timer or the network, the others run.

docs.title: The one rule: don't block
docs.text:
Everything shares one event loop. A handler that stops and waits without handing control back stops every other handler too. In a function node, that means no time.sleep() and no long loops.

To wait, use a node built for it: delay waits, timer repeats. They hand control back while they wait. Inside a function node, await asyncio.sleep(1) does the same:

await asyncio.sleep(1)
return msg

docs.title: More
docs.text:
Further reading:

  • MicroPython's asyncio
  • Peter Hinch's asyncio tutorial for MicroPython

docs.title: Flows, nodes and messages
docs.text: A ThingStudio program is a flow: a set of nodes joined by wires. You build it by dragging nodes onto a canvas and wiring them together, rather than writing a program top to bottom.

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
A node does one job. Most fall into three kinds:

  • Sources start things off: timer fires on an interval, interrupt fires when a pin changes, mqtt subscribe fires when a message arrives.
  • Transforms change or filter what passes through: function, filter, delay.
  • Sinks do something at the end: gpio out switches a pin, display spi draws, mqtt publish sends.

Each node has properties, set in the editor's property panel: a pin number, an interval, a topic.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text:
Nodes pass messages along wires. A message is a Python dict with two standard keys:

  • payload: the main value, such as a reading, a count or a string
  • topic: a short label saying what the message is about
{'payload': 21.5, 'topic': 'kitchen/temperature'}

Nodes may add other keys. A node reads the ones it needs and passes the rest on.

docs.title: Wires
docs.text:
A wire joins an output to an input. One output can feed several inputs, and each gets its own copy of the message. Several outputs can feed one input, and the node runs once per message, whichever wire it came in on.

Each port has a type, such as int, number, bool, string or any. The editor refuses a wire between ports whose types don't fit.

docs.title: Config nodes
docs.text: Settings that several nodes share, like a WiFi network or an MQTT broker, live in a config node. You set it up once and pick it from each node that uses it. See Editor in depth.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: Node-and-wire programming has a long history, from J. Paul Morrison's flow-based programming to tools like LabVIEW, Max and Node-RED. ThingStudio follows Node-RED's version of the idea, with the same message shape and very similar nodes.

docs.title: MicroPython
docs.text: MicroPython is a version of Python 3 made to run on microcontrollers. It fits in hundreds of kilobytes and runs directly on the chip, with no operating system underneath.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
You flash MicroPython onto the board once, like any firmware. After that the board runs Python files from its own filesystem, and gives you a Python prompt, the REPL, over USB. You can type Python at the board and see the result at once.

MicroPython keeps most of the Python language and part of its standard library. It adds modules for hardware: machine for pins, I2C, SPI and PWM, network for WiFi, and asyncio for running several tasks at once.

from machine import Pin
led = Pin(15, Pin.OUT)
led.on()

docs.title: The limits
docs.text: Microcontrollers are limited. A board typically has hundreds of kilobytes of RAM, and MicroPython itself uses some of it. Python is also much slower than C, though fast enough for most sensing, switching and networking jobs.

docs.title: Where ThingStudio fits
docs.text:
ThingStudio runs on top of MicroPython. It installs a runtime onto the board, and turns each flow you deploy into MicroPython code. The function node runs your own MicroPython. See installing MicroPython to get it onto your board.

If you already use MicroPython, see if you know MicroPython for how ThingStudio uses your board.

docs.title: More
docs.text:
Further reading:

  • MicroPython documentation
  • MicroPython quick reference for ESP32 and for RP2

docs.title: Node-RED
docs.text: Node-RED is a free tool for wiring together devices, web services and APIs. You build programs, called flows, in a browser by dragging nodes onto a canvas and wiring them up. It was created at IBM in 2013 and is now an OpenJS Foundation project.

docs.title: What people use it for
docs.text: Node-RED is popular for home automation and IoT. A typical flow might take sensor readings from MQTT, check them, store them in a database and send an alert when something is out of range. It has thousands of add-on nodes and a dashboard for building web UIs.

docs.title: Where it runs
docs.text: Node-RED runs on Node.js, on a server, a PC or a Raspberry Pi. Microcontrollers usually talk to it over the network, often by MQTT, and run their own separate firmware.

docs.title: Where ThingStudio fits
docs.text:
ThingStudio takes Node-RED's way of working onto the microcontroller. The flow runs on the board itself, so the board doesn't need a server to decide what to do. The two work well together: a ThingStudio board can publish readings over MQTT to a Node-RED flow on your server.

If you already use Node-RED, see if you know Node-RED for what's different.

docs.title: More
docs.text:
Further reading:

  • Node-RED concepts
  • Node-RED getting started

docs.title: If you know Arduino and C
docs.text: If you've written setup() and loop() in C or C++, ThingStudio will feel different in three ways. It uses Python rather than C, you wire events together instead of writing a loop, and a change goes to the board in seconds without reflashing.

docs.title: Python instead of C
docs.text:
The board runs MicroPython, which you flash once in place of an Arduino sketch. Your own code, in function nodes and custom nodes, is Python.
