Python is slower than C and uses more memory. That's fine for sensing, switching, displays and networking. It's the wrong tool for tight timing, such as bit-banging a protocol at microsecond precision or sampling at high rates.

docs.title: Events instead of a loop
docs.text:
There's no loop(). Each job is its own chain of nodes, started by an event: a timer, a pin change, a network message. Jobs don't wait for each other. See event-driven programming.

The interrupt node works like attachInterrupt(). The difference is that your code runs safely in the main program, not inside the interrupt, so you can do anything there.

docs.title: No compile-and-flash cycle
docs.text: The firmware stays the same. Deploying a flow sends a compiled file to the board, over USB or WiFi, and the board swaps it in. Changing a flow and trying it again takes seconds.

docs.title: What stays the same
docs.text:
ThingStudio checks your pin numbers against the board before deploying, and refuses pins that would crash it, such as those wired to the flash chip. See boards and processors.

Next: getting started.

docs.title: If you know MicroPython
docs.text: ThingStudio sits on top of the MicroPython you already have. It doesn't replace your firmware. It adds a runtime and a way to write programs as flows, while the REPL and your own Python stay within reach.

docs.title: What goes on the board
docs.text:
Tools → Install runtime… copies a set of Python files onto the board's filesystem, including a main.py that starts the ThingStudio runtime at boot. The runtime listens on USB or WiFi for the editor, and runs the last flow you deployed.

If your board already has a main.py of your own, copy it off first.

docs.title: What a flow becomes
docs.text:
When you deploy, the editor turns the flow into MicroPython source. Each source node, such as a timer or an interrupt, becomes an asyncio task. The other nodes become async functions that each task calls in turn. The editor compiles the result to .mpy bytecode with mpy-cross and sends it to the board, which swaps it in without a reset. Compiling on your computer means the board never needs RAM for the compiler.

The board saves the flow and runs it again after a restart.

docs.title: Your own code
docs.text:
• Function nodes run your Python on each message. They're called from the event loop, so don't block: no time.sleep(), no long loops. See event-driven programming.
  • Custom nodes turn your own code, such as a sensor driver, into a node with its own properties. See writing custom nodes.

docs.title: The REPL
docs.text: The command box under the editor's console runs Python on the board while the flow runs, for checks like gc.mem_free(). For the full >>> prompt, click Stop flow & open prompt. To use Thonny or mpremote, click Disconnect first. See commands and the Python prompt.

docs.title: Memory
docs.text:
A flow, its nodes and the runtime all share the board's RAM. If a deploy fails for lack of space, the console says so. See debugging.

Next: getting started.

docs.title: If you know Node-RED
docs.text: Most of what you know carries over. You drag nodes onto a canvas, wire them, set properties and click Deploy. Messages carry payload and topic. Config nodes hold shared settings like an MQTT broker. The differences come from where the flow runs: on a microcontroller, not on a server.

docs.title: Where the flow runs
docs.text: The editor runs on your computer, but the flow runs on the board. Deploy compiles the flow to MicroPython and sends it to the board, which then runs on its own. Close the editor, unplug the USB cable, and the flow carries on.

docs.title: Function nodes are Python
docs.text:
Function nodes run MicroPython, not JavaScript. A message is a Python dict, so write msg['payload'], not msg.payload.

if msg['payload'] > 30:
    msg['topic'] = 'alarm'
    return msg

Much else is the same. return msg passes the message on, and returning nothing stops it. Return a list to route to several outputs. context.get()/context.set() and flow.get()/flow.set() work as you'd expect. There's no global, since there's only one flow. See the function node.

Don't use time.sleep() in a function node. It stops the whole board, not only that node. Use await asyncio.sleep() or a delay node instead. See event-driven programming.

docs.title: Messages
docs.text: A message carries a payload and usually a topic; the built-in nodes that start a flow set topic to an empty string. Ports also have types, such as int, bool and string, and the editor refuses a wire between types that don't fit. See Editor in depth.

docs.title: Nodes
docs.text:
The palette is smaller, and made for hardware. timer, interrupt, gpio out, pwm out and the sensor and display nodes work with the board directly. inject, debug, function and delay will look familiar, and so will the network nodes: mqtt publish, mqtt subscribe, http request, http in, http response, udp send and udp receive.

A flow has one MQTT broker and one WiFi network, set on any MQTT or WiFi node and shared by all of them. Node-RED's broker per node doesn't carry over. See Config nodes.

You add node types by writing a JSON file and a Python file. See writing custom nodes.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text: debug output appears in the editor's console, not a sidebar. An error in one node is reported in the console, saying which node, and the rest of the flow keeps running. See debugging.

docs.title: Using both
docs.text:
Node-RED is the better place for dashboards, databases and cloud services. A common setup is ThingStudio boards publishing over MQTT to a Node-RED flow on a server or Raspberry Pi.

Next: getting started.

docs.title: Node reference
docs.text: Every built-in node has its own page, covering what it does, its properties and its output. This page lists them all, grouped as in the editor's palette: General, Network and Hardware.

docs.title: Kinds of node
docs.text:
Each node is one of three kinds. The kind decides where it can sit in a flow.

  • Source: starts a message. Has no input. Every chain in a flow begins with one.
  • Transform: takes a message in, and passes it on, changed, delayed or not at all.
  • Sink: takes a message in and acts on it. Has no output.

See flows, nodes and messages for how they fit together.

docs.title: Which node do I need?
docs.text: To… Use do something at a fixed interval timer do something once, when the flow starts startup send a test message by hand inject respond to a pin changing interrupt, eswitch respond to presses, long presses and double clicks ebutton read an analog input adc read a rotary knob encoder drive an LED strip neopixel switch an LED or relay gpio out dim an LED or set a motor's speed pwm out read a temperature, humidity or pressure sensor bme280 talk to another I2C device, or find its address i2c device draw on a display display spi, display i2c show readings as pages on a display GUI nodes change a message, or decide where it goes function set or clear a value between messages change send only changes, or limit the rate filter keep a number's history and show its histogram journal show the time of day ntp wait before passing a message on delay see what's in a message debug send or receive MQTT messages mqtt publish, mqtt subscribe call a web API http request serve a web page or API from the board http in and http response send or receive UDP packets udp send, udp receive read BLE beacons and sensors ble scan broadcast a reading over Bluetooth ble advertise let a phone, computer or another board read or set a value ble characteristic out, ble characteristic in send and receive text with a Bluetooth terminal app ble uart in, ble uart out read from, write to, or listen to a BLE sensor or another board ble read, ble write, ble notify know when WiFi connects or drops wifi status stop messages while WiFi is down wifi gate

docs.title: General
docs.text:
Nodes that don't need a network or hardware:

Node Kind What it does inject source Sends one message with a fixed payload when you click it in the editor. startup source Sends one message each time the flow starts. timer source Sends a rising count at a fixed interval. function transform Runs your own MicroPython on each message. delay transform Passes each message on after a set wait. filter transform Passes a message on only if it changed enough, or enough time has passed. change transform Sets or deletes one message property or flow variable. journal transform Keeps the recent history of a number as average, min and max rows, for a histogram. debug sink Prints a message to the editor's console.

docs.title: Network
docs.text:
These nodes share the flow's WiFi network. A flow has one, set on any WiFi node's WiFi field.

Node Kind What it does wifi status source Reports when the WiFi connection comes up or goes down. wifi gate transform Passes a message on only while WiFi is connected. ntp in and out Sets the board's clock from the internet and sends the time. mqtt subscribe source Sends a message for each MQTT message on a topic. mqtt publish sink Publishes a message's payload to an MQTT topic. http request transform Makes an HTTP request per message and passes on the response. http in source Serves HTTP from the board, sending a message for each request. http response sink Answers a request that arrived through http in. udp receive source Sends a message for each UDP packet received on a port. udp send sink Sends a message's payload as a UDP packet.

docs.title: Bluetooth
docs.text:
These nodes need a board with Bluetooth LE: ESP32, ESP32-S3, ESP32-C3 or ESP32-C5. They share the board's one radio.

Node Kind What it does ble scan source Sends a message for each Bluetooth LE advertisement nearby. ble advertise sink Advertises the board's name and a payload over Bluetooth LE. ble characteristic in source Sends a message when a connected device writes a characteristic. ble characteristic out sink Sets a characteristic a connected device can read, and notifies it. ble uart in source Receives text lines from a Bluetooth terminal app. ble uart out sink Sends text to a Bluetooth terminal app. ble read transform Reads a characteristic of another BLE device. ble write sink Writes to a characteristic of another BLE device. ble notify source Sends each value another BLE device notifies.

The board's Bluetooth name is set once, in the BLE config. The devices the board connects to are BLE peers.

docs.title: Hardware
docs.text:
Pin numbers are checked against your board before a deploy. See boards and processors.

Node Kind What it does interrupt source Fires the moment a pin changes. eswitch source Reports a debounced switch opening or closing. ebutton source Reports presses, releases, long presses and double clicks. adc source Reads an analog pin, sending when the reading moves past its bounds. encoder source Reports a rotary knob's value as it turns. neopixel sink Lights a WS2812 / NeoPixel strip. gpio out sink Sets a pin high or low. pwm out sink Drives a pin with a variable duty cycle. bme280 source Reads a BME280 or BMP280 sensor at a fixed interval. i2c device transform Reads, writes or scans an I2C device that has no node of its own. display spi sink Sends a frame to an SPI color display (ST7789). display i2c sink Sends a frame to an I2C OLED display (SSD1306).

docs.title: Hardware is shared
docs.text:
Each pin, PWM output, I2C bus and SPI bus is set up once, and every node that uses it shares that one setup. Two nodes can use the same pin only if they set it up the same way. For example, an interrupt and an eswitch can both read an input pin with no pull, but a gpio out can't drive a pin an eswitch reads. When two nodes clash, the compile stops and names both.

A function or custom node gets the same objects with runtime.shared(), for example runtime.shared('i2c', 0).

docs.title: Shared settings
docs.text:
Some settings are set once and shared by the nodes that use them:

  • WiFi network and MQTT broker: config nodes, with the real passwords kept outside the flow file. See config nodes.
  • I2C bus: the pins and clock for a bus, shared by every I2C node on it. See I2C bus.
  • BLE: the board's Bluetooth name, shared by the ble nodes. See BLE.
  • BLE peer: a device the board connects to, shared by the nodes that use it. See BLE peer.
  • Touch panel: the controller, bus and size of a touch screen, used by a gui screen or a touch node. See touch panels.

docs.title: Something missing?
docs.text: A function node covers most gaps: a comparison, a sum, a calculation on a reading. For something you'll use again, write a custom node.

docs.title: adc
docs.text: Reads an analog pin, and sends the reading when it moves past the set bounds, and at a fixed interval if one is set.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• pin — the ADC pin. Default 34. Kitchen-sink board shows a potentiometer wired to one.
  • mode — what counts as a change. Default relative.
    • relative — the reading has moved more than delta from the last one sent.
    • absolute — the reading crosses lower or upper: out of the range, or back into it (see sense).
  • delta (counts) — for relative. Default 2000. Must be 1 or more.
  • lower / upper — for absolute, in counts from 0 to 65535. Defaults 0 and 50000. lower must be less than upper.
  • sense — for absolute: outside to send when the reading leaves the range, inside to send when it comes back. Default outside. Leave it at outside in relative mode.
  • poll (ms) — also send the reading at least this often. Default 0, which sends only on a change.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — none. adc is a source.

Output — a message with payload a dict, and topic an empty string:

{'raw': 31250, 'volts': 1.572, 'percent': 47.7}

raw is the reading, 0 to 65535. volts is the pin voltage, to 3 decimal places; on a board that can't measure it, it is worked out as raw over 65535 times 3.3 V. percent is raw as a percentage of 65535, to 1 decimal place.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
A raw reading is noisy, so relative with a delta of a few thousand counts suits most sensors. absolute suits an alarm or a threshold.

In absolute mode the node sends once per crossing. After a message it waits for the reading to go back to the other side before it can send again, so a reading that stays outside sends nothing more. If the reading is already on the sense side when the flow starts, the first message goes out at once.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• The pin can't be read. The node's status dot turns red with the error, and the reading is dropped. See Node status.
  • An ESP32 ADC2 pin in a flow that uses WiFi. Deploy stops: ADC2 can't be read while WiFi is on. Use an ADC1 pin.
  • lower is not less than upper, in absolute mode. Deploy stops with adc lower (100) must be less than upper (50).
  • A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently. Deploy stops and says why. See What gets checked and Hardware is shared.

docs.title: ble advertise
docs.text: Advertises over Bluetooth LE: the board's name, and each message's payload as manufacturer or service data.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• payload goes in — manufacturer data, service data, or nothing (name only). Default manufacturer data.
  • manufacturer id — for manufacturer data, in decimal or hex. Default 0xFFFF, which is reserved for testing; a product uses its maker's id from the Bluetooth SIG.
  • service UUID — for service data: 16-bit (fcd2 is BTHome) or 128-bit. Default fcd2.
  • interval (ms) — how often the advertisement is sent, 20 to 10240. Default 500. Shorter is found faster and uses more power.
  • BLE — the flow's BLE config, whose name is advertised. Without one, the name is thingstudio.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — payload replaces the data: bytes as they are, text as UTF-8. With nothing (name only) it's ignored. Pack a number with struct.pack in a function node first, for example struct.pack('<h', round(t * 100)). Unwired, the node advertises the name only.

This node has no output.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The board advertises the name from the moment the flow starts. Each message replaces the data, and the board sends the new advertisement until the next one. Phones and computers (nRF Connect, for example) and other boards with a ble scan node see it without connecting. When the flow also has characteristic or UART nodes, the advertisement accepts connections, so other devices can connect to them.

An advertisement holds 31 bytes. The flags take 3, the name its length plus 2, and the data's header 4 (manufacturer or 16-bit service) or 18 (128-bit service). The node's status says how many are left for the payload.

A flow has one ble advertise node. It runs on the processors Supported hardware lists for the ble nodes.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A name with no room left for data, a bad id or UUID, a second ble advertise node, or a board without the ble nodes stops the deploy. A payload that isn't bytes or text, or that doesn't fit, is reported on the console with its size, and the board keeps sending the last advertisement.

Anyone nearby can read an advertisement. Don't put anything private in it.

docs.title: ble characteristic in
docs.text: Sends a message each time a connected device writes a Bluetooth LE characteristic.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• service UUID — the service the characteristic belongs to: 16-bit (181a) or 128-bit. Required. Use the same service on the nodes for its other characteristics.
  • characteristic UUID — 16-bit (2a6e) or 128-bit. Required.
  • encoding — how the bytes written become payload: bytes, text (UTF-8), int8, uint8, int16, uint16, int32, uint32 or float32, little-endian. Default bytes. It also sets the output's type, so a number encoding can wire into a number input.
  • BLE — the flow's BLE config, for the board's name. Optional.

For your own service, pick a random 128-bit UUID (an online UUID generator, or python3 -c "import uuid; print(uuid.uuid4())"). 16-bit UUIDs belong to services the Bluetooth SIG has defined.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — none. ble characteristic in is a source.

Output — payload is the value. The message also carries conn, the connection's number, and uuid, the characteristic.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The board becomes a GATT server when a flow has any characteristic or UART node. It advertises its name, accepts connections, and starts advertising again when a device disconnects. Any Bluetooth LE device that can connect and write works: an app on a phone or a computer, such as nRF Connect, or another board's ble write node. All the flow's characteristics are registered once, when the flow starts. Pair a ble characteristic out with the same UUIDs to make one characteristic a connected device can read, write and subscribe to.

A connected device can write up to 244 bytes at a time. A node keeps up to 20 writes waiting; if they come faster than the flow handles them, the oldest are dropped.

The node's status shows advertising, no one connected or 1 connected.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A missing or malformed UUID, two nodes using one characteristic with different encodings, or a board without the ble nodes stops the deploy. A write that doesn't decode (2 bytes sent to an int32, text that isn't UTF-8) is reported on the console with its size and dropped.

Anyone in range can connect and write: there's no pairing. Treat what arrives as untrusted input.

docs.title: ble characteristic out
docs.text: Sets a Bluetooth LE characteristic to each message's payload, for a connected device to read, and notifies the devices that subscribed.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• service UUID / characteristic UUID — as for ble characteristic in.
  • encoding — how payload becomes bytes: the same choices. Default bytes. A number must fit: 70000 doesn't fit an int16.
  • notify — also push each new value to the devices subscribed to it. Default on.
  • BLE — the flow's BLE config.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — payload is the new value. Unwired, the characteristic exists but stays empty.

This node has no output.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Each message replaces the value. A device that reads gets the whole value; a notification carries up to 20 bytes unless the device has agreed a larger MTU (most do, up to 244). Only devices connected at the time are notified.

One characteristic out node per characteristic: two would fight over its value. A ble characteristic in on the same UUIDs makes it writable too.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A missing or malformed UUID, two out nodes on one characteristic, or a board without the ble nodes stops the deploy. A payload that doesn't fit the encoding is reported on the console and dropped, and the last value stays.

Anyone in range can connect and read: don't put anything private in a characteristic.

docs.title: ble notify
docs.text: Subscribes to a characteristic of another Bluetooth LE device and sends a message each time it sends a new value.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• BLE peer — the device to listen to. Required.
  • service UUID / characteristic UUID — the characteristic: 16-bit or 128-bit. Required. It must support notify or indicate; nRF Connect shows which.
  • encoding — how each value becomes payload, as for ble read. Default bytes. It also sets the output's type.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — none. ble notify is a source.

Output — payload is the value. The message also carries peer, the device's address or name, and uuid, the characteristic.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The board turns notifications on when it connects, and again after each reconnect. It uses indications when the characteristic offers no notifications. Up to 20 values wait if they come faster than the flow handles them; then the oldest are dropped.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: A characteristic that can't notify or indicate is reported when the board connects. A value that doesn't decode is reported and dropped.

docs.title: BLE peer
docs.text:
Another Bluetooth LE device the board connects to, such as a sensor or another board. The ble read, ble write and ble notify nodes name one.

Each of those nodes has a BLE peer field. Pick a peer, or add one with +. A flow can have several, one per device. Nodes that name the same peer share one connection.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
• address — the device's address, aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff. Default blank. A ble scan node into a debug node shows the addresses nearby.
  • name starts with — default blank. Used when the address is blank: the first device whose advertised name starts with this. Phones change their address every few minutes, so find a phone by name; most sensors and boards keep theirs.
  • timeout (ms) — how long finding the device and connecting to it may each take. Default 10000.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The board finds the device, connects, finds the services and characteristics the flow's nodes use, and turns on notifications for the ble notify nodes. The nodes' status follows each step: finding, connecting, discovering, connected. If a step fails or the link drops, the status says why, and the board starts again from finding after 10 seconds. It never connects to a different device instead.

An ESP32 holds at most 4 Bluetooth connections at once, counting its peers and the devices connected to the board. A peer over that limit reports a failure at connecting.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: A peer with neither an address nor a name, a malformed address, or a timeout outside 1000 to 60000 ms stops the deploy. A step that fails on the board, such as the device not being found or a service it doesn't have, is reported once on the console, naming the device and the step.

docs.title: ble read
docs.text: Reads a characteristic of another Bluetooth LE device for each message that arrives, and sends the value on.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• BLE peer — the device to read from. Required.
  • service UUID / characteristic UUID — the characteristic to read: 16-bit (2a6e) or 128-bit. Required. Apps such as nRF Connect list a device's UUIDs.
  • encoding — how the bytes read become payload: bytes, text, int8 to uint32, or float32, little-endian. Default bytes. It also sets the output's type.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — any message starts a read. Wire a timer in to read at an interval.

Output — the incoming message, with payload set to the value read.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The read waits up to 5 seconds for the device's answer, and the message's chain waits with it. For a device that pushes its values, a ble notify node needs no polling.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A message that arrives while the peer isn't connected, a read that times out or fails, or a value that doesn't decode (1 byte for a uint16) is reported on the console and the message is dropped.

What a device sends is untrusted input: check it before acting on it.

docs.title: ble scan
docs.text: Listens for Bluetooth LE advertisements, such as beacons and BLE sensors, and sends one message per advertisement.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• name starts with — only devices whose advertised name starts with this. Default blank. Many devices send their name only in reply to an active scan.
  • address — only this device, as aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff. Default blank.
  • manufacturer id — only advertisements with this manufacturer id, in decimal or hex (0x0499 is Ruuvi). Default blank.
  • service UUID — only advertisements that list this service or carry data for it: 16-bit (fcd2 is BTHome) or 128-bit. Default blank.
  • active scan — also ask each device for its scan response, which usually holds its name. Default off.
  • repeat window (ms) — drops an advertisement identical to the same device's last one within this time. Default 1000. 0 sends every one; a changed advertisement is always sent.
  • scan interval (ms) / scan window (ms) — the radio listens for the window once every interval, from 2.5 to 10240 ms. Defaults 320 and 30. A longer window misses fewer advertisements and leaves WiFi less time.

A blank filter lets everything through. The filters combine: an advertisement must pass every one that is set.

With active scan on, a device's scan response arrives as a second message, usually a few milliseconds after its advertisement, with scanResponse set. That's where most devices put their name. Empty scan responses are dropped.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — none. ble scan is a source.

Output — payload is the advertising data as bytes. The message also carries:

field addr the sender's address, aa:bb:cc:dd:ee:ff addrType public or random (phones use random addresses that change) rssi signal strength in dBm, such as -60 connectable whether the device accepts connections; None for a scan response scanResponse True for a device's reply to an active scan, sent as its own message name the advertised name, or '' mfrId, mfr the manufacturer id and the bytes after it, or None and b'' svcData service data, by UUID: {'fcd2': b'...'} services the service UUIDs it lists

Decode the bytes in a function node, with struct.unpack.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Every ble scan node in a flow shares one scan, so they must have the same scan interval, scan window and active scan settings. Each node applies its own filters. A node keeps up to 20 advertisements waiting; if they come faster than the flow handles them, the oldest are dropped.

The radio is shared with WiFi on an ESP32. A long scan window slows WiFi and MQTT.

It runs on the processors Supported hardware lists for the ble nodes.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
A bad address, manufacturer id, UUID or scan setting stops the deploy, naming the value. So do two ble scan nodes with different scan settings, and a board without the ble nodes. The status shows scanning, or scan stopped by the radio if the radio ends the scan. If the radio can't start, often because the board is short of memory, the console says so: hard-reset the board.

An advertisement is untrusted input: anyone nearby can send one, with any name or address.

docs.title: ble uart in
docs.text: Receives text from a connected device over Bluetooth LE, through the Nordic UART Service that terminal apps use.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• one message per line — default on: text is gathered until a newline (\n; a \r is dropped), and the line is sent without its line ending. Off: one message per write.
  • BLE — the flow's BLE config.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — none. ble uart in is a source.

Output — payload is the text. The message also carries conn, the connection's number.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Any UART node adds the Nordic UART Service to the board's GATT server. Terminal apps that speak it, on phones and computers, such as nRF Connect, Serial Bluetooth Terminal and Adafruit Bluefruit, find the board by its name and connect. Pair it with ble uart out to answer.

A line over 512 bytes is sent as it is, so a device that never sends a newline still gets through.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Bytes that aren't UTF-8 text are reported on the console and dropped. Anyone in range can connect and send: there's no pairing.

docs.title: ble uart out
docs.text: Sends text to the devices connected over Bluetooth LE, through the Nordic UART Service.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• end with a newline — add \n after each payload. Default on.
  • BLE — the flow's BLE config.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — payload as text. Bytes are sent as they are; anything else is sent as str(payload).

This node has no output.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The text goes to every connected device, split into pieces that fit each connection: 20 bytes until the device agrees a larger MTU. With no device connected, nothing is sent and nothing is kept.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: A board without the ble nodes stops the deploy. Anyone in range can connect and read what's sent: there's no pairing.

docs.title: ble write
docs.text: Writes each message's payload to a characteristic of another Bluetooth LE device.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• BLE peer — the device to write to. Required.
  • service UUID / characteristic UUID — the characteristic to write: 16-bit or 128-bit. Required.
  • encoding — how payload becomes bytes: the same choices as ble read. Default bytes. A number must fit.
  • wait for the peer's response — default on: the device confirms each write, and a write it refuses is reported. Off: write without response, which is faster; the characteristic must allow it.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — payload is the value to write.

This node has no output.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: Nothing is queued: a message that arrives while the peer isn't connected is reported and dropped, so a stale value is never written after a reconnect.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: Not connected, a write the device refuses or doesn't confirm within 5 seconds, or a payload that doesn't fit the encoding is reported on the console.

docs.title: BLE
docs.text:
The board's Bluetooth name, shared by every ble node in a flow. Optional: without it, the board is called thingstudio.

Each ble node has a BLE field. Pick the flow's BLE config, or add one with +. A flow has one, since a board has one radio.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: • name — what other devices show when they find the board, up to 26 bytes. Default thingstudio. A ble advertise node shares the 31 bytes of an advertisement between the name and its payload, so a shorter name leaves more room.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: Once a ble node has started the radio, it stays on until the board resets, through every redeploy. A deploy stops the old flow's scans, advertising and connections, not the radio. It keeps some ESP-IDF memory meanwhile: a hard reset gives it back.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: A name over 26 bytes, or two BLE configs in a flow, stops the deploy.

docs.title: bme280
docs.text: Reads a BME280 or BMP280 temperature, humidity and pressure sensor at a fixed interval. Supported hardware lists the chips.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• I2C bus — the bus the sensor is wired to. Required. See I2C bus.
  • address — 0x76 (SDO to ground, most boards) or 0x77 (SDO to VCC). Default 0x76. In the flow file, a plain number: 118 or 119.
  • interval (ms) — how often to read. Default 5000. Must be 100 or more.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — none. bme280 is a source.

Output — one reading per interval, with topic an empty string:

msg['payload'] == {'temperature': 21.43, 'humidity': 48.2, 'pressure': 1012.6}

Temperature is in °C, humidity in %, pressure in hPa, each to 2 decimal places. On a BMP280, humidity is None. To use one value, pick it out in a function node: msg['payload'] = msg['payload']['temperature'].

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The first reading goes out when the flow starts. The status dot shows which chip answered, BME280 or BMP280. A failed read sends nothing; the node tries again at the next interval, so a sensor connected after the flow starts is picked up.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• Nothing answers. The dot shows disconnected, no reply at 0x76 on I2C bus 0. Check the wiring, pins and address; see I2C device not answering.
  • A different chip at the address. The dot shows error, no BME280/BMP280 at 0x76 (chip id 0x..).
  • No I2C bus. Deploy stops with bme280 has no I2C bus. Pick one, or add one with +.

docs.title: change
docs.text: Sets or deletes one value, on the message or in a flow variable, then passes the message on.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• operation — set or delete. Default set.
  • target — msg property or flow variable. Default msg property.
  • property / name — the message property or flow variable to change. Default payload. Required. A leading msg. or flow. is dropped. The name is one top-level key: payload.temp names a property called payload.temp, not temp inside payload.
  • value from — with set: a literal value, another msg property or a flow variable. Default a literal value.
  • literal type — with a literal: string, number or bool. Default string.
  • value / source property — with set: the literal, or the name of the message property or flow variable to copy. Default empty. A literal is read as the literal type (see Typed values).

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — any message.

Output — the same message, changed when the target is a message property.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
One rule per node. Chain change nodes for more than one change.

A flow variable is shared by name with every other change node and with a function node's flow.get and flow.set. There is no node-private store here; use a function node's context for that.

Copying a property or flow variable that doesn't exist sets the target to None. Deleting one that doesn't exist does nothing.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
These stop the deploy:

  • No property or flow variable name: change needs a property or variable name.
  • No source name when copying: change needs a source property or variable name.
  • A number literal that isn't a number: change value "abc" is not a valid number.

docs.title: debug
docs.text: Prints each message's payload to the console, to see what is flowing through a wire.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: • full message — default off. When on, prints the whole message, with topic and any other fields the source adds, instead of only payload.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — any message.

This node has no output.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Each message prints one line: DEBUG node=ID payload=VALUE, or DEBUG node=ID msg=MESSAGE with full message on. The value is printed as Python shows it, so a string is in quotes: payload='hello'. Click the line in the console to find the node on the canvas.

The board prints the line, so the console shows it only while the editor is connected.

docs.title: delay
docs.text: Passes each message on unchanged, after a wait.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: • delay (ms) — how long to hold each message, in milliseconds. Default 1000. Must be 1 or more. A fraction is rounded down.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — any message.

Output — the same message, after the wait.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The wait holds the whole chain the message is in, back to its source. The source sends nothing new until the message has gone all the way through. A timer set to 200 ms, wired into a 5000 ms delay, sends a message every 5.2 seconds, not every 200 ms.

Messages from different chains don't wait for each other, even when they pass through the same delay node.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: • The delay is less than 1. Deploy stops with property "delayMs" 0 is below its minimum, 1, naming the node.

docs.title: display i2c
docs.text: Shows a frame on an I2C monochrome OLED panel. The frame is drawn upstream, usually in a function node with framebuf. Supported hardware lists the display chips.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
The property panel's preset picker saves a panel's setup under a name and loads it on another node (see Presets).

  • controller — the display chip. Default SSD1306.
  • I2C bus — the bus the panel is wired to. Required. See I2C bus.
  • address — the I2C address, 0 to 127. Default 0x3C, the usual SSD1306 address. In the flow file addr, a plain number: 60 is 0x3C.
  • width (px) — default 128.
  • height (px, multiple of 8) — default 64.

A flow saved before I2C bus settings existed has its pins on the node. The editor moves them into an I2C bus when it opens the flow; save the flow to keep the change.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — payload is the frame: a MONO_VLSB buffer of exactly width * height / 8 bytes, bytes or bytearray, as framebuf.FrameBuffer makes for a 1-bit surface. Send the buffer, not the FrameBuffer object.

This node has no output.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Each message replaces the whole picture. The node only shows frames; it has no drawing of its own.

framebuf's text() draws a fixed 8x8 font, so a 128x64 panel holds 16 characters on each of 8 lines. This function node draws a temperature from a bme280 and sends the frame:

import framebuf
buf = context.get('buf')
if buf is None:
    buf = bytearray(128 * 8)
    context.set('buf', buf)
fb = framebuf.FrameBuffer(buf, 128, 64, framebuf.MONO_VLSB)
fb.fill(0)
fb.text('%.1f C' % msg['payload']['temperature'], 0, 28, 1)
msg['payload'] = buf
return msg

A panel can share a bus with a sensor, at the bus's one clock; the default 100000 Hz suits both.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• A frame of the wrong size. The console shows a [NODE_ERROR] naming this node and display_i2c: expected 1024 bytes (128x64 MONO_VLSB), got 1000. See Reading a node error.
  • No I2C bus, or an address over 127. Deploy stops and says which.

docs.title: display spi
docs.text: Shows a frame on an SPI color TFT panel. The frame comes from a gui screen, or from a function node that draws with framebuf. Supported hardware lists the display chips.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
The property panel's preset picker saves a panel's whole setup under a name and loads it on another node (see Presets). Pins, size, rotation and color settings differ from board to board, so check them against your own panel, or use a board's labelled pins (see Seeing a board's pins).

  • controller — the display chip: ST7789 or ST7796 (320x480). Default ST7789.
  • frame format — the frame the node takes. Default rgb565, full color at 2 bytes a pixel. The indexed formats use less memory and fewer colors: gs4 (16 colors, a quarter of the memory), gs2 (4 colors, an eighth) and mono (2 colors, a sixteenth). A gui screen wired to the display draws in this format.
  • palette — the 16 RGB565 colors the indexed formats use: gs4 all 16, gs2 the first 4, mono the first 2. Shown as swatches under frame format when an indexed format is picked; click one to change it, or reset for the built-in colors. While a gui screen with a theme is wired to the display, the theme sets the palette and this one is ignored.
  • SPI bus — the hardware SPI peripheral. Default 2.
  • baudrate — the SPI clock in Hz. Default 40000000.
  • sck pin / mosi pin / dc pin — required. Defaults 12, 11 and 13.
  • cs pin / reset pin / backlight pin — -1 when not wired, the default for all three. Some boards tie reset or CS in hardware, or have no backlight control.
  • width (px) / height (px) — the panel's own size. Defaults 135 and 240. A gui screen wired to the display takes this size.
  • orientation — default off. 0, 90, 180 or 270 turns the picture clockwise, and a gui screen wired to the display turns its size and touch to match. With an orientation, set width and height to the panel's own size, rotation to how the panel is mounted (0 to 3), and xstart and ystart to -1. See Rotating the screen. A flow that reads touch with a touch node sets the same angle on that node.
  • rotation (0-7) — the controller's own orientation code. Default 1.
  • color order — BGR or RGB, as the panel is wired. Default BGR.
  • invert colors — for a panel that shows the negative. Default off.
  • data latch order (MH bit) — a controller bit some panels need, with rotation, for the right left-to-right order. Default on.
  • xstart / ystart — the panel's offset in the ST7789's larger frame memory. Default -1, which takes it from the driver's table: 0, 0 for 240x240, 52, 40 for 135x240. Any other ST7789 size needs both set. A wrong offset doesn't raise an error: the picture shows clipped or shifted. An ST7796 has no offset; leave both at -1.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — payload is the frame, in the frame format. A whole frame is exactly the size the format needs: width * height * 2 bytes for rgb565; for the indexed formats, see Indexed formats below.

A message with a y field is a strip: whole rows, written from row y down. A gui screen sends strips, so a large display never needs a whole frame in memory.

This node has no output.

docs.title: RGB565 byte order
docs.text:
framebuf.RGB565 stores each pixel in the processor's byte order, little-endian on an ESP32, but the panel expects big-endian. The node sends the bytes as they are, so a buffer drawn with framebuf.FrameBuffer(..., framebuf.RGB565) comes out with its colors wrong: an intended green shows red. Swap each pair of bytes after drawing, before msg['payload'] = buf:

for i in range(0, len(buf), 2):
    buf[i], buf[i + 1] = buf[i + 1], buf[i]

A color whose two bytes are the same, such as white 0xFFFF or black 0x0000, looks right either way, so text on a plain background can hide the problem.

docs.title: Indexed formats
docs.text:
Draw an indexed frame with framebuf.FrameBuffer(..., framebuf.<FORMAT>), with the constant that matches frame format:

frame format framebuf constant bits per pixel palette entries used 240x320 frame rgb565 RGB565 16 none, real color 153,600 bytes gs4 GS4_HMSB 4 0–15 38,400 bytes gs2 GS2_HMSB 2 0–3 19,200 bytes mono MONO_HMSB 1 0–1 9,600 bytes

Pixel values are palette entries, not colors; the node turns each into its palette color as it writes. The indexed formats have no byte-order problem.

Each row is padded to a whole byte, so a width that isn't a multiple of the pixels per byte (2 for gs4, 4 for gs2, 8 for mono) needs a little more than width * height * bits / 8. On a wrong size the node names the size it expects.

mono needs framebuf.MONO_HMSB. MONO_VLSB (the display i2c layout) and MONO_HLSB give a garbled picture with no error, because the node can't tell which one was used.

Send the bytearray itself (msg['payload'] = buf): bytes(buf) makes a second copy the board may not have memory for. For a flow that redraws often, keep the buffer in context and reuse it.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• A frame or strip of the wrong size. The console shows a [NODE_ERROR] naming this node, such as display_spi: expected 64800 bytes (...), got 64000, or for a strip display_spi: a strip must be whole rows of 270 bytes inside the 240-row screen, .... See Reading a node error.
  • An ST7789 size other than 240x240 or 135x240, with xstart and ystart at -1. The board reports Unsupported display. Only 240x240 and 135x240 are supported without xstart and ystart provided when the flow starts.
  • An orientation with a panel offset, including the default 135x240 size. Deploy stops: clear the orientation, or set rotation by hand.
  • An orientation with a rotation of 4 to 7. Deploy stops; with an orientation, rotation is 0 to 3.
  • A baudrate too fast for the board or for these pins. Deploy stops and gives the board's limit.
  • A changed palette while a themed gui screen is wired. Deploy warns that the theme sets the palette.
  • A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently. Deploy stops and says why. See What gets checked and Hardware is shared.

docs.title: ebutton
docs.text: Reports presses, releases, long presses and double clicks from one button, ignoring contact bounce.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• pin — the GPIO pin. Default 5. Kitchen-sink board shows a button wired to one.
  • pull — the pin's own pull resistor: none, up or down. Default none, for a button with an external pull resistor or a module that has one.
  • sense — the pin level when the button is not pressed: auto, 0 or 1. Default auto, which takes the level when the flow starts as not pressed. Set it if the button may be held down at start.
  • suppress — default off. When on, a click that may be the first half of a double click is held back (see Behavior).
  • debounce (ms) — default 50. Must be 1 or more.
  • long press (ms) — how long a press must last to count as long. Default 1000.
  • double click (ms) — how soon a second press must follow the first to count as double. Default 400. Must be less than long press.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — none. ebutton is a source.

Output — a message for each event, with payload one of press, release, long or double, and topic an empty string.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The events each action sends depend on suppress:

Action suppress off suppress on a click press, release press and release together, after double click has passed a double click press, release, then press and double together, then release double, release a long press press, long, release long, release

With suppress off, every press is reported at once. With it on, a click arrives later but never as part of a double click or a long press, and a press held longer than double click but released before long press sends only release.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• double click is not less than long press. Deploy stops with property "doubleClickMs" 1000 must be less than longPressMs (1000), naming the node.
  • A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently. Deploy stops and says why. See What gets checked and Hardware is shared.

docs.title: encoder
docs.text: Reads a rotary encoder (a quadrature knob) and sends its value each time it turns.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• pin x / pin y — the encoder's two switch pins. Defaults 10 and 11. Both are read with the pins' own pull-ups. If the value counts the wrong way, swap them.
  • divide by (div) — pulses per step of the value: 4 or 2 for a knob that clicks, so one click is one step; 1 counts every pulse. Default 1.
  • start value — the value when the flow starts. Default 0.
  • lowest (blank for none) / highest (blank for none) — whole numbers the value stops at. Default blank.
  • wrap at (blank for none) — a whole number: the value counts from 0 to one less than it, then wraps. Default blank.
  • settle (ms) — how long to wait after the knob moves before sending the value. Default 100. Must be 0 or more.

The value is divided first, then held within lowest and highest, then wrapped.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — none. encoder is a source.

Output — a message with payload set to the value, delta set to how far it moved since the last message (negative when it went down), and topic an empty string.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: When the knob moves, the node waits settle, then sends the value it has reached. A fast turn gives about one message per settle, not one per pulse. A turn that ends where it started sends nothing.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• start value is below lowest or above highest. The board reports Incompatible args: must have vmin <= v <= vmax when the flow starts.
  • lowest, highest or wrap at isn't a whole number. Deploy stops with property "vmin" "x" must be a whole number (decimal or 0x hex), naming the node.
  • A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently. Deploy stops and says why. See What gets checked and Hardware is shared.

docs.title: eswitch
docs.text: Reports when a switch opens or closes, ignoring contact bounce.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• pin — the GPIO pin. Default 4.
  • pull — the pin's own pull resistor: none, up or down. Default none, for a switch with an external pull resistor or a module that has one.
  • open level (lopen) — the pin level that means open: 1 for a switch to ground with a pull-up, 0 for a switch to 3V3 with a pull-down. Default 1.
  • debounce (ms) — how long a level must hold before it counts. Default 50. Must be 1 or more.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — none. eswitch is a source.

Output — a message for each change, with payload True when the switch closes and False when it opens, and topic an empty string. payload is a bool, so it can wire straight to a gpio out to mirror the switch.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The node checks the pin every debounce interval. It sends nothing when the flow starts, only on a change.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: • A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently. Deploy stops and says why. See What gets checked and Hardware is shared.

docs.title: filter
docs.text: Passes a message on only when it's worth sending, and drops the rest. Messages that pass are unchanged.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• mode — what counts as worth sending. Default change.
    • change — the payload differs from the last one passed.
    • deadband — the payload is a number that has moved at least threshold from the last one passed, up or down.
    • rate — at least interval has passed since the last message passed.
  • threshold — for deadband. Default 1. Must be 0 or more. With 0, every number passes, changed or not.
  • interval (ms) — for rate. Default 1000. Must be 1 or more.
  • ignore first message — for change and deadband. Default off. When on, the first message only sets the starting value.
  • separately for each topic — default on. Each msg.topic is filtered on its own, with its own last value and its own first message.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — any message.

Output — the message, unchanged, when it passes.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
change compares payloads with Python's ==, so 1 and 1.0 count as the same.

deadband compares with the last value it let through, not the last one it received, so a slow drift passes once it adds up to the threshold. It reads text such as "21.5" as a number, so it works on MQTT payloads; the message still goes out as the original text. Anything else, including true and false, is dropped.

rate drops extra messages. It doesn't queue them or send them later. The first message always passes.

The node tracks up to 32 topics. After that it forgets them all and starts again, and prints FILTER_INFO node=ID more than 32 topics, starting again once.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• deadband gets something that isn't a number. The message is dropped and the console shows a [NODE_ERROR] naming this node and deadband needs a number, got str 'abc'. It is reported once, then again only after a number has arrived. The chain keeps running.
  • A threshold below 0 or an interval below 1. Deploy stops, naming the node and the property.

docs.title: function
docs.text: Runs your own MicroPython on each message, for anything no other node does.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• code — the body of a Python function, run once for each message. Default msg['payload'] = msg['payload'] followed by return msg. Required.
  • outputs — how many outputs the node has, 1 to 10. Default 1. outputCount in the flow file.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — any message, as msg: a dict with the main value in msg['payload'].

Output — what the code returns. Return the message to pass it on, or return None or nothing to stop it. Every output has type any (see Wiring).

With more than one output, return a list with one entry per output, as in Node-RED:

if msg['payload'] > 100:
    return [msg, None]   # output 1 only
return [None, msg]       # output 2 only

The returned list is read entry by entry:

  • None sends nothing on that output.
  • A list of messages sends each of them on that output, in order: return [[msg1, msg2], None].
  • A list shorter than the number of outputs leaves the rest empty. Entries past the last output are ignored.
  • A plain return msg, not in a list, goes to output 1.

With one output, a returned list is passed on as the message itself. Set outputs to 2 or more to use the list.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The code is the body of an async def, so return and await work at its top level. asyncio and runtime are already defined; import anything else in the code, such as import machine. A library ThingStudio provides, such as mqtt_as, is installed on the board when you deploy (see Libraries).

Don't call time.sleep() or run a long loop: either stops every other chain while it runs. Use await asyncio.sleep(1) instead (see The one rule: don't block).

Local variables start again for every message. Keep values between messages in context, flow or settings.

docs.title: Context, flow and settings
docs.text:
Three stores keep values between messages, each with get(name, default) and set(name, value):

  • context — this node only. Two function nodes using the same name don't share it.
  • flow — shared by every function and change node in the flow, by name.
  • settings — saved on the board, so it survives a restart and a redeploy of the same flow. It is runtime.settings; see Persisting values for what else it does.

context and flow start empty each time the flow starts.

count = context.get('count', 0) + 1
context.set('count', count)
msg['payload'] = count
return msg

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• The code is empty. Deploy stops with function node's code is empty.
  • The code has a syntax error. Deploy stops and highlights the node.
  • The code raises an exception. The console shows a [NODE_ERROR] naming this node and the exception, and the chain stops. See Reading a node error.

docs.title: gpio out
docs.text: Sets a pin high or low from each message.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: • pin — the GPIO pin. Default 12.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — payload, read with Python's bool(): a true value sets the pin high, a false one (False, 0, "", None, an empty list) sets it low. A message with no payload sets it low. The input is type bool, so any output can wire to it.

This node has no output.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The pin stays where the last message set it. It is set up as an output when the flow starts, before any message arrives.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: • A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently. Deploy stops and says why. See What gets checked and Hardware is shared.

docs.title: GUI nodes
docs.text:
Provisional

The GUI nodes are provisional: their properties and the page layout may change between releases.

The GUI nodes show readings on a display as pages of numbers, text, bars, lights, histograms and buttons. A gui screen draws the pages and sends them to a display spi node; each widget node shows the payload of the messages wired to it. Lay out the pages in the gui screen's property panel: see Laying out pages.

The nodes on this page:

  • gui screen — one per display.
  • gui readout — a number with units.
  • gui label — text.
  • gui bar — a bar between two values.
  • gui light — on or off.
  • gui button — a touch button.
  • gui histogram — the recent history of a number.

On a classic ESP32 without PSRAM, a GUI flow needs the custom firmware for classic ESP32: stock MicroPython runs out of memory loading the display stack.

docs.title: gui screen
docs.text: Draws a display's pages of widgets and sends them to a display spi node.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
The screen takes its width, height and frame format from the display it is wired to, so set them once on the display.

  • name — the screen's name, sent as topic. Default screen.
  • fastest redraw (ms) — the shortest time between two redraws. Default 200.
  • next/prev wrap round — whether next on the last page goes to the first, and prev on the first to the last. Default on.
  • grid columns — the layout grid's columns, 2 to 48. Default 12. See Laying out pages.
  • grid rows (0 = from the display's shape) — 0 to 64. Default 0, which keeps the cells roughly square.
  • touch panel (blank: no touch) — the touch panel the screen reads, for buttons. Default blank.
  • theme and the ten role colors — the screen's colors. Default blank, the GUI's own colors. See Themes.
  • shared theme config (older flows) — used only when the theme fields are empty, so a flow saved with a shared theme still draws.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — none. The widgets on its pages get their own wires.

Output — the picture, in strips of about 5 KB, each with y set to its first row, so a whole frame never has to fit in memory. Wire it to a display spi node.

docs.title: Laying out pages
docs.text:
A display is one fixed panel of a known size, filled by one flow. A page fills it, and its size never changes while the flow runs. The layout is worked out when the flow compiles: the compiler turns each element's cells into pixel positions and picks the font for each piece of text, and Deploy sends those numbers. Nothing reflows at runtime, and the board carries no layout engine. That differs from a web page: nothing responds to a resize or an orientation change while the flow runs, and a layout is for one panel. A display of a different size means compiling for that display.

Every screen has a cell grid: grid columns on the gui screen (12 by default) and grid rows (0 means "work them out from the display's shape", so cells stay roughly square). A position is a row and a column, 0-based; a size is a row span and a column span. Nothing is in pixels, so the same layout works on a different panel.

Select the gui screen node and open Properties: each page lists its elements. ⚙ on an element opens row, col, rows and cols; tick panel to draw a card behind those cells. + add… puts a widget, text, page dots or a panel on the page (it starts at row 0, column 0 — set its cells after). The same widget can be on several pages of a screen (a navigation button on every page, say), and it must have the same span on each. A widget belongs to one screen.

Text sizes itself: the compiler picks the largest font that fits the element's cells, and Deploy says which element, on which page, when even the smallest does not fit. Two elements on the same cells, a span outside the grid, or a panel on top of another panel are also Deploy errors naming the element. The editor doesn't draw the page; the outline is a view of the flow file's "screens" section, which you can also edit by hand.

To put the page dots in a footer, give them the last grid row. The current page's dot is drawn as a pill.

docs.title: Widgets
docs.text:
The readout, label, bar, light, button and histogram are widgets: each sits on a page and shows the payload of each message that arrives on its input.

  • A widget shows -- until a value arrives. A payload of None shows -- again.
  • stale after (s, 0 = never), default 0: a value not updated in that time is dimmed (or underlined, on a black-and-white display), so an old reading never looks current.
  • name is how Deploy names the widget in an error, after its flow label.
  • font (blank = fit the cells), where a widget has one: default blank, the largest font that fits its cells.
  • A widget that can't draw its value, such as a bar given text, is crossed out and the console shows a [NODE_ERROR] naming it. The other widgets carry on.

A widget belongs to one screen, and can be on several of its pages.

docs.title: gui readout
docs.text:
Shows payload as a number with units. A number is drawn with decimals places; anything else is drawn as text.

  • caption (above the number) — a small muted line above the number, such as Temperature. Default blank.
  • units — text after the number. Default blank.
  • decimals — 0 to 6. Default 1.
  • lowest value / highest value — the range it will show. Defaults 0 and 100. The number's space is sized for this range, so the layout doesn't shift as the value changes.

docs.title: gui label
docs.text:
Shows payload as text.

  • room for (characters) — how many characters its space is sized for. Default 8.

docs.title: gui bar
docs.text:
A bar that fills between two values. A value below empty at shows empty, one above full at shows full.

  • style — solid (an outline and a fill) or segments (a row of cells, lit in the accent color and unlit in the track color). Default solid.
  • cells — for segments, 1 to 40. Default 10.
  • empty at / full at — defaults 0 and 100. full at must be above empty at.

docs.title: gui light
docs.text:
On when payload is true, off when it is false, by Python's bool().

  • style — light (a circle) or chip (a filled pill showing a word). Default light.
  • chip when on / chip when off — the chip's words. Defaults On and Off.

docs.title: Buttons
docs.text: A touch button. Its input sets what it shows, and its output sends when it is tapped. A button needs a touch panel on its screen to be pressed.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• topic — the topic of the messages it sends. Default blank, the node's id.
  • mode — what a tap does. Default momentary.
    • momentary — sends its sends value.
    • toggle — sends the opposite of its state, and shows its on shows or off shows text.
    • navigate — changes page, to goes to. It needs no wires.
  • style — box (outline and text), filled (a solid accent button, for the main action) or switch (a track and knob; it needs toggle). Default box.
  • value type — true / false, text or number: the type of what it sends. Default true / false.
  • send on — release (when your finger lifts inside the button; lifting outside sends nothing) or press. Default release. The button is drawn inverted while held.
  • board label (drawn on the button) — momentary: the text drawn on it. Default blank, the flow label. A payload on its input replaces it.
  • sends (the payload) — momentary: what it sends. Default blank.
  • room for (characters, if no text) — momentary: default 8.
  • on sends / off sends — toggle: what it sends to turn on and off. Default blank.
  • on shows / off shows — toggle: its text. Defaults ON and OFF.
  • starts on (when nothing is wired in) — toggle: default off.
  • wait for confirmation (s, 5 or more) — toggle with a wired input: how long a tap waits for the input to agree. Default 5.
  • goes to — navigate: next, prev, back, home or a page name.

A blank value field sends true and false for true / false, ON and OFF for text, and 1 and 0 for number. The gray placeholder shows which.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — for momentary, a payload replaces the text drawn on it. For toggle, the real state of the thing it switches; see below.

Output — {'topic': <topic>, 'payload': <value>} on each tap. A navigate button sends nothing.

Deploy warns when a screen has buttons and no touch panel, and when a momentary or toggle button's output goes nowhere. A navigate button whose goes to isn't next, prev, back, home or a page on its screen stops the deploy.

docs.title: A toggle that follows the real device
docs.text:
Wire the toggle's input to the device's real state, and its output to whatever switches it:

mqtt subscribe (stat/plug/POWER) -> toggle -> mqtt publish (cmnd/plug/POWER)

With the input wired, the flow owns the state:

  • Before the first report the toggle shows -- (a dashed outline).
  • A tap shows the state you asked for, with a dotted outline, until the input confirms it.
  • If the input says something different, the toggle shows what the input says.
  • If nothing comes back in time, it returns to the last known state, shows a cross for a moment, and the console reports it. See a toggle goes back.

The input is matched against the toggle's on sends and off sends values. MQTT delivers text, so the text true matches a true/false toggle and 1 matches a number toggle. Anything else shows --. Tasmota reports ON and OFF as text, so for a Tasmota plug set the value type to text and use ON and OFF.

Unwired, the toggle keeps its own state and starts as set by starts on.

docs.title: Histogram
docs.text:
A moving histogram: a row of bars, oldest on the left, newest on the right. It shows what a number can't: which way it is heading. Wire it to the first output of a journal, or to any node that sends a list of numbers (a None is a gap), such as a spectrum from a function node.

Each bar is a row's average, in the theme's accent color, with a thin line from the row's minimum to its maximum in the muted color, so the range reads as context behind the value. A gap is empty. A wider space shows more history: it draws as many bars as fit, newest at the right edge.

  • bottom at / top at — the range of the bars. Defaults 0 and 100. Values outside are cut off at the edge.
  • columns (natural width), column width (px), height (px) — the natural size, defaults 60, 3 and 48: as wide as columns times column width, plus the border. In a layout it can stretch, and then shows more rows.

It shows only the rows its journal kept. With fewer rows than the space holds, the bars sit at the right edge and the left of the card stays empty; the compiler says how many rows to keep. Raising rows kept on the journal fills it.

docs.title: Themes
docs.text:
By default a screen draws in the GUI's own colors: white text, gray for stale values, and a green accent for bars and lights that are on. Full color needs the display's frame format set to rgb565; the gray formats use less memory and send faster, so use them on boards with little RAM. To choose your own colors, select the gui screen and set theme (a starting point) and any of the role colors in its Properties: the screen owns its look, and a screen with no theme keeps the default colors.

A theme is ten roles, so the widgets stay consistent and one theme works on different panels: background, card, foreground, muted (stale values), track (a bar's empty part), accent (bar fill, lights on), text on accent, ok, warn and alarm. Start from dark slate, light paper or vivid and change any color; the preset is a starting point, not a lock. Vivid has a near-black background, violet cards and a cyan accent.

Use the preset control in the theme's edit form to save your colors by name under ~/.thingstudio/presets/gui_theme/, and apply them to another theme later (Presets). The three starting points are built in, so a flow that names one still compiles without a backend.

A panel with fewer colors than that folds the roles onto the ones it has, rather than refusing the theme:

  • a gs4 panel (16 colors) gets every role as its own color;
  • a gs2 panel (4 colors) keeps background, foreground, muted and accent — cards fold to the background, the track to muted, ok/warn/alarm to the foreground;
  • a mono panel (2 colors) is ink and paper: text, bars and lights are ink, backgrounds are paper.

A panel is a card behind a group of widgets: tick panel on an element in the layout outline and the cells it covers sit on a filled, rounded rectangle in the theme's card color. It follows the theme.

On an indexed panel (gs4, gs2 or mono) the theme also sets the display's palette while a screen is wired to it — one theme is the whole color scheme, not two lists to keep in step. A palette set on the display itself is ignored while a themed screen is wired to it, and Deploy says so in the console.

docs.title: Rotating the screen
docs.text: The screen follows its display's orientation (see display spi). It takes the display's size and turns its layout and its touch to match. At 90 or 270 the usable picture is the panel turned: 480 wide by 320 high on a 320x480 panel. A flow that reads touch with a touch node instead of a gui screen sets the same angle on that node, since there is no display for it to follow.

docs.title: Seven-segment digits
docs.text: The seg7 fonts (font_seg748, font_seg764, font_seg796) have only 0-9 : . - and a space, so they suit the time and time_seconds formats of the ntp node. On a 320-pixel-wide screen font_seg764 fits 14:05 (221 px) and font_seg748 fits 14:05:09 (254 px). font_seg796 is for wider screens. The font is DSEG by Keshikan (SIL Open Font License 1.1); see third-party licenses.

docs.title: http in
docs.text: Starts a web server on the board and sends a message for each request to a path.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• port — the TCP port to listen on (1–65535). Default 8080.
  • path — the exact path to match, such as /status. It must start with /. A pattern such as /user/:id isn't supported.
  • method — GET or POST. Default GET.
  • response timeout (ms) — how long to wait for an http response node before the client gets a
  • Default 10000.
  • WiFi — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Output — one message per matching request:

Field Value payload None. The request body isn't read. topic an empty string req.method GET or POST req.path the path requested, without any query string

Every chain that starts here must end at an http response node. The message carries a hidden link to the client's connection, and http response uses it. A node that returns a new message instead of the one it received, such as a function node, drops the link.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Several http in nodes can share one port. Each claims its own method and path. Two nodes claiming the same method and path on one port is a compile error.

A request that matches no node gets a 404: that includes a method other than GET or POST. A query string is dropped, so /status?x=1 matches /status, and the value isn't available to the flow. Request headers are ignored.

If no http response node replies within the response timeout, the client gets a 500 with the body Internal Server Error: no response. The connection closes after each reply.

The server speaks plain HTTP and has no login. It limits neither the number of requests in flight nor their size, apart from the board's own memory and sockets. Use it on a network you trust.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
These stop the compile:

  • the port isn't a number from 1 to 65535
  • the path doesn't start with /
  • the response timeout isn't a positive number
  • two nodes claim the same method and path on one port. The error names both.

A client that doesn't finish sending its request line and headers within 5 seconds gets a 400.

docs.title: http request
docs.text: Makes one HTTP request per incoming message and returns the response.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• url — http://host[:port]/path. HTTPS isn't supported.
  • method — GET or POST. No other methods are supported.
  • timeout (ms) — how long to wait for the whole request and response. Default 5000.
  • WiFi — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — any message. For a POST, payload is the request body: a string is UTF-8 encoded, and other types are converted.

Output — the response:

  • payload — the decoded body, as a string.
  • status — the HTTP status code, an integer.

A response with any status (404, 500, …) is sent on. Test msg['status'] == 200 yourself.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The first request goes out when the first message arrives, so with a timer it is one full interval after the flow starts.

The server must send Content-Length: chunked transfer-encoding isn't supported. Redirects aren't followed. The body must be valid UTF-8.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
If the connection fails, the request times out or the reply can't be read, nothing is sent on. The console shows the error, and the next message tries again. There is no failure output. To act on a failure, watch the console.

  • A body that isn't valid UTF-8 raises an error.
  • The whole body is read into memory at once. A response larger than the board's largest free block fails with MemoryError. Request a smaller response, or use a board with PSRAM.

docs.title: http response
docs.text: Sends the reply to a request that arrived through an http in node.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: None. The reply comes from the message.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — a message that started at an http in node:

Field Value payload the reply body. A string is sent as UTF-8, bytes as they are, and None as an empty body. Anything else is converted to text. statusCode the HTTP status, a whole number. Default 200.

This node has no output.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The reply has no Content-Type header. A client that needs to know the body is JSON has to assume it.

Send one reply per request. Once a reply has gone, another for the same request does nothing. A reply that arrives after the response timeout is too late: the client has already received a 500.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• The message didn't come from an http in node. The console shows http_response: msg did not come from an http_in node (no request to respond to). The same happens when a node between the two built a new message and dropped the link. Change the message you received and pass it on.
  • statusCode isn't a whole number. The node raises an error and the client gets the 500 after the timeout.

docs.title: I2C bus
docs.text:
The pins and clock of one I2C bus, set once and shared by every node on it. A display and a sensor can sit on the same bus, each at its own address.

Each I2C node has an I2C bus field. Pick a bus, or add one with +. A new bus takes the lowest bus number not yet used in the flow.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
• bus — the chip's I2C peripheral number. Default 0. Each bus number is used once per flow.
  • scl pin / sda pin — the GPIO pins. Required, and different from each other.
  • frequency (Hz) — the clock. Default 100000, which suits most sensors. Displays that can take it run at 400000.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
Changing a bus changes it for every node on it. The bus's two pins are claimed like any other pin, so no other node can use them (see Hardware is shared).

runtime.shared('i2c', 0) in a function node returns the flow's bus 0, already set up, to talk to a device that has no node of its own. It raises KeyError if no node in the flow uses that bus.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
These stop the deploy:

  • No SCL or SDA pin: I2C bus 0 has no SCL pin set.
  • The same pin for both: I2C bus 0 uses pin 5 for both SCL and SDA.
  • Two bus settings with the same number, both in use: Two I2C bus settings both say bus 0.
  • A pin or bus number the board can't use for I2C. See What gets checked.

docs.title: i2c device
docs.text: Talks to an I2C device that has no node of its own. Each message that arrives does one transfer.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• I2C bus — the bus the device is wired to. Required. See I2C bus.
  • operation — read bytes, write msg.payload or scan the bus (read, write, scan in the flow file). Default read.
  • address — the device's 7-bit address, such as 0x29 or 41. Up to 0x7f. Required except for scan.
  • register — the register to read or write, such as 0x80. Up to 0xff. Leave it empty for a device without registers.
  • length (bytes) — for read, how many bytes, 1 to 256. Default 1.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — any message starts a transfer. For write, payload is what to send: bytes, a list of numbers 0 to 255, or one number 0 to 255.

Output — the same message, with other fields kept:

  • read: payload is the bytes read. Reading register 0x92 at address 0x29 (a TCS34725's ID) gives b'D'.
  • write: payload is unchanged.
  • scan: payload is the list of addresses that answer, as numbers.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The status dot shows whether the device answers. A transfer that fails sends nothing, and the next message tries again.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• Nothing answers at the address. The dot shows disconnected, no reply at 0x29 on I2C bus 0, and the message is dropped. For scan, I2C bus 0 not responding.
  • A payload that can't be written, such as a bool or a number over 255. The dot shows error with the reason, and the message is dropped.
  • No address, for read or write. The first message fails with a [NODE_ERROR]: i2c: set the device address (7-bit, e.g. 0x29).
  • No bus, a bus without pins, or an address or register out of range. Deploy stops and says which.

docs.title: inject
docs.text: Sends one message with a fixed payload each time you click its ▶ icon while the editor is connected to the board.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• payload type — bool, number or string. Default bool. The output's type follows it, so the editor checks the wire against the input it feeds (see Wiring).
  • value — the value to send, read as the payload type (see Typed values). Default true.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — none. inject is a source.

Output — a message with payload set to the value and topic set to an empty string.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The ▶ icon and the rest of the node are separate click targets. The ▶ fires the node. A click anywhere else on the node opens its property panel, connected or not.

Each click sends one message. inject never fires on its own, neither on a schedule nor when the flow starts, so a flow whose only sources are inject nodes does nothing until you click one. To send a message when the flow starts, use startup. To send one repeatedly, use timer.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• The editor isn't connected. The console shows [inject: connect to a device first -- clicking only fires while live] and nothing is sent.
  • The value isn't a number, with payload type number. The deploy goes through; the click fails on the board with a [NODE_ERROR] naming this node and inject value 'abc' is not a valid number. See Reading a node error.
  • A node error in this node's chain stops the chain. See Reading a node error.

docs.title: interrupt
docs.text: Sends a message the moment a pin changes state.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• pin — the GPIO pin. Default 4.
  • edge — the change to react to: rising, falling or both. Default rising.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — none. interrupt is a source.

Output — a message with payload set to the pin's level, True or False, read when the node handles the change. topic is an empty string.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The pin's interrupt wakes the node, and the node reads the pin then. Changes that come faster than the flow handles them are collapsed into one message, so payload is the level at that moment, not a record of every change.

The pin has no pull resistor. Wire an external one, or use a module with one built in. For a button or switch, use ebutton or eswitch, which ignore contact bounce and can use the pin's own pull resistor.

docs.title: Errors
