docs.text: • A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently. Deploy stops and says why. See What gets checked and Hardware is shared.

docs.title: journal
docs.text: Keeps the recent history of a number, as rows of average, minimum and maximum, the way RRDtool and Cacti do. Wire it to a histogram to see the history, and to another journal for a longer time scale.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• rows kept — how many rows the history holds, 1 to 256. Default 60. At 12 bytes a row, 156 rows is under 2 KB.
  • seconds per row — a row closes once this much time has passed, and holds the average, minimum and maximum of the readings in it. Default 60. 0 makes every message one row, which is what a journal fed by another journal wants.
  • rows per roll-up — how many rows go into each roll-up on output 2. Default 0, which sends no roll-up.
  • gaps allowed in a roll-up — shown when rows per roll-up is above 0. From 0 to 1, default 0.5. If more than this fraction of the rows in a roll-up are gaps, the roll-up is a gap too. Averages use the known rows only; a gap is never counted as zero.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — msg.payload is a number. Text such as "21.5" is read as a number, and True and False as 1 and 0. A message that also carries min and max, such as another journal's roll-up, is folded in with them, so a longer time scale keeps the spikes. With seconds per row at 0, a payload of None records a gap.

Output 1, series — sent each time a row is added. The payload is the journal itself, to wire to a histogram. It is the live history, not a copy, so it costs no memory per row.

Output 2, roll-up — sent every rows per roll-up rows: payload the average, min, max, and the input's topic. A gap roll-up has None in all three. Wire it to another journal, a readout or MQTT.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
A gap is empty, never a copy of the last value. A row with no readings in it is a gap, so choose a row longer than your sensor's interval: 10 seconds for a reading every 5.

With seconds per row set, a row closes when a message arrives after its time is up. A sensor that has gone quiet adds no rows until it sends again; then the rows it missed are added as gaps, at most one full history's worth. Set the histogram's stale after to dim it meanwhile.

A sensor display wires two journals in a row, for a 26-minute and a 2.6-hour history.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• The payload isn't a number. The message is dropped and the console shows a [NODE_ERROR] naming this node and journal needs a number, got str 'abc'. It is reported once, then again only after a number has arrived. The chain keeps running.
  • Rows kept outside 1 to 256, or a negative seconds per row. Deploy stops, naming the node and the property.

docs.title: mqtt publish
docs.text: Publishes each message's payload to an MQTT topic.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• topic — the topic to publish to. Required. It is fixed: a message's topic is ignored. To publish to several topics, use one node for each.
  • retain — ask the broker to keep the message and give it to later subscribers. Default off.
  • QoS — 0 or 1. Default 0. QoS 2 isn't supported.
  • MQTT Broker — the flow's MQTT broker, shared by every MQTT node in the flow: change it on one and it changes on all (see Editor in depth). Required.
  • WiFi — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow. unmanaged isn't accepted in a flow with MQTT nodes, because they manage the connection themselves.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — any message. payload is the message sent: bytes as they are, a string as UTF-8, and anything else converted to text first. None sends the text None.

This node has no output.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: Nodes on the same broker share one connection. The node connects when the first message reaches it, so its status dot stays blank until then (see node status). It shows this node's own view of the connection, even when an mqtt subscribe node shares the broker.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• The board can't reach the broker. The dot turns red and the console shows mqtt connect to HOST:PORT failed after 3 attempts, with the reason for each attempt. See MQTT broker unreachable.
  • The publish fails. The console shows mqtt publish to HOST:PORT failed, with the system's error.

These stop the compile: no MQTT broker or no WiFi network in the flow, an empty topic, a QoS other than 0 or 1, an unmanaged WiFi network.

docs.title: mqtt subscribe
docs.text: Sends a message for each message that arrives on an MQTT topic.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• topic — the topic to subscribe to. Required. + matches one level and # the rest, as usual in MQTT.
  • QoS — 0 or 1. Default 0. QoS 2 isn't supported.
  • dynamic subscription — let messages on the input change the subscriptions (see below). Default off.
  • MQTT Broker — the flow's MQTT broker, shared by every MQTT node in the flow: change it on one and it changes on all (see Editor in depth). Required.
  • WiFi — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow. unmanaged isn't accepted in a flow with MQTT nodes, because they manage the connection themselves.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — only with dynamic subscription on. See below.

Output — one message per message received:

Field Value payload the message body, decoded as UTF-8 text topic the topic it arrived on, which can differ from the subscription when that has a wildcard retained True when the broker sent it as a retained message

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The node subscribes to topic when the flow starts and keeps the subscription across reconnects. Nodes on the same broker share one connection and subscribe independently.

The node holds up to 20 messages that haven't been sent on yet. When more arrive, the oldest is dropped.

A subscription may not be confirmed by the broker before an mqtt publish node on the same broker sends its first message. An early publish can go unheard.

The status dot shows this node's own view of the connection, as for mqtt publish.

docs.title: Dynamic subscription
docs.text:
With it on, an input message changes what the node listens to:

Field Value action subscribe or unsubscribe topic a topic string, a {topic, qos} object, or a list of either

An unsubscribe stops this node receiving that topic. Another node subscribed to the same topic keeps receiving it. The configured topic can be unsubscribed too, until the flow is next reloaded.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• The board can't reach the broker. The dot turns red and the console shows mqtt connect to HOST:PORT failed after 3 attempts, with the reason for each attempt. See MQTT broker unreachable.
  • The subscribe fails. The console shows mqtt subscribe to HOST:PORT failed, with the system's error.
  • A message arrives on the input with dynamic subscription off. The node raises an error rather than ignoring it.
  • An action message has no topic, an unknown action, or a QoS other than 0 or 1. The node raises an error.

These stop the compile: no MQTT broker or no WiFi network in the flow, an empty topic, a QoS other than 0 or 1, an unmanaged WiFi network.

docs.title: neopixel
docs.text: Lights a WS2812 (NeoPixel) strip: sets its pixels from each message, then writes the strip.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• pin — the strip's data pin. Default 13. Kitchen-sink board shows one LED wired to one.
  • count — how many pixels the strip has. Default 8. Must be 1 or more.
  • order — the color order of your strip: GRB, RGB, RGBW or GRBW. Default GRB, which most WS2812 strips use. The W orders are for strips with a white channel.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — payload in one of three forms:

msg['payload'] = 0xff4400                            # one color for the whole strip
msg['payload'] = [0xff0000, 0x00ff00, 0x0000ff]      # one color per pixel, from the first
msg['payload'] = {'index': 2, 'colour': 0x00ff00}    # one pixel; 'color' works too

A color is 0xRRGGBB, 0 to 255 for each of red, green and blue. A strip with a white channel takes 0xWWRRGGBB; a plain 0xRRGGBB leaves white off. A list shorter than the strip leaves the other pixels as they were; one longer than the strip is cut off.

This node has no output.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: Each message sets the pixels it names and writes the whole strip. Pixels a message doesn't name keep their color.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• A payload that isn't a color, or an index past the end of the strip. The node's status dot turns red with the error, and nothing is written. See Node status.
  • A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently. Deploy stops and says why. See What gets checked and Hardware is shared.

docs.title: ntp
docs.text: Sets the board's clock from the internet and sends the time, as text for a display or as Unix time.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• NTP server — a host name. Default pool.ntp.org.
  • UTC offset (hours) — your standard time, from -12 to 14 in half hours: 1 for central Europe, 5.5 for India. Default 0.
  • daylight saving — UK / EU: automatic adds an hour from 01:00 UTC on the last Sunday of March to 01:00 UTC on the last Sunday of October. none adds nothing. Default UK / EU: automatic. For other countries' rules, choose none and change the offset yourself.
  • format — what goes in payload. Default time. Every message also carries all seven formats, as fields of the same names.
  • WiFi — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow (see Config nodes). Required.

The seven formats, for 14:05:09 on 14 October 2026 at UTC+1:

format payload time 14:05 time_seconds 14:05:09 time_12h 2:05 pm date Wed 14 Oct date_iso 2026-10-14 iso 2026-10-14T14:05:09+01:00 unix 1791983109, an int: seconds since 1970 UTC, whatever the offset

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — any message asks for the time now. Wire a timer in for a clock that ticks: every second for a format with seconds, otherwise every 1 to 5 seconds.

Output — a new message, not the input one: one after each sync, and one for each input once the board has the time. Nothing is sent before the first sync, so a label shows -- rather than a wrong time. To show the time and the date on one screen, use two ntp nodes, one with time and one with date.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The node joins the flow's WiFi itself. Once WiFi is up it asks the server for the time, tries again every 30 seconds until that works, then syncs every hour. Between syncs the board's own clock keeps time. A sync takes up to a second and holds up the flow while it runs.

The board's clock is kept in UTC. The offset and summer hour are added to each message, so the hour changes on time.

The status dot shows waiting for WiFi until the first sync, then synced.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• The sync fails. The dot shows NTP from pool.ntp.org failed, and the first failure in a row also goes to the console as a [NODE_ERROR] with the reason. A board whose MicroPython has no ntptime module gives the reason this firmware has no ntptime module.
  • No WiFi network, a server that isn't a host name, or an offset outside -12 to 14. Deploy stops and says which.
  • The output isn't wired. Deploy warns sends the time nowhere: wire its output to something.

docs.title: pwm out
docs.text: Drives a PWM signal on a pin, for dimming an LED, setting a motor's speed, or any other variable duty cycle.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• pin — the GPIO pin. Default 12.
  • frequency (Hz) — the PWM frequency. Default 1000. Must be 1 or more.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — payload is the duty cycle as a fraction, from 0.0 (always off) to 1.0 (always on). A value below 0 is taken as 0 and one above 1 as 1. True and False work as 1 and 0. A string, even "0.5", fails: convert it first, in a function node. A message with no payload sets the duty to 0.

This node has no output.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The duty cycle stays where the last message set it.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• The payload is a string or another non-number. The console shows a [NODE_ERROR] naming this node. See Reading a node error.
  • A pin the board can't use, or one another node sets up differently. Deploy stops and says why. See What gets checked and Hardware is shared.

docs.title: startup
docs.text: Sends one message with a fixed payload each time the flow starts.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• payload type — bool, number, string or start reason. Default bool.
  • value — the value to send, read as the payload type (see Typed values). Default true. Hidden with start reason.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — none. startup is a source.

Output — a message with payload set to the value, topic set to an empty string, and reason saying why the flow started. With payload type start reason, the payload is that same string.

reason the flow started because deploy you clicked Deploy power_on the board was powered up hard_reset the reset button was pressed watchdog a watchdog timer reset the board deep_sleep the board woke from deep sleep soft_reset software restarted the board, for example machine.reset() unknown the board can't tell

Not every board reports every reason. ESP32 boards report the reset button as power_on, because on those chips the button cuts power to the core.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The flow starts after every deploy and each time the board starts (see Deploy), so startup fires even when the editor isn't connected. Use it for setup work, such as setting an output to a known state or drawing a first screen.

It fires once per start and never repeats. For a message you send by hand, use inject. For a repeating one, use timer.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text: • The value isn't a number, with payload type number. The deploy goes through; when the flow starts, the console shows a [NODE_ERROR] naming this node and startup value 'abc' is not a valid number.

docs.title: timer
docs.text: Sends a count that goes up by one at a fixed interval.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: • interval (ms) — the time between messages, in milliseconds. Default 1000. A whole number, 1 or more.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — none. timer is a source.

Output — a message with payload set to the count, an int: 1, 2, 3 and so on. topic is an empty string.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The first message goes out as soon as the flow starts, then one each interval. The interval starts once the previous message has finished going through the chain, so a slow node after the timer, such as a delay, adds its time to every interval.

Each timer node keeps its own count, starting at 1 when the flow starts, even when two share an interval.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• The interval is less than 1. Deploy stops with property "intervalMs" 0 is below its minimum, 1, naming the node.
  • The interval isn't a whole number. Deploy stops with "intervalMs" must be a whole number of milliseconds, naming the node.
  • A node error in this node's chain stops the chain. See Reading a node error.

docs.title: touch
docs.text:
Raw touch input, for flows that don't use the GUI: sends a message when a finger lands on a touch panel and when it lifts.

A gui screen reads its own panel, so buttons on a screen don't need this node. One panel feeds either one gui screen or one touch node.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• Touch panel — the touch panel to read. Required. Pick one, or add one with +.
  • orientation — the turn of the picture the touches should match: 0, 90, 180 or 270 degrees clockwise, the angles a display spi's orientation takes. Default off, which leaves the panel's own axes. Set it when the screen is turned and the flow reads touch through this node; a flow with a gui screen sets the orientation on the display instead.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — none. touch is a source.

Output — one message when a finger lands and one when it lifts:

{'payload': {'x': 120, 'y': 340}, 'topic': 'down'}   # a finger lands
{'payload': {'x': 121, 'y': 338}, 'topic': 'up'}     # it lifts, where it was last seen

The coordinates are screen pixels in the turned picture when orientation is set, and in the panel's own axes when it is off. There is nothing to calibrate.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The node reads the panel at the panel's poll every (ms). Nothing is sent while the finger moves, and only one finger is followed. The status dot shows FT6336U while the panel answers.

A panel that stops answering sends nothing until it answers again. A touch that was down at the time gets its up then.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• The panel doesn't answer. The dot shows disconnected, no reply from FT6336U at 0x38 on I2C bus 0.
  • No touch panel, or a panel also used by a gui screen or another touch node. Deploy stops and names them.

docs.title: Touch panels
docs.text:
The settings of a capacitive touch panel on an I2C bus, set once in a config node. A gui screen or a touch node picks it.

A gui screen reads its panel itself and turns touches into button presses, with no wire to draw. If the panel stops answering, the screen's status dot says so, and a button being held is let go without sending.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
• controller — the touch chip. Default FT6336U. Supported hardware lists the chips.
  • I2C bus — the bus the panel is wired to. Required. See I2C bus.
  • address — the chip's 7-bit I2C address, from 0x08 to 0x77. Default 0x38, the FT6336U's.
  • reset pin — the panel's reset pin. Default blank, for none.
  • poll every (ms) — how often to read the panel. Default 20; above 50 starts to feel slow.
  • panel width / panel height — the panel's own size in pixels. Defaults 320 and 480.
  • swap x and y / flip x / flip y — turn the panel's coordinates into the display's. Default off. If the display is turned, tick these until a touch lands where you pressed.

A board definition that has a touch panel labels its pins; see Seeing a board's pins.

docs.title: Presets
docs.text: The edit form has a preset control, as the display nodes do. Fill in the settings once, press the disk button and give the set a name, such as freenove-4in. In another flow, open a new touch panel and pick that name to fill the form. The I2C bus isn't saved with it, since it belongs to the flow: pick or add it after loading.

docs.title: Rotated screens
docs.text: When the display a gui screen is wired to has an orientation, the screen turns its touches to match the picture. A touch node turns them by its own orientation.

docs.title: Other touch chips
docs.text: For another chip, such as a GT911 or CST820, read it from a function node with runtime.shared('i2c', 0), using the chip's datasheet and a MicroPython driver for it. See MicroPython's machine.I2C for the I2C calls.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
These stop the deploy:

  • No I2C bus: the touch panel has no I2C bus. Pick one, or add one with +.
  • An address outside 0x08 to 0x77.
  • A controller other than FT6336U.

docs.title: udp receive
docs.text: Listens on a UDP port and emits one message per datagram received.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• port — local port to listen on (1–65535).
  • poll interval (ms) — how often the node checks for datagrams. Default 20.
  • WiFi — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Output — one message per datagram:

  • payload — the raw bytes received, not parsed. To read text or a structured format, decode it in a function node.
  • host and port — the sender's address.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text: The node takes at most one datagram each time its loop runs, and the loop runs about every 10 ms: the output stops at roughly 100 messages a second. Datagrams that arrive meanwhile wait in the socket for the next turn. Poll interval (ms) is how long a wait sleeps before checking again when nothing has arrived; lowering it does not raise that ceiling. A sender that outruns the node fills the socket and loses datagrams.

docs.title: udp send
docs.text: Sends a message's payload as a UDP datagram to a fixed host and port.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• host — the destination hostname or IP address. Required.
  • port — the destination port (1–65535). Default 9999.
  • timeout (ms) — how long to wait for the board's network stack to accept the datagram. Default 2000.
  • WiFi — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — any message. payload is the datagram: bytes are sent as they are, a string as UTF-8, and anything else is converted to text first. None sends the text None.

This node has no output.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
UDP has no acknowledgement. A send that succeeds doesn't mean the datagram arrived, and sending to an IP address that nobody is listening on raises no error.

A hostname is looked up again for every message.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
• The name can't be resolved. The console shows udp_send: could not resolve HOST:PORT. Check the name, or use the IP address.
  • The send fails. The console shows udp_send to HOST:PORT failed, with the system's error.
  • The network stack doesn't take the datagram within the timeout. The console shows a timeout error, without the host or port.

These stop the compile: an empty host, a port outside 1–65535, a timeout that isn't a positive number.

docs.title: wifi gate
docs.text: Passes a message through unchanged while the board's WiFi is connected, and drops it while it isn't.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text: • WiFi — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Input — any message.

Output — the same message, unchanged, while the link is up. While it is down, nothing is sent on, as when a function node returns None.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
The gate checks the live WiFi link as each message arrives. It doesn't use the last message from wifi status, which sends only when the connection changes and can be out of date.

Put it between a source that fires on its own schedule, such as a timer or a sensor, and a node that sends over the network. Messages that arrive while the link is down are dropped instead of failing downstream.

It checks the WiFi link only, not whether a given MQTT broker or HTTP server can be reached. mqtt publish, mqtt subscribe and http request handle their own connections on top of a working link.

docs.title: wifi status
docs.text: Reports the board's WiFi connection state. In a flow with no other WiFi node, it also brings the connection up.

docs.title: Properties
docs.text:
• poll interval (ms) — how often to check the connection. Default 5000.
  • WiFi — the flow's WiFi network, shared by every WiFi node in the flow (see Editor in depth). Pick unmanaged to stop this node connecting: use it when something else manages the connection, or to leave the network out of the flow and enter it on the board. See WiFi provisioning.

docs.title: Wiring
docs.text:
Output — a message when the connection changes:

Field Value payload True when connected, False when disconnected ip, subnet, gateway, dns the connection's addresses; empty strings when disconnected rssi signal strength in dBm; None when disconnected, or when the board can't read it (ESP32 only)

A debug node prints only payload. Tick full message on it to see the other fields.

docs.title: Behavior
docs.text:
This node is optional: other network nodes don't need it. In a flow with MQTT nodes, MQTT manages the WiFi connection and this node only reports on it.

It sends a message when the connection changes: a connect or disconnect, or a new ip, subnet, gateway or dns. It doesn't send on every poll, except the first, which always reports.

rssi drifts constantly, so a change in it sends nothing by itself. It is included, as read at that poll, whenever a message goes out for another reason. It is a snapshot, not a live reading.

If no connection is ever made, the node reports disconnected, as for any failed connect. Provisioning changes how the board gets its credentials, not what this node reports.

Once the board is connected, the node shows a status dot on the canvas (see node status). While the node has the board on a network, the editor can connect to the board over WiFi. See Connecting over WiFi.

docs.title: Tutorials
docs.text:
Getting started ends with a blinking LED. The first two tutorials continue from it, each starting from the flow the last one ends with. The MQTT tutorial starts a new flow, and the sensor display is a separate project.

  1. Two more blinks — the blink again, two more ways: one with the LED's state on the hardware, one keeping it in the function node with context.

  2. Web Blink — the same LED, driven by an http in node arriving over WiFi: putting the board on your network, finding it again, and what an open port on the board means.

    More tutorials coming

    Web Blink is the last finished tutorial. The two after it are still being worked on, and more are on the way.

  3. Blink from anywhere — the same LED through an MQTT broker: publishing from the board, subscribing to switch it, and why every topic carries a number of your own.

  4. A sensor display — read a sensor and show it on a touch display. It is a work in progress.

The finished flow for each tutorial is in the tutorials folder. Tutorial flows says where the folder is and what to change in each flow.

If you've built something past the tutorials, what worked and what stalled is a useful report: what you tried next, and what happened. File it on the issue tracker.

docs.title: Blink from anywhere
docs.text:
Work in progress

This tutorial is still being checked on a board. The example flow compiles, but some steps may not match the editor.

If you've worked through Web Blink, you have a board on your WiFi that switches its LED when a browser on your network asks. Here an MQTT broker sits in the middle. A broker passes messages between clients, so your phone or laptop doesn't have to be on the board's network. You'll publish a message from the board, switch the LED by sending one to it, and see why every topic here carries a number of your own.

This is a new flow, on an empty canvas, with two halves: inject → mqtt publish sends a message when you click the button in the editor, and mqtt subscribe → function → gpio out switches the LED when a message arrives on another topic. The board joins your WiFi with the saved credential from Web Blink.

You can build the flow step by step, or start from the finished flow, blink-from-anywhere.flow.json, in the tutorials folder, with File → Open…. Before you deploy, replace change-this-number in both topics (see below), and set the WiFi network and broker as Tutorial flows describes.

If a step misbehaves on the way, start at Debugging & troubleshooting.

docs.title: Pick a topic prefix
docs.text:
This tutorial uses test.mosquitto.org, a public broker. Anyone who knows or guesses a topic can read it and publish to it, so every topic starts with a number nobody else will pick: a random one of six or seven digits. Here it is written 4821937; use your own.

  • thingstudio/4821937/button is where the board publishes.
  • thingstudio/4821937/led is where the board listens.

docs.title: Build the flow
docs.text:
Start with an empty canvas (File → New flow).

  1. Drag an inject onto the canvas. Set payload type to string and value to pressed.
  2. Drag an mqtt publish. Set topic to thingstudio/4821937/button. Click + next to MQTT Broker: the form asks for a name, a host, a port and an optional username and password. Name it test-mosquitto, set the host to test.mosquitto.org and the port to 1883, and leave the rest blank. Wire inject → mqtt publish.
  3. Drag an mqtt subscribe. Set topic to thingstudio/4821937/led. Its MQTT Broker field already shows the broker from step 2, because a flow has one.

  4. Drag a function and replace its code with:

    msg['payload'] = str(msg['payload']).lower() in ('on', '1', 'true')
return msg

  5. Drag a gpio out and set pin to your LED's GPIO number. Wire mqtt subscribe → function → gpio out.

  6. Drag a debug and wire mqtt subscribe → debug, to see what arrives in the console.
  7. On either MQTT node, pick your WiFi credential in the WiFi field: the one from Web Blink, or make one with +. A flow has one WiFi network, so the other node shows the same one.

docs.title: Deploy
docs.text: With the board connected, click Compile → Deploy. When mqtt subscribe's dot turns green, the board is connected to the broker. mqtt publish's dot stays blank until its first message.

docs.title: Board to world
docs.text:
On your computer, subscribe to everything under your prefix:

mosquitto_sub -h test.mosquitto.org -t 'thingstudio/4821937/#' -v

Click the ▶ on the inject node. The terminal prints the topic and pressed. A phone does the same with any MQTT client app: connect to test.mosquitto.org on port 1883 and subscribe to the same topic.

docs.title: World to board
docs.text:
Publish to the LED topic from the same terminal, or from the phone:

mosquitto_pub -h test.mosquitto.org -t 'thingstudio/4821937/led' -m on
mosquitto_pub -h test.mosquitto.org -t 'thingstudio/4821937/led' -m off

The LED follows, and the editor's console shows each message from the debug node. The function node is there because gpio out treats any non-empty text as true, so off would switch the LED on. It turns on, 1 and true into true and every other message into false.

docs.title: Nothing arrives?
docs.text:
• Check that the number in the topics matches everywhere, and that the last part is button on the publisher and led on the subscriber.
  • A red dot on an MQTT node, or a console line starting mqtt connect to, means the board can't reach the broker. See MQTT broker unreachable, which also covers networks that block port 1883.
  • If compile stops with "needs a WiFi network", a WiFi field is empty. See Why does compile fail with "needs a WiFi network"?.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
A topic is a label on a message. mqtt publish sends each message that reaches it to its topic, and mqtt subscribe emits each message that arrives on its topic, with the text as payload and the topic it came in on as topic. The broker sits between them and between any other clients.

Both nodes use the flow's one broker, which is why the second node showed the first one's settings.

docs.title: The broker is public
docs.text: Anyone who knows your topic can switch your LED, which is why the topic carries a number and why the messages here carry nothing private. For anything that matters, use a broker on your own network with a password: set its address in the broker form instead. The nodes work the same way.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:
• mqtt publish and mqtt subscribe — every property, including QoS and retain.
  • Tutorial flows — the finished flows for the tutorials, and what to change in each.
  • Tutorials — the other tutorials.

docs.title: Web Blink
docs.text:
If you've worked through Two more blinks, you have a board whose LED blinks on a timer. Here the timer goes, and a web browser does the switching. You'll put the board on your WiFi network, find it from your computer, and see what it means for a board to have an open port.

The blink flow was a timer → function → gpio out. The timer gives way to an http in node, which runs a web server on the board, and the function gains a second output for the reply that goes back to the browser.

You can build the flow step by step, or start from the finished flow, http-blink.flow.json, in the tutorials folder, with File → Open…. Tutorial flows says what to change before you deploy.

If a step misbehaves on the way, start at Debugging & troubleshooting.

docs.title: Build the flow
docs.text:
On the network the request is the event, so the timer goes and the LED holds the level you last asked for.

  1. Delete the timer.
  2. Drag an http in onto the canvas. Set port to 9999 and path to /toggle. Leave method as GET.

  3. Select the function. Set outputs to 2 and replace its code with:

    on = not context.get('on', False)
context.set('on', on)
msg['payload'] = on
reply = dict(msg)
reply['payload'] = 'LED ' + ('on' if on else 'off')
return [msg, reply]

  4. Drag an http response onto the canvas.

  5. Wire http in → function. Wire the function's first output to gpio out and its second output to http response.
  6. Drag a wifi status and a debug onto the canvas. Tick full message on the debug node and wire wifi status → debug.

docs.title: The board joins WiFi
docs.text:
The board joins the network named in the flow — so tell the flow which network. Flow files hold no passwords or other secrets: the WiFi details live in the .thingstudio folder in your home directory (~/.thingstudio/credentials/), as credentials. Each credential is named, and you can keep several — one per network — and pick the right one per flow. See The ThingStudio folder.

  1. On the http in node's property panel, click + next to the WiFi field to make a new credential (✎ edits an existing one). Give the credential a name, your network's SSID and its password, and save.
  2. The WiFi field on the http in node (and on the wifi status node) picks that credential — one WiFi network per flow, shared by every WiFi node in it.

Compile stops with a one-line error if the flow's WiFi has no saved network behind it; the FAQ's needs-a-WiFi-network entry is that error.

docs.title: Name the board, then deploy
docs.text:
1. Connect the board over USB, as in Connect your board, and choose Tools → Board settings…. Give the board a network name, such as blink. A name lets your computer find the board without an IP address.
  2. Click Compile → Deploy. The board swaps in the flow and joins your WiFi.

A few seconds after the deploy, the console prints the wifi status message, with a payload of true, and the node's dot shows connected (see node status when the dot is something else). The LED is dark: nothing drives the pin until a request does.

docs.title: Find the board
docs.text:
• By name: open http://blink.local:9999/toggle in your browser. The name is the one from Board settings plus .local; port 9999 and path /toggle are the port and path of the http in node.
  • By IP: the debug node prints the whole wifi status message, which includes ip. (In the example file, tick full message on the debug node first; it prints only the payload otherwise.) The fields are listed under wifi status. Open http://<ip>:9999/toggle.

If .local names don't resolve on your network (they don't everywhere, and they don't across VPN tunnels at all — multicast doesn't pass), the IP address is the dependable one.

The page answers LED on or LED off, and the LED does what it says. Expect the first answer after an idle stretch to take up to a second: the board's WiFi wakes on the request (see Why do http in requests take a second to answer?).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
The request is the only event this flow gets, and each one is handled on its own: between requests the LED holds its level, remembered in the context toggle from the last tutorial.

The function has two outputs. The first carries the new state to gpio out. The second carries reply to http response, which answers the browser. return [msg, reply] routes one message to each output, as in Node-RED; see the function node.

docs.title: The server is open
docs.text: http in runs an unauthenticated server on the board: whatever reaches that network can call every path. Keep those routes non-sensitive, or keep the board off shared networks. See http in for what the server does and doesn't do.

docs.title: Next
docs.text:

  • Blink from anywhere — the next tutorial: the same LED through an MQTT broker.
  • mqtt publish and mqtt subscribe — the nodes behind it.
  • Connecting over WiFi — the board as an editor peer on your network, not just a web server.

docs.title: Two more blinks
docs.text:
If you've followed the steps in Getting started you'll now have a board with a blinking LED. This tutorial starts from there and shows you two other methods to get the same effect. In the process you'll directly access the hardware through MicroPython and see how ThingStudio nodes and flows can keep track of past events.

The Blink an LED flow contained three nodes, a timer → function → gpio out. We'll just be changing the function node in this tutorial.

The first variant is Read the pin, write it back: the blink's state lives on the board, in the pin, and the function node runs your own MicroPython to reach it.

The second variant is Keep the state in the node: the state lives inside the function node itself, in context.

You can build this flow up yourself or start from the finished flow, two-more-blinks.flow.json, in the tutorials folder, with File → Open…. It carries the first of the two blinks: change 15 in machine.Pin(15) to your LED's GPIO number.

If a step misbehaves on the way, start at Debugging & troubleshooting.

docs.title: Read the pin, write it back
docs.text:
Each message so far decides the LED by counting. Let the pin say where it is instead. Replace the function's code with this, using your LED's GPIO number in place of PIN:

import machine
msg['payload'] = 0 if machine.Pin(PIN).value() else 1
return msg

Deploy. The LED blinks as before, but the reason has changed: each message now reads the pin and writes back the opposite of what it found. The state, what the LED is actually showing, lives on the board between messages, so the flow can't contradict it.

machine.Pin is MicroPython's own pin API. Constructed with a number and no other settings, it takes the pin as it is and .value() reads the level the gpio out node has written. The write itself goes out of the function's output, through to gpio out.

The pin fields on gpio nodes are checked against your board at compile time, but code inside a function isn't. If PIN isn't a pin number your board has, the compile check passes and the error arrives when the flow runs, as a [NODE_ERROR] in the console. See Reading a node error; Pins… next to the Board menu lists your board's pins.

docs.title: Keep the state in the node
docs.text:
An important point to understand

A flow is stateless: each event is handled on its own, without regard to what came before. In general this is a good thing:

  • An error shows up with the message that caused it, not in some state built over earlier operations.
  • Recovery is doing nothing: the next message starts clean. A crashed stateful component needs its data restored to an acceptable earlier version, with nothing to say which that is.

When a flow does need to remember, ThingStudio's answer is a context — state held between messages, either private to one node (context) or shared across the whole flow (flow). This blink's LED level belongs to one function node, so its private store is the one to use. All three stores, context and flow among them, are in Context, flow and settings; settings even survives a reboot.

The pin held the state on the board. The other place is inside the function node itself:

on = not context.get('on', False)
context.set('on', on)
msg['payload'] = on
return msg

Deploy again: the same blink. Nothing outside the node holds the state now. context.get('on', False) reads this function node's own memory; context.set('on', on) writes it; the False is what .get answers when nothing is stored yet, which is why the first message turns the LED on.

For state kept without code, the change node stores a flow variable, the same store a function's flow.get()/flow.set() reads. A change node can store a flow variable but can't flip it, so a toggle needs a function node.
